en: The summary verse of the collection:
Saṃmata, Devapāla, Niryūha, Jīrṇa, and Bhadraka.
The assembly, Kauṇḍinya, the supernatural power, Kauśika, Bhukpuha...
and Sāvīci—among these, which one is the last?
The summary verse: Mahāsaṃmata, Siṃhahanu, and likewise Suprabuddha;
the Tuṣitas, the longing, the birth, the aspiration, Asita, and then Pātrī.
Then Kṛmivarman, followed by Baddhālī and likewise Sahadeva;
then the covering, the instruction of the Vaiśālakas, and finally the propitiation.
Yaśodharā, Haṃsa, and Kalyāṇī Gopikā;
Nirdeśana and Jambū; Mṛgajā as the seventh; the Bhārgava clan; Rājagṛha; asceticism; Ārāḍa; difficult practices; and Nandā. (SBV I 3)
Likewise, Kālaka and Svastika, having brought about the destruction of Māra,
[attained] the western assembly of the four.
In the lineage of kings at Potalaka, there were one hundred and one Arciṣmantas;
in Ayodhyā, there were fifty-four Arindamas.
Ajitañjaya [reigned] sixty-three times in Vārāṇasī;
Duṣprasaha eighty-four times in Kiṃpilā;
and Brahmadatta thirty-two times in Hastināpura.
Hastidatta had five thousand in Takṣaśilā;
Kālīśa had thirty-two in Urasā;
and Nagnajit had thirty-two in Ajitañjaya.
Jayadatta [ruled] twelve years in Kanyākubja,
Jayasena eighteen years in Campā,
and Nāgadeva twenty-five years in Tālipta.
Naradeva [ruled] for twelve years in Tāmaliptī;
Sāgaradeva for eighteen years in Dantapurī; and Sumati for twenty-five years in Rājagṛha.
Tamonuda [reigned] for one hundred years in Vārāṇasī;
Mahendrasena for eighty-four [years] in Kuśāvatī;
and Samudrasena for one thousand [years] in Potalaka.
Tapaścara performed eighty-four thousand [offerings] at Kusāvatī;
Mahīmukha, the lord of the earth, performed one hundred thousand at Vārāṇasī;
and Mahīpati performed one hundred thousand at Ayodhyā.
Mahīdhara [ruled] eighty-four times in Mithilā;
Mahādeva again [ruled] eighty-four times in Mithilā;
Mahādeva, Nimi... [and so on] ... Dṛḍharatha [ruled] seventy-seven times in Sāṃkāśya.
Ambarīśa was Nāgasaṃpāla in Vārāṇasī;
Kṛkī was Sujāta in Potalaka; and Karṇa was Ikṣvāku in Potalaka—each having one hundred [sons].

Virūḍhaka was of the Ikṣvāku lineage; Gopūraka [ruled] in Kapilavastu; Daśaratha [ruled over] fifty-five thousand [villages], and so forth... Siṃhahanu; Siṃhahanu had four sons; from the four [sons] came Dvikayukti. The bhikṣus wish to know.
The Origin of the Śākyas:
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Monastery.
Now, while many Śākyans of Kapilavastu were seated and assembled together in their assembly hall, this kind of conversation arose among them.
"From where were you Śākyas born? Who are your leaders? What is your lineage? And what is the ancient family line of the Śākyas?
If someone were to approach us and ask: 'From where were you Śākyas born? Who are your leaders? What is your lineage? And what is their ancient family line? [how would we answer?]"
Being asked this, what could we possibly say?
Furthermore, we do not know from where the Śākyas originated, who their ancestors were, what their lineage was, or what their ancient family history is.
Therefore, let us approach the Blessed One.
"Having approached the Blessed One, we shall ask him about this very matter; and we will retain it exactly as the Blessed One explains it to us.
Then a great multitude of Śākyas from Kapilavastu approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the many Śākyas of Kapilavastu said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, while we many Śākyas of Kapilavastu were sitting and assembled together in the assembly hall, this kind of conversation arose among us."
"From where were the Śākyas born? Who is their leader? What is their lineage? And what is their ancient family line?
If someone were to approach us and ask: 'From where were you Śākyas born? Who is your leader? What is your lineage? And what is your ancient family line? [we would have to answer]."
Being asked this, what could we possibly explain?
Furthermore, we do not know from where the Śākyas originated, who their leader was, what their lineage was, or what their ancient family line was.
Therefore, let us approach the Blessed One.
"Having approached the Blessed One, we shall ask him about this very matter;
and just as the Blessed One explains it to us, so shall we remember it.
Thus, we ask the Blessed One about this very matter.
“Blessed One, from where were the Śākyas born? Who is their leader? What is their lineage? And what is the ancient family line of the Śākyas?
Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One:
“If I were to deliver a discourse on the Dharma concerning the ancient family line of the Śākyas, it is possible that [the assembly] would become distracted.”

"If other non-Buddhist wanderers were to say, 'The ascetic Gautama is a self-praiser who explains things only according to his own whims,' then which of my disciples would be capable of delivering a discourse on the Dharma to the monks concerning the ancient lineage of the Śākyas?"
Now at that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was seated and present in that very assembly. Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"May it be inspired in you, Maudgalyāyana, to deliver a discourse on the Dharma to the monks concerning the ancient family lineage of the Śākyas;
my back is aching,
so I shall stretch it for a moment."
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana consented to the Blessed One by remaining silent.

Then the Blessed One, perceiving the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana’s consent through his silence, placed his outer robe folded in four over his head and lay down on his right side, placing one foot upon the other, mindful of the perception of light.
Mindful and clearly comprehending, he directed his attention solely to the perception of rising.
Then, this thought occurred to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "What if I were to enter such a state of meditative concentration? (SBV I 7)

"By means of a concentrated mind, I shall examine the ancient family lineage of the Śākyas: from where were the Śākyas born, who are their ancestors, what is their descent, and what is the ancient family lineage of the Śākyas?
Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana entered such a state of meditative concentration that, with his mind thus concentrated, he examined the ancient family lineage of the Śākyas.

The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having observed the ancient family lineage of the Śākyas— from which the Śākyas were born, who their ancestors were, and what that ancient family lineage of the Śākyas was—
arose from that meditative concentration and sat down on the seat prepared in front of the community of monks.
Having sat down, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the Śākyas of Kapilavastu.
Maudgalyāyana narrates:
"The beings in the realm of the Ābhāsvara devas..."
O Gautamas, there comes a time when this world dissolves;
as the world dissolves, for the most part, sentient beings are reborn in the Ābhāsvara realm of gods.
There they exist as embodied beings, mind-made, without deficiency, with unimpaired faculties, complete in all limbs and minor members, and beautiful.
Abiding in their respective colors, self-luminous, moving through the sky, feeding on joy and having joy as their sustenance, they live long lives and remain for a long duration of time.
At that time, indeed, this great earth becomes a single body of water, a single ocean.
Indeed,

that which on the great earth consisting of a single expanse of water— becoming a single ocean— comes together with the wind, coalesces, and extends, just as a film comes together upon boiled milk that has cooled down through the action of the wind; [that is the subtle element of air].
It coagulates, it extends.
Thus, upon the great earth which is a single mass of water and a single ocean, a film is formed by the wind; it coagulates, it consolidates, and it extends.
That becomes the essence of the earth, endowed with excellence of color, excellence of fragrance, and excellence of taste.
It is such in color, Gautamas, as fresh butter;
it is such in taste, as pure honey.
There comes a time, Gautamas, when this world evolves.

When the world is evolving, some beings, due to the exhaustion of their lifespan, the exhaustion of their karma, and the exhaustion of their merit, pass away from the Ābhāsvara host of gods and come here into the common lot of human beings.
Here they become possessed of form, mind-made, complete, with unimpaired faculties, endowed with all major and minor limbs, and beautiful.
Abiding in their own radiance, moving through the sky, feeding on joy and nourished by joy, they were long-lived and remained for a long duration.
At that time, indeed, there was no appearance of the sun and moon in the world.
not of the constellations; not of the moments, instants, or hours;
not of nights and days;
In that world, there was no appearance of months, fortnights, seasons, or years;
neither woman nor man was known, but rather beings were reckoned simply as "beings.
[This concludes] the section on the tasting of the earth-essence (*pṛthivīrasa*).

Then, a certain being of a greedy disposition tasted the essence of the earth with the tip of his finger; as he tasted it, so he relished it; as he relished it, so he began to consume it by way of solid food.
Other beings also saw that being tasting the essence of the earth with the tip of his finger; as he tasted it, so it pleased him; as it pleased him, so he began to consume it by way of mouthfuls.
Having seen this, those beings also began to taste the essence of the earth with the tips of their fingers.
Just as they tasted it, so did they find it pleasing;
just as they found it pleasing, they then began to consume it by way of mouthfuls.
And because those beings consumed the essence of the earth by way of mouthfuls as food, coarseness and heaviness entered their bodies.
That auspicious radiance of theirs vanished,
and darkness appeared in the world.
Indeed, Gautamas, it is the natural law that when darkness appears in the world, the sun and moon appear in the world.
The appearance of the constellations, of moments, instants, and hours, of nights and days, of months, fortnights, seasons, and years occurs in the world.
They feed on that, they subsist on that, and being long-lived, they remain for a long duration.
Among them, whoever consumes less food becomes more beautiful in complexion.
He who consumes excessive food becomes ill-favored in complexion; thus, in dependence upon this twofold state of food, a twofold state of complexion is perceived.
When there is this twofold state of complexion, one being despises another being:

"O beings! I am handsome; you are ugly. Because those beings were thus conceited regarding their appearance, and due to their undertaking of those very same evil and unwholesome qualities, the essence of the earth disappeared.
When the essence of the earth had disappeared, those beings, gathering together and coming together, grieved, languished, and lamented, saying: "Oh, the taste! Oh, the taste!
Just as people nowadays, having eaten some delicious, fine food, recall that very same old expression and say: "Oh, the taste! Oh, the taste!"
Thus, O Gautamas, when the essence of the earth had disappeared, those beings gathered together and, being distressed, exhausted, and lamenting, cried out, "Oh, what flavor! Oh, what flavor!
yet they did not understand its true meaning.
"This is the meaning of what was said; this is the meaning of what was said.
When the essence of the earth had disappeared, for those beings, the *pṛthivīparpaṭaka* appeared, endowed with excellence of color, excellence of fragrance, and excellence of taste.
Such was its color, like that of a *karṇikāra* flower;
such was its taste, like that of pure, unadulterated honey.
Having that as their food and that as their sustenance, they were long-lived and remained for a long duration of time.
Among them, he who consumes less food becomes handsome,
while he who consumes more food becomes ugly; thus, depending on the duality of food, the duality of complexion is perceived.
When there is a twofold distinction of complexion, one being despises another being, saying: "O being, I am well-colored; you are ill-colored."
Because those beings, being conceited regarding their own caste, took up those very same evil and unwholesome qualities, the earth-crust disappeared.
When the earth-crust had disappeared, those beings gathered together and, in their grief, exhaustion, and lamentation, cried out:
"Alas! Oh, alas!"

Just as people today, when touched by some suffering or mental distress, repeat those very same ancient syllables, phrases, and phonemes, saying, "Alas! Oh, alas!"— in the very same way, when the crust of earth had disappeared, those beings gathered together and, being stricken with grief, grew weary and lamented.
And they say, "O, alas! O, alas!
yet they do not understand its meaning, [thinking]:
"This is the meaning of what he has said; this is the meaning of what he has said."
When the crust of the earth had disappeared, a forest creeper appeared for those beings, endowed with color, endowed with fragrance,
and endowed with flavor; such was its color, like the *kadamba* flower, and such was its flavor, like pure, unrefined honey.
Subsisting on that and feeding upon that, they lived for a long time and remained for a long duration.

Among them, whoever consumed less food became beautiful in color, while whoever consumed more food became ugly in color; thus, based on the duality of their food, the duality of their complexion was perceived.
When there is a twofold difference in complexion, one being disparages another, saying: "O being, I am well-colored; you are ill-colored."
Because those beings, being conceited regarding their caste, took up those very same sinful and unwholesome qualities, the forest creepers vanished.
When the forest creepers had vanished, those beings gathered together and, meeting one another, grieved, were distressed, and lamented, saying: "Move aside! Move aside from our front!"
In the same way, when the forest creeper has vanished, those beings gather together and, meeting one another, grieve, languish, and lament; they say, "Move aside! Move aside!
yet they do not understand its meaning.
"This is the meaning of what he said; this is the meaning of what he said.

Gautamas, when the forest creeper had disappeared, for those beings there appeared rice with grains of *taṇḍula* that was unplowed and unsown—without husks, without chaff, pure, clean, four fingers in length, and growing in clusters; it would grow back ripe by morning once it was harvested in the evening.

And as it grew back, what was harvested in the morning would be ripe by evening and have grown back again; thus, as it was harvested, it grew back, and it remained visible even when not harvested. Having that as their food and that as their sustenance, they lived for a long time and endured for a long duration.
Then those beings began to consume the rice-fruit that grew without being ploughed or sown by way of solid food;
consequently, a diversity of sense faculties appeared among them:
some possessed the female faculty, and others the male faculty.
Therein, those who possess the female faculty and those who possess the male faculty look at one another’s eyes with their own eyes.
To the extent that they look at one another’s eyes with their own eyes, to that extent they become impassioned;
to the extent that they are impassioned, to that extent they are tormented.
To the extent that they were torn asunder, to that same extent they fell into misconduct.
Other beings also saw one being behaving improperly toward another being;
having seen this, they even threw dust at them.
Clods of earth, pebbles, and potsherds as well; and they spoke thus:
"Shame on you, village being, for doing what should not be done! Shame on you, village being, for doing what should not be done! How is it now, O being, that you defile another being?
It is just as people nowadays throw powder, incense, garlands, and nets of cloth over a bride when she is being led away in marriage.
And they say, "Be happy, little bride! Be happy, little bride!
In this very same way, when those beings see one being behaving improperly toward another being, they throw even dust at them, even clods of earth, even gravel, and even potsherds; and they say:
"Shame on you, vulgar being!
(Shame on you, vulgar being who commits what should not be done! O being, how is it that you now defile another being?"

For thus, O Gautamas, that which was formerly considered contrary to the Dharma is now considered in accordance with the Dharma; that which was formerly considered contrary to the Vinaya is now considered in accordance with the Vinaya; and that which was formerly considered censurable is now considered praiseworthy.
They banish them for even one day, or they banish them for two, three, or even seven days.

And because those beings have fallen into such an excessively sinful vow regarding that evil, non-dharma, they become intent on building houses, thinking, "We shall do what is improper here; we shall do what is improper here."
The notion "house, house" arose;
O Gautamas, this was the ancient precursor to the appearance in the world of household occupations within the home.
And since they [acted] by means of righteousness (*dharma*) and not by unrighteousness (*adharma*), therein this is the supreme dharma of the Lords of Jinas:
they would assemble in the evening for the sake of their evening meal from the rice-field, and in the morning for the sake of their morning meal.
Then, a certain being of a lazy disposition brought the rice from both the evening and the morning harvest at once.
Then another being said this to that being: "Come, O being, let us go together for the sake of the rice. Then that being said this to him:
"O being, you must acknowledge your own rice! I have brought back rice for both evening and morning.
Then this thought occurred to that being:
"Ah, this would indeed be excellent; ah, this would be truly good—what if I were to bring back rice that is two days old, three days old, up to seven days old?
He then brought back rice that was two days old, up to seven days old.
Then another being said this to that being:
"Come, O being, let us go together for the sake of the rice.
Then that being said this to him: "Promise me, O being, [the right to] your own rice."
"I have brought this rice that lasts for two days, three days, and so on, up to seven days.
Then this thought occurred to that being:
"Ah, how excellent! Ah, how wonderful!"
"It would be well if I were to bring rice every half-month or every month.
So he brought rice every half-month or every month.
And because those beings consumed that non-plowed, non-sown rice with the grain by means of hoarding for use, the husk and the bran came to envelop the rice grain.
As each stalk was harvested, it did not grow back, and it became known as "weak.
The rice remained established in groves and thickets of reeds.
Then those beings, gathering together and coming together, grieved, were exhausted, and lamented: "Sirs, formerly we..."

We were embodied beings, mind-made, complete, with unimpaired faculties, endowed with all major and minor limbs, beautiful, abiding in a state of radiant color, self-luminous, moving through the air, feeding on joy, nourished by joy, long-lived, and remaining for a long duration. Then, for us, the essence of the earth appeared, perfect in color, perfect in fragrance, and perfect in taste.
We, having consumed that essence of the earth by way of solid food, and because we had consumed that essence of the earth by way of solid food, coarseness and heaviness entered our bodies;
that beautiful, radiant complexion vanished.
Darkness appeared in the world.
We, feeding on that and subsisting on that, lived for a long time and remained for a long duration.
Among us, whoever had taken up a small amount of food became possessed of a fine complexion.
He who has taken abundant food becomes ill-colored; thus, depending on the duality of food, the duality of complexion is perceived.
When there is this duality of complexion, one being despises another being, saying: "O being, I am well-colored!"
"You are ill-colored.
Because of that, for us who were possessed of pride in our own complexion, due to the undertaking of those very same evil and unwholesome qualities, the essence of the earth disappeared.
When the essence of the earth had disappeared, a crust of earth appeared, endowed with excellence of color, excellence of fragrance, and excellence of taste.
Because we, being conceited regarding our physical appearance, undertook those very same evil and unwholesome qualities, the crust of earth disappeared.
When the crust of earth had disappeared, forest creepers appeared, endowed with excellence of color, fragrance, and flavor.
Because we, being conceited regarding our physical appearance, undertook those very same evil and unwholesome qualities, the forest creepers disappeared.
When the forest creeper had vanished, rice with grains of grain appeared, sown without being ploughed; it was without husk, without chaff, pure, clean, four fingers in length, and fully encased.
When reaped in the evening, it was ripe and grown back again by morning; thus, as it was reaped again and again, it grew back, and it remained known even when not reaped.
Subsisting on that and taking that as our food, we lived for a long time and remained for a long duration.
Because we consumed the rice-fruit of the *śāli* grain— which had not been ploughed or sown— by means of storing it up for use, thereupon the husk and the chaff appeared upon this *śāli* grain.
It is encircled;
as it is reaped, it does not grow back again, and it is known to be weak—
the rice situated in thickets of reeds.
The establishment of boundary lines, limits, and so forth,
and the origin of property.
And the first king [thought], "What if we, having gathered and come together, were to measure out the fields, establish boundaries, and set up limits, saying, 'This is yours; this is mine'?
They, having gathered and come together, measured out the fields.
And they bound the boundary;
they established the limit.
Gautamas, this ancient leader appeared in the world as the originator of the practice of establishing limits.
And that was done through righteousness, not through unrighteousness;
for this is the supreme righteousness of the Lords of Jinas.
Now, a certain being, while staying in his own field of rice, took another's rice without it being given.
Another being saw that being standing in his own rice field taking another's rice that had not been given;
having seen him, he spoke thus to that being:
"Why, O being, do you take another's rice while standing in your own rice field?"
"Go, O being, do not do this again!

A second and even a third time, that being remained in his own rice field and took another's rice without it being given. That [other] being saw him remaining in his own rice field and taking another's rice without it being given, a second and even a third time.
Having seen that being, he spoke to him thus:
"O being, why do you remain in your own field of rice and take the rice of another without it being given?
He dragged him here and there, even leading him into the midst of the assembly, saying: "Sirs, this being remains in his own field of rice and takes the rice of another without it being given!"
Then those beings said this to that being:
"Why, O being, do you remain in your own rice field while taking the rice of another three times over without it being given?
Go away, O being, and do not do such a thing again."
Then that being said this to those beings:
"Sirs, by this being I have been dragged and pulled away for the sake of some śāli rice, even unto being reviled in the midst of the assembly.
Then those beings said this to that being:
"Why, O being, do you pull, drag away, and even bring this being from the rice-field into the midst of the assembly?
Go, O being, and do not do so again!
Then, this thought occurred to those beings:

Indeed, it is observed that because of the cultivation of rice, there is even the drawing [of water], as well as the driving away [of weeds], and even the leading [of people] into the midst of the assembly.

What if we, having gathered and come together, were to appoint as the lord of the fields whichever among us is the most handsome, the most beautiful to behold, the most pleasing, and the most renowned? Whosoever—
"He will restrain those among us who deserve restraint and support those who deserve support;
and whatever shall be produced from our fields, we shall grant him a lawful portion thereof."
Having gathered together and assembled, they appoint as the lord of those fields whichever being among them is most handsome, most beautiful to behold, most gracious, and most influential.
And they say: "Come, O being, subdue those who are to be subdued by us."
"Take up those who are to be taken up;
and whatever shall be produced from our fields, we shall grant you a righteous portion thereof.
Thus he punishes those among them who are to be punished and favors those who are to be favored.
And whatever was produced from those fields, they bestowed upon him a lawful portion of it;
because he was highly esteemed by the great multitude, the designation "Mahāsaṃmata" (Greatly Esteemed) arose for him as "Mahāsaṃmata, Mahāsaṃmata.
Because he was the lord of the fields (*kṣetra*) and protected (*trāyate*) them from injury (*kṣata*), the designation "Kṣatriya" arose for him as "Kṣatriya, Kṣatriya."
Because he delighted the subjects through righteousness, through the practice of virtuous conduct, and through the practice of wise conduct, the designation "King, King" arose.
Among the people of King Mahāsaṃmata, Gautamas, the designation "beings, beings" came into existence. Among the people of King Mahāsaṃmata, Gautamas...
Roca was the son;
during the reign of King Roca, the designation "ehikā" arose among human beings;
O Gautamas, Kalyāṇa was the son of Roca.
Among the humans of King Kalyāṇa, Gautamas, the designation "tilakas, tilakas" arose; and among the humans of King Varakalyāṇa,
Gautamas, the designation "cloud-necks, cloud-necks" arose.
Varakalyāṇa’s son was Upoṣadha.
O Gautamas, during the reign of King Upoṣadha, humans came to be known as "stālajaṅghas" (pillar-leggeds).
[This was] of Upoṣadha. (SBV I 16)
A tumor grew on the king’s head— soft, very soft, like a tuft of silk-cotton or a tuft of cotton;
it never caused any pain.
Through the process of ripening, it burst open;
a prince was born, handsome, beautiful, and pleasing to behold, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
Because he was born from the crown of the head, the name "Mūrdhāta" arose.
As soon as he was born, the prince was brought into the inner apartments; at that moment,
the breasts of all sixty thousand women of King Upoṣadha began to flow with milk.
Each one said, "Nourish me! Nourish me!
Thus, the name Māndhātṛ arose.
At the time when King Māndhātṛ ruled his kingdom, at that time human beings were reflective, deliberative, and investigative.
Having reflected, weighed, and examined [the matter], they established various sites for crafts and sites for occupations; thus, the designation "human beings, human beings" arose for them.
Thus, O Gautamas, these six kings were of immortal lifespan and immeasurable lifespan. This is the intermediate summary verse.
The Satvas, the Ehikas, the Tilakas, the Abhrakaṇṭhas,
and likewise the Stālajaṅghas— these six are declared to be the lineages of men.
O Gautamas, on King Māndhātṛ’s right thigh a tumor arose— soft, very soft, like a tuft of cotton or a tuft of silk-cotton;
it caused him no affliction whatsoever.
Through the process of ripening,
it burst open and a prince was born, handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man;
because he was born from the right thigh, the name "Cāru" (the Beautiful One) arose for him.
That prince was possessed of great supernatural power and great majesty;
he has now exercised sovereign lordship and dominion over the four continents.
Gautamas, a soft and very tender tumor arose on Cāru’s left thigh, just like a tuft of silk-cotton or a tuft of cotton wool.
It caused no pain whatsoever,
and having burst open through the process of ripening, a prince was born— handsome, beautiful, pleasing, and adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
Born from the left thigh, he was given the name Upacāru.
That prince, possessed of great supernatural power and great majesty, now exercised sovereign authority and lordship over the three continents.
Gautamas, on King Upacāru’s right foot, a swelling arose—soft and very soft, like a tuft of cotton or a tuft of silk-cotton.
It caused no pain whatsoever,
but burst open as a result of its maturation;
a prince was born, handsome, beautiful, and pleasing to behold, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
Born from the right foot, the name Cārumān arose for him.
That prince was possessed of great supernatural power and great majesty; even now, he exercises sovereignty, lordship, and dominion over two continents.
Gautamas, on the left foot of King Cārumān a tumor arose, soft and very soft, like a tuft of cotton or a tuft of silk-cotton.
It caused no pain whatsoever,
for it burst open as a result of its full maturation;
a prince was born, handsome, beautiful to behold, gracious, and adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
From his left foot was born Upacārumān, and thus the name Upacārumān arose.
That prince was possessed of great supernatural power and great majesty; even now he exercises sovereignty, lordship, and dominion over one continent.
Thus, O Gautamas, Rocas was the son of King Mahāsaṃmata; Kalyāṇa was the son of Rocas; and Varakalyāṇa was the son of Kalyāṇa.

Varakalyāṇa’s son was Upoṣadha; Upoṣadha’s was Māndhātṛ; Māndhātṛ’s was Cāru; Cāru’s was Upacāru; Upacāru’s was Cārumān; Cārumān’s was Upacārumān; Upacārumān’s was Ruci; Ruci’s was Suruci; Suruci’s was Muci; Muci’s was Mucilinda; Mucilinda’s was Aṅga; Aṅga’s was Aṅgīratha; Aṅgīratha’s was Bhṛṅga; Bhṛṅga’s was Bhagīratha; Bhagīratha’s was Sagara; Sagara’s was Sāgara; Sāgara’s was Mahāsāgara; Mahāsāgara’s was Śakuni; Śakuni’s was Mahāśakuni; Mahāśakuni’s was Kuśa; Kuśa’s was Upakuśa; Upakuśa’s was Mahākuśa; Mahākuśa’s was Sudarśana; and Sudarśana’s was Mahāsudarśana.

Praṇaya, Mahāpraṇaya, Praṇāda, Mahāpraṇāda, Prabhaṅkara, Pratāpavat, Meru, Merumān, Merumant, Arcis, Arciṣmat, and Arciṣmant; O Gautamas, through the lineage of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants of King Arciṣmant—
In the city of Potalaka there were one hundred and one kings;
the last of them was a king named Arindama.
Because he tamed his enemies, he was known as Arindama, and thus the name "Arindama" arose.
O Gautamas, through the lineage of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants of King Arindama, there were fifty-four thousand kings in Ayodhyā.
The last of them was a king named Ajitañjaya;
he was called Ajitañjaya because he conquers the unconquered. Ajitañjaya...
Thus the tradition arose:
through the lineage of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants of King Ajitañjaya Gautama, sixty-three thousand kings ruled in Vārāṇasī;
the last of them was a king named Duṣprasaha.
Gautamas, through the succession of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants of King Duṣprasaha, there were eighty-four thousand kings in the city of Kiṃpilya;
the last of them was a king named Brahmadatta.
Gautamas, through the succession of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants of King Brahmadatta, there were thirty-two thousand kings in Hastināpura.
The last of them was a king named Hastidatta.
Gautamas, through the succession of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants of King Hastidatta, there were five thousand kings in Takṣaśilā;
the last of them was a king named Kālīśa.
O Gautamas, through the succession of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants of King Kālīśa, there were thirty-two thousand kings in the city of Urasā;
the last of them was a king named Nagnajit.
O Gautamas, through the succession of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants of King Nagnajit, there were thirty-two thousand kings in the city of Ajitañjaya.
The last of them was a king named Jayadatta.
Gautamas, through the succession of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and great-great-grandsons of King Jayadatta, there were twelve thousand kings in the city of Kanyakubja;
the last of them was a king named Jayasena.
Gautamas, through the succession of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants of King Jayasena, there were eighteen thousand kings in the city of Campā;
the last of them was a king named Nāgadeva.
Gautamas, through the succession of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants of King Nāgadeva, there were twenty-five [thousand kings] in the city of Tāliṣya.
There were thousands of kings;
their last was a king named Naradeva.
Gautamas, through the succession of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants of King Naradeva, there were twelve thousand kings in the city of Tāmaliptī.
The last among them was a king named Sāgaradeva.
Gautamas, through the lineage of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and great-great-grandsons of King Sāgaradeva, there were eighteen thousand kings in the city of Dantapurī;
the last among them was a king named Sumati.
Gautamas, through the succession of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants of King Sumati, there were twenty-five thousand kings in the city of Rājagṛha;
the last of them was a king named Tamonuda.
Gautamas, through the succession of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants of King Tamonuda, there were again one hundred and one kings in the city of Vārāṇasī.
The last of them was a king named Mahendrasena.
Gautamas, through the succession of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants of King Mahendrasena, there were eighty-four thousand kings in the city of Kuśāvatī;
the last of them was a king named Samudrasena.
Gautamas, through the succession of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants of King Samudrasena, there were once again a thousand kings in the city of Potalaka;
the last of them was a king named Tapañcara.
Gautamas, through the succession of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants of King Tapañcara, there were eighty-four thousand kings in the city of Kuśāvatī.
The last of them was a king named Mahīmukha.
Gautamas, through the succession of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants of King Mahīmukha, there were again one hundred thousand kings in the city of Vārāṇasī;
the last of them was a king named Mahīpati.
O Gautamas, through the succession of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants of King Mahīpati, there were again one hundred thousand kings in the city of Ayodhyā;
the last of them was a king named Mahīdhara.
O Gautamas, through the succession of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants of King Mahīdhara, there were eighty-four thousand kings in the city of Mithilā.

The last of them was a king named Mahādeva. Gautamas, through the succession of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants of King Mahādeva, eighty-four thousand royal seers likewise practiced the holy life in the city of Mithilā.

The last among them was a king named Nimi. From Nimi came Nimagha, Dṛḍhanemi, Khanu, Upakhanu, Khanumān, Khanumanta, Sudṛśa, Samadṛśa, Śrutasena, Dharmasena, Vidita, Mahāvidita, Viditasena, Aśoka, Vigataśoka, Dṛḍhasena, and Jarāsaṃdha.
Dhundhumāra, Aruṇa, Diśāmpati, Eṇḍa, Saṃkakāraka, Ānanda, Ādarśamukha, Janaka, Sañjanaka,
Janarṣabha, Annapāna, Pracurānnapāna, Ajita, Aparājita, Pratiṣṭhita, Supratiṣṭhita, Mahābala,
Mahābalavāhana, Sumati, Dṛḍhavāhana, Śatadhanu, Citradhanu, and Navatidhanu.
Vijitadhanu, Dṛḍhadhanu, Daśaratha, Śataratha, Navatiratha, Nararṣabha, Citraratha, Vicitraratha,
and Dṛḍharatha; O Gautamas, through the succession of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants of King Dṛḍharatha, there were seventy-seven thousand kings in the city of Sāṃkāśya.
The last of them was a king named Ambarīṣa.
Gautamas, King Ambarīṣa had a son named Nāgasampāla.
Gautamas, through the succession of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants of King Nāgasampāla, there arose once again one hundred and one kings in the city of Vārāṇasī.
The last of them was a king named Kṛkin.
At that time, a teacher named Kāśyapa appeared in the world:
a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, Sugata, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, Buddha, Blessed One.
In whose presence the Blessed One, as a bodhisattva, having made a vow for awakening in the future and having practiced the holy life, was reborn in the Tuṣita host of gods;
he was Sujāta, the son of King Kṛkī, O Gautamas.
Gautamas, through the succession of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants of King Sujāta, there were once more one hundred kings in the city of Potalaka;
the last among them was a king named Karṇa.
The progenitor of Ikṣvāku was King Karṇa Gautama; he had two sons, Gautama and Bharadvāja.
Of these two, Gautama delighted in the state beyond action (*naiṣkarmya*).
Bharadvāja was one who delighted in sovereignty;
he saw his father exercising sovereignty through both dharma and adharma,
and he reflected:

Thinking, "I too, upon the passing of my father, shall become king; I too, having ruled the kingdom through both righteousness and unrighteousness, shall be destined for hell; what is the timely course here? I shall go forth from the home to the homeless life," he approached King Karṇa.
Having approached and prostrated at his feet, he made this request:
"Father, grant me leave; out of faith, I shall go forth from the home to the homeless life.
He replied:
"Son, that for the sake of which sacrifices are offered, oblations are poured, and austerities are practiced—that kingdom is already in the palm of your hand."
"After my passing, you shall become king;
for what purpose, then, do you renounce the world?
He replied:
"Father, it is not possible for me to rule the kingdom through both dharma and adharma;
therefore, grant me permission, for I shall go forth. Then, the king, recognizing his firm persistence, gave him leave.
Now at that time, a seer named Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana was dwelling in a certain hermitage.

Then the youth Gautama, having been granted permission by the king, being thrilled, satisfied, joyful, and filled with an exalted sense of rapture and gladness, approached the seer Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana; having approached him, he performed a prostration at his feet with a disciplined deportment.
Having done so, he said, "I am seeking the going forth; let me go forth. He was ordained by him;
the seer Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana subsisted on fruits, roots, and water.
For him too, the name "Gautama Rishi" became established as his designation.
Then, at another time, King Karṇa passed away;
Bharadvāja Kumāra was installed in the sovereignty and lordship of the kingdom, and he ruled over the paternal realm.
Then, at another time, the seer Gautama said to his preceptor:
"Preceptor, I am unable to subsist on forest herbs;
I shall go to the vicinity of a village."
He said: "Son, well said!
Whether dwelling in a village or in the forest, a seer must at all times guard his sense faculties."

"Go, and having constructed a leaf-hut among the surroundings of Potalaka, make it your dwelling. "So be it, Preceptor," said the seer Gautama, and having constructed a leaf-hut among the surroundings of Potalaka, he settled there.
Now at that time, a courtesan named Bhadrā resided in the city of Potalaka.
And there was a rogue named Mṛṇāla;
he sent garments and ornaments for her enjoyment,
and she, having put on those garments and ornaments, set out.
A certain man approached, bringing five hundred kārṣāpaṇas, saying, "Noble lady, come, let us enjoy ourselves";
she reflected:
"If I go, I shall obtain five hundred kārṣāpaṇas;
moreover, it would be a lack of hospitality to turn away one who has come to my house and go elsewhere.
She then spoke to her maidservant:
"Go and tell Mṛṇāla: 'The noble lady says, "I am not yet ready; I will come later. She went and informed him of this.
That man, however, had many duties to attend to. He— (A 356b)
Having attended to her, he departed during the very first watch of the night.
She reflected:
"A long time has passed; I shall be able to win over his heart as well."
She spoke again to that girl:
"Go and inform Mṛṇāla: 'The noble lady has become ready; tell him which park he should come to. She went and informed him accordingly.
He said, "In one moment your noble lady is ready, and in another moment she is not.
That girl was her confidante, and she explained the matter to her.
"Noble son, she was not unfaithful;
rather,
she enjoyed herself with another man using your own clothes and ornaments."
Whatever obsession of sensual desire he had, that departed; an obsession of ill will arose.
Filled with indignation, he said:
"Girl, go and tell Bhadrā that Mṛṇāla says she should go out to such-and-such a park. She went and informed Bhadrā.
Then she went out from that garden;
there she was addressed by the rogue Mṛṇāla:
"Is it right for you to enjoy yourself with another man while wearing my clothes and ornaments?"
She said:
"Noble son, there truly is my fault;
however, women are constantly prone to offense, so please forgive me."
Then, filled with rage, he drew his sword from its scabbard and deprived her of life.
Thereupon, that maidservant raised a great outcry, crying out, "The noble lady has been murdered! The noble lady has been murdered!
Hearing this, a multitude of people rushed from all directions toward that very hermitage where the seer Gautama resided.
Then that rogue Mṛṇāla, terrified, cast his blood-stained sword before the seer Gautama and entered the midst of that very great crowd of people;
and the great crowd of people, seeing the blood-stained sword, said:
"This renunciant has deprived Bhadrā of her life."
Then, surrounding the seer Gautama, they spoke with rising indignation:
"O renunciant, you bear the banner of a seer, yet you perform such an act!
He replied:
"What was done? They replied, "You enjoyed yourself with Bhadrā, and she has been deprived of life.
He said:
"I am not the doer of this deed; it is peaceful," he said.

Yet, although he spoke thus peacefully, he was bound behind the back with tight bonds by that great crowd of people and brought before the king, who declared: "O King, this renunciant has dallied with Bhadrā; she has been deprived of life by him."
"Kings are unexamining," he said;
"if it is so, go! Impale him upon a stake!"

"This renunciant has been abandoned by me. Then that renunciant, with a garland of *karavīra* flowers draped around his neck and surrounded on all sides by men dressed in blue garments who held upraised weapons, was paraded through the streets, lanes, crossroads, and junctions— places unpleasant to hear—
while being proclaimed [of his crimes], and led along the right-hand path.
Having been led out through the city gate, he was impaled alive upon a stake.
His preceptor, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, would from time to time visit his hermitage;
however, on another occasion, when he arrived and did not see him, he began to search here and there until he saw him impaled upon the stake.
With his throat choked with tears and his eyes clouded with weeping, he spoke in piteous, wretched, and faltering syllables:
"Alas, my child! What is this?
He too, with a choking voice and despondency born from the obstruction of agonizing pain, replied: "Preceptor, it is my karmas."
"What else could it be?
he said,
"My child, you are neither wounded nor injured."
"Father, I am wounded in body, but not in mind.
"My child, how is this known?
"Preceptor, I shall make a vow of truth; listen: by that truth, by that word of truth, I am wounded in body."
But by that mind, by that truth, by that word of truth, may this dark-complexioned skin of my preceptor become golden-colored;
for that Great Being has cultivated a resolute intention.
Immediately upon the conclusion of his speech, the dark complexion of the seer Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana vanished, and he became golden-hued.
A cry spread throughout the surrounding area: "The seer Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana has become golden-hued!"
The name Suvarṇadvaipāyana, "Golden Dvaipāyana," became established for him;
he was filled with supreme wonder,
and then that seer Gautama said:
"Preceptor, when I have passed away from here, what will be my destination, what my rebirth, and what my future state? He replied, "Child, the brahmins say:"
"There is no destination for one who has no son;
have you produced any offspring?
"Preceptor, I am indeed a prince."
Unacquainted with the nature of women,
he was incited by his father for the sake of the kingdom and went forth as a renunciant; how, then, could there be the birth of offspring for me?
"My child, if that is so, then recollect the objects of enjoyment you experienced in the past.
"Preceptor, for one like me who is now struck by intense pain, with my vital organs being torn asunder and my joints being loosened,
and whose mind is fixed solely on death, how can there be recollection of objects of enjoyment experienced in the past?"
His preceptor was one who had attained the five superknowledges;
he created a great wind and rain by means of his supernatural power,
and drops of that rain fell upon [the monk's] body.
Then, due to the touch of cool water and wind, his agony was stilled;
he began to remember the sensory objects he had previously enjoyed,
until, from recollecting sexual passion, two drops of semen fell along with blood.
There are four things that are inconceivable:
reflection on the self, reflection on the world, reflection on the ripening of the karma of sentient beings, and reflection on the domain of the Buddhas.
Those two drops of semen appeared as two eggs.
At the time of sunrise, when [the fruit] had ripened by the rays of the sun and burst open,
two boys were born;
not far from there was a sugarcane plantation.
The two of them entered there;
then the sun's rays became even more brilliant,
and the seer Gautama, scorched by the sun's rays, passed away.
Then the seer Suvarṇadvaipāyana arrived; he saw that [the child] had passed away;
he saw that near the stake, the egg had burst open.
The skull-bowls were lying there;
following them here and there, he entered a sugar-cane field until he saw two young boys.
He began to reflect: "Whose sons are these? He saw:
"They are the sons of the seer Gautama."
Thereupon, an even greater love arose within him;
he took the two of them to his hermitage, where he suckled, nourished, and raised them.
He then proceeded to establish names for the two of them.
At the time of the sun’s rising, they were born fully ripened by the rays of the sun;
therefore, the designation "Sūryagotra" (of the Solar Lineage) came to be. Since they were the sons of the seer Gautama, the second designation "Gautama" also came to be.
Because they were born from his own body, the third designation "Āṅgīrasas" came into being;
because they were obtained from the sugarcane field (ikṣuvāṭa), the fourth designation "Ikṣvākus" came into being;
and later, at another time, King Bharadvāja passed away while still childless.
The ministers assembled and began to deliberate:
"Sirs, whom shall we now consecrate as king?
Others said, "His brother Gautama has gone forth among the sages."
"This kingdom has come down to him by hereditary succession;
let us consecrate him.
Having thus consulted together, they approached the seer Suvarṇadvaipāyana.
Having approached and prostrated at his feet, they said,
"Great Seer, where has Gautama gone?
He replied, "He was killed by you yourselves."
"Great Seer, we do not even remember seeing him;
how then shall we kill him? "I shall remind you," he said.
"Excellent!
Thus reminded, they said:
"Great Seer, if that is so, enough of mentioning his name."
This man is an evildoer and beyond reproach;
what evil deed has he committed? This and that.
That man was not a doer of evil deeds;
he was killed by you even though he had done you no wrong and had harmed none.
How so?
He related everything exactly as it had happened;
they, overcome with dejection, said:
"Great Seer, if this is so, we are the ones who committed the evil deed, not he."
While they were conversing in this manner,
those two boys approached the presence of the ṛṣi;
the ministers said:
"Great Seer, whose children are these two boys? "He replied, 'They are his very own sons. 'How were they born, and what are their names?
He then related the account of their birth in detail."
Having heard this, the ministers were filled with great wonder;
they took leave of that ṛṣi and consecrated the elder of the two princes with the royal inauguration.
He too died without having had a son.
Then that second younger son was consecrated;

the name Ikṣvākurāja came to belong to him. Gautamas, through the succession of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants of King Ikṣvāku, there arose once again in the city of Potalaka one hundred kings named Ikṣvāku.
The Story of Virūḍhaka:
Among them, the last was a king of the Ikṣvāku lineage named Virūḍhaka.
Gautamas, King Ikṣvāku Virūḍhaka had four sons:
Ulkāmukha, Karakarṇī, Hastiniyaṃsa, and Nūpuraka.
At a later time, his chief queen passed away.
Placing his cheek upon his hand, he remained lost in thought;
the ministers asked,
"For what reason, O Lord, do you stand with your cheek resting on your hand, absorbed in anxiety?"
He said:
"My chief queen has passed away;
how could I not remain absorbed in grief?"
"Your Majesty, if this is so, why is the King's chief queen not sought after?
There are daughters available among the neighboring kings."
The king said:
"These princes are seekers of sovereignty;
while they exist as my adversaries, who will give their daughter to me?"
"Let Your Majesty direct his mind [to this matter];
we shall search for one.
Until now, there has been the daughter of a certain king, who is beautiful, lovely to behold, gracious, and worthy to be a queen."
Having found her, they went into the presence of that king;
they reported it to the king by word of mouth, and the king gave the command: "Let her be summoned."
Then they were sent into the presence of the king; having prostrated at his feet, they sat down after exchanging greetings.
When the opportunity for conversation arose, seeing the king before them face-to-face, they said:
"O King, may there be well-being! May there be well-being!
The king said: "Sirs, what do you ask for?"
The chief queen of King Ikṣvāku Virūḍhaka had passed away;
for her sake, he requested a maiden as alms,
to which the king replied:
"He is handsome, worthy, and excellent;
however, I shall grant him [my daughter] on one condition: if a son is born to my daughter, and if he establishes that son in the sovereignty, lordship, and authority of the kingdom."
"Your Majesty, let it be so; we shall go and inform the King.
Having gone, they reported to Virūḍhaka, the Ikṣvāku king, exactly what had occurred.
The king said:
"Sirs, it is not fitting to set aside the elder princes who desire the kingdom and establish a younger one instead.
Your Majesty, this matter is uncertain; let the Queen be summoned first, so that Your Majesty may sport, enjoy, and amuse yourself with her."
"It is not known whether she will give birth to a son, or a daughter, or whether she will be barren.
The king said, "Sirs, if that is the case, go!"
"Therefore, let her be established [as his wife].
Having gone there, they accepted her;
eventually, she was married by the king with a great display of royal splendor.
She became dear to the king;
he played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
While he was thus playing, dallying, and enjoying himself, in the course of time the queen became pregnant.
When eight or nine months had passed, she gave birth;
a boy was born who was handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing.
Upon his birth, a birth-festival was held, and they deliberated on the naming of the child, asking, "What shall be the name of this boy?"
"Your Majesty, since this boy rejoices in the kingdom even while unborn, let the child's name be Rājyābhinandin.
That boy was entrusted to eight nurses, and as before, he grew quickly like a lotus in a pond.
The king did not establish him in the position of crown prince;
his maternal grandfather, the king, heard of this and dispatched a messenger to him.
And it was written quite harshly:
"It was already authorized by you previously;
if you act according to what was promised, that would be well."
"If you do not stand firm with whatever strength, heroism, and prowess you possess,
[know that] here I have come, saying, 'I shall bring about the destruction of your kingdom';
for that king has arisen with a great army."
Having heard this, he was distressed;
having assembled his ministers, he asked: "Sirs, such is the letter written to me by that king."
"How should we proceed in this matter? they asked.
They replied, "Your Majesty, let Rājyābhinandin be consecrated in the position of crown prince."
He said:
"Sirs, it is not proper to reject the elder princes who desire the kingdom and instead consecrate the younger one for the kingship.
They replied:
"Your Majesty, that king has mobilized his forces and vehicles; it is possible that he will come and surely inflict a crushing defeat upon our kingdom.
Therefore, let the one who delights in sovereignty be consecrated to the lordship and power of the kingdom."
"Let the princes be exiled from the kingdom.
The king said:
"Sirs, how can these princes, who are blameless and have done no wrong, be banished?"
"O King, we ministers, though intent on promoting your welfare, blameless and harmless, are being banished;
while those who are corrupt and harmful are being established.
Even the King remains indifferent and silent."
The ministers, having assembled, began to consult with one another: "Sirs, a strategic plan must be devised by which the king may turn his face away from the princes.
Thereupon, they had the park cleaned and decorated it with various beautiful paintings.
It was delightful, furnished with incense burners emitting fragrant smoke, draped with bundles of silk ribbons, and strewn with various flowers; then,
those ministers saw from afar that park thus prepared,
and the princes, out of restlessness, set out toward the park.
The ministers, having had the beauty of the park prepared, went out;
when questioned by the princes as to whose park this was, they replied, "It belongs to Your Majesty."
They began to turn back;
the ministers said, "Princes, enter! For what reason do you turn back?"
They said, "This is the king's garden;
how shall we enter?
The ministers replied:
"Whether it be a god playing or a prince, what contradiction is there in this?
Having entered, they began to play;
the ministers then addressed the king:
"Your Majesty, the garden is beautiful and has been prepared;
it is time for Your Majesty to go and see it.
The king set out.
He heard a tumultuous noise in the park;
having heard it, he questioned his ministers: "Sirs, what is this tumult in the park?"
A sound is heard;
"Who is staying here?
the ministers replied:
"O King, the princes! If the princes have thus been abandoned by me," the ministers, falling at his feet, said:
"Your Majesty, let it be forgiven for the princes; let them not be abandoned.
The king said, "So be it."
They began to banish them, but falling at the feet of the king, they said:
"Your Majesty, if this is the case, you ought to grant an order such that the attendants who go along with us are not prevented from returning.
The king gave his command.
They set out;
they were beloved by the people of the countryside,
and a great multitude of people set out along with them.
For seven days, the city gate of Potalaka remained open for the multitude of people to depart;
the ministers informed the king:
"Your Majesty, if the city gate is not closed, before long Potalaka will become uninhabited."
"If that is so, then close the gates.
Thereupon those princes, taking each his own sister, proceeded by stages to the slopes of the Himalayas, reaching the bank of the river Bhāgīrathī not far from the hermitage of the seer Kapila.
Having constructed leaf-huts there, they made it their dwelling; and by repeatedly slaughtering deer, they sustained their livelihood.
They would go to the hermitage of the seer Kapila three times a day;

being seized by the intoxication of fresh youth and excessively oppressed by the passion of desire, they became extremely pale and emaciated. Then, at another time, the seer Kapila saw them in such a state and questioned them:
"Why are you so pale and wan?
They replied,
"Great Seer, we are being excessively tormented by sensual desire."
He said:
"Abandoning each your own sisters, dwell together with your half-sisters. "Great Seer, it is possible for us to do so," they replied.
"Sirs, it is possible for Kṣatriyas who have been deprived of their kingdom to do as you have said.

Then, taking the words of the ṛṣi as authoritative, they became intent upon sensual passion; filled with joy and gladness, they played, dallied, and enjoyed themselves together with their half-sisters.
As they played with those [women], took their pleasure, and enjoyed themselves, sons and daughters were born to them;
these grew up. [The cities of] Kapilavastu and Devadṛśa.
The seer Kapila, because words were like thorns to his meditations, could not attain one-pointedness of mind;
he said: "Sirs, look upon me!"
"I shall go elsewhere.
"For what reason, Great Seer?
"I am unable to attain one-pointedness of mind."
"Meditations have sounds as their thorns;
O Great Seer, you remain right here;
we shall go elsewhere."
"But grant us a portion of land;
you are most excellent,
for those great-souled sages are the fulfillers of one's desired wishes."
Taking a golden pitcher, he laid out the city by means of streams of water falling in the shape of a city;
because the seer Kapila had relinquished the site for them to dwell in, it became known as Kapilavastu, "the Abode of Kapila";
they flourished there.
A great multitude of people had gathered;
because of the congestion, they could not find space to grow.
Having understood their thoughts with his own mind, deities pointed out another location to them.
Having gone there, they built a second city;
it became known by the name Devadriśa, "Gazing upon the Gods.
Then, having gathered and assembled together, they began to hold a consultation:
"Gentlemen, the reason we have been exiled is our taking of a second wife who was our equal;
therefore, none of us should take a second wife who is our equal;
we should be content with only one."
They marry only one wife who is their equal, and not a second;
then, at another time, King Virūḍhaka, remembering his beloved sons, addressed his ministers:
"O village headman, where are those princes now?
They reported in detail:
"Your Majesty, they have been banished on account of a certain legal matter."
Taking each their own sister, they departed from here;
on the slopes of the Himalayas, on the bank of the river Bhāgīrathī, not far from the hermitage of the seer Kapila, they established their dwelling.
Having rejected each their own sisters, they played, took pleasure, and amused themselves together with the half-sisters born of different mothers.
As they were playing, sporting, and enjoying themselves, sons and daughters were born to them;
it is possible, O village headman, for princes to act in this way.
"It is possible, O King.
Then Virūḍhaka, the Ikṣvāku king, raised his upper body, extended his right arm, and uttered this exclamation:
"The princes are indeed capable!"
"Ah, the Kumāras are supremely capable!"—thus was the speech uttered by a being of great majesty: "Ah, the Śākyas!
Ah, the Kumāras are supremely Śākyas! And so the designation "Śākyas" came into being.
As for the successors of Virūḍhaka:
at a later time, King Virūḍhaka of the Ikṣvāku lineage passed away,
and Rājyābhinandin was consecrated in the kingdom.
He too died without a son;
Ulkāmukha was established in the sovereignty and lordship of the kingdom;
he too died without a son.
Karakarṇī became king;
he too died without a son;
Hastiniyaṃsa became king.
He too died without a son,
and Nūpuraka became king;
his son was Opuraka.
Gopuraka was the son of Gopuraka. From King Gopuraka’s lineage, through sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and great-great-grandsons, there were fifty-five thousand kings in the city of Kapilavastu.
The last of them were Daśaratha, Śataratha, Navatiratha, Citraratha, Vijitaratha, Dṛḍharatha, Daśadhanus, Śatadhanus, Navatidhanus, Vijitadhanus, and Citradhanus.
Gautamas, Dṛḍhadhanus had two sons: Siṃhahanu and Siṃhanādī.
O Gautamas, among all the archers in Jambūdvīpa, Siṃhahanu was proclaimed the foremost.
O Gautamas, Siṃhahanu had four sons: Śuddhodana, Śuklodana, Droṇodana, and Amṛtodana;
and his daughters were Śuddhā, Śuklā, Droṇā, and Amṛtikā.
Śuddhodana had two sons: the Blessed One and the Venerable Nanda;
Śuklodana had two sons.
The Venerable Tiṣya and Bhadraka were the Śākya kings;
Droṇodana had two sons, Mahānāman and the Venerable Aniruddha;
Amṛtodana had two sons, the Venerable Ānanda and Devadatta.
Suprabuddha was the son of Śuddhā;
Mālin was the son of Śuklā; and Bhāddālī was the son of Droṇā.

"O Gautamas, Śaivala was the son of Amṛtikā and the son of the Blessed One Rāhula; thus the lineage of Mahāsaṃmata was established in Rāhula. The conduit to existence is cut off, the cycle of birth is exhausted, and now there is no further becoming."—the Buddha’s remarks.
Then the Blessed One, perceiving that the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had finished his discourse, rose from his seat and sat down; having sat down, he addressed the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Excellent, excellent, Maudgalyāyana! It is indeed excellent, Maudgalyāyana, that you have delivered a discourse on the Dharma before the monks concerning the ancient family lineage of the Śākyas."
"Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana, you should frequently deliver a discourse on the Dharma concerning the ancient family lineage of the Śākyas;
that will be for their long-term welfare, benefit, and happiness.
Then the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, you should take up, maintain, master, and recite the Dharma discourse concerning the ancient lineage of the Śākyas.
For what reason?
Because, monks, the Dharma discourse concerning the ancient lineage of the Śākyas is endowed with meaning."
It is connected with the goal and connected with the holy life;

it is indeed fitting, monks, for a son of good family who has gone forth out of faith to uphold, cause others to grasp, or recite a discourse on the Dharma concerning the ancient lineage of the Śākyas.

Then the Śākyas of Kapilavastu, having rejoiced and delighted in the words spoken by the Blessed One, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from his presence. [This concludes the account of] Siṃhahanu’s reign.
At that time, in the city of Kapilavastu, a king named Siṃhahanu reigned; his kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people.
In the city of Devadṛśa, King Suprabuddha reigned; his kingdom was likewise prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people.
King Suprabuddha had a chief queen named Lumbinī, who was beautiful, lovely to behold, gracious, and the most excellent woman in the land.

In Devadṛśa there lived a certain householder, wealthy, of great fortune and great enjoyment, possessing vast and extensive holdings, endowed with wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, and rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa himself. His park was abundant in flowers, abundant in fruits, abundant in rice, and resounded with the songs of various birds.
Because of its delightful beauty, the king would go there from time to time together with his harem to experience pleasure and sport.
Having seen it, Lumbinī conceived a longing for it;
she said,
"Your Majesty, please grant this grove to me."
The king said:
"This monastery belongs to the householder; how can I give it away?"
"If you desire a grove, I shall have another, even more beautiful one made for you";
thereupon, King Suprabuddha had a grove even more excellent than that built for Lumbinī,
and it became known by the name "Lumbinī Grove."
For a long time, Siṃhahanu had this aspiration:
"O, would that a universal monarch might be born into my family!
And for a long time, King Suprabuddha also had this aspiration: [the same].
"O, would that I might have a connection with Siṃhahanu!
Then, at another time, while he was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself with his queen, after some time his wife became pregnant;
and when eight or nine months had passed, she gave birth.
A daughter was born, beautiful, lovely, pleasing, and endowed with all major and minor limbs;

by the splendor of her form, King Suprabuddha, along with his harem, the inhabitants of Devadṛśa, and the multitude of people, were struck with supreme wonder, and he became filled with doubt, thinking:
"Is this a girl, or is she a magical illusion created by Viśvakarman?
For her, after performing the birth ceremony in detail for three times seven—that is, twenty-one days—the naming was established:
"What shall be the name of this girl?"
The ministers said:
"Your Majesty, the body of people residing in Devadṛśa are disputing in the streets, lanes, squares, and crossroads;
some say:"
"This girl possesses such beauty of complexion and form as a result produced by the ripening of her past karma";
others say,
"This is not a girl."
"What then? That illusion was created by Viśvakarman; therefore, let the girl's name be Māyā. Thus, the name Māyā was given to her.
The girl Māyā was entrusted to eight nurses, and as before, she grew until she became a young woman.
She was prophesied by the soothsayers:
"She will give birth to a son endowed with many auspicious marks;
he will become a king, a powerful universal monarch."
Furthermore, while he was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, a daughter was born to him— well-proportioned, beautiful, pleasing, and endowed with the highest excellence of complexion;
at her birth, that entire city was illuminated by a sublime radiance.
And it was impossible to describe her beauty of form in every respect;
just as [was done] for Māyā, so too, when her birth festival had been performed in detail, her name was established,
[the king asking], "What shall be the girl's name?"
The ministers said:
"Since the beauty of her form surpasses that of Māyā, let her be named Mahāmāyā.
She was then raised and nurtured until she had grown up and reached maturity.
She was prophesied by the soothsayers:
"She will give birth to a son adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man;
he will become a universal monarch (cakravartin)."
King Suprabuddha dispatched a messenger to Siṃhahanu, reporting:
"Two daughters have been born, Māyā and Mahāmāyā;
among them, one has been prophesied that she will give birth to a son endowed with the [major] marks."
"He shall become a powerful universal monarch";
the second was prophesied: "She will give birth to a son adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man."
"He shall become a universal monarch (cakravartin)";
"Of these two, bring whichever one Śuddhodana desires for the sake of the prince";
thus Siṃhahanu gave this reply.
The prince has need of both;

however, two similar wives should not be presented to one man. For it was thus prophesied: "She who shall give birth to a son adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man will have a son who shall become a universal monarch (cakravartin)."
"This one has already been accepted;
for the sake of a second, I shall look for a group.
He then sent her forth with a retinue of five hundred.
At that time, the Śākyas were opposed by the Khaṣas known as the Pāṇḍavas;
the Śākyas, having gathered together, approached King Siṃhahanu and said,
"O Lord, we are being harassed by the Pāṇḍava Khaṣas."
"Provide assistance," they said.
He replied, "Sirs, I am old and I am unable to fight with them;
Your Majesty, please send Prince Śuddhodana."
"I send you on this condition: if you grant whatever boon the prince requests according to his desire.
They replied, "Your Majesty, let it be so; we shall grant it."
The king, having provided a fourfold army, dispatched Prince Śuddhodana;
by him those Khaṣas were struck down, slaughtered, and utterly destroyed.
Thereupon, the Śākyas, being highly gratified, approached King Siṃhahanu.
"O King, the Pāṇḍavas and the Khaṣas have been struck down, slaughtered, and utterly destroyed by the prince;
we are well-pleased.
Tell us, what boon shall we grant to the prince?"
"Sirs, an agreement has been made by the Śākyas that no one shall take two wives who are alike. Your Majesty, why should this agreement not be rescinded?
He replied:
"He must be bound even more firmly and not released;
however, grant one boon to the prince, that you provide him with a second wife who is his equal."
"Your Majesty, it is excellent;
let it be done so.
Then Siṃhahanu dispatched a letter to Suprabuddha, which was read by Avalokita.
"I have [already] a group [of followers]; send me your second daughter.
He then sent her as well, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred;
both were married by Prince Śuddhodana.
Śuddhodana succeeds Siṃhahanu and the descent of the Buddha: at a later time, King Siṃhahanu passed away;
in Kapilavastu, King Śuddhodana ruled the kingdom, which was prosperous, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people.
And at another time, he went with Queen Mahāmāyā to the upper terrace of the palace and sported, enjoyed himself, and dallied there with music performed by women alone.

For it is the natural law that a Bodhisattva dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven surveys the world with five observations: the observation of the [proper] birth, the observation of the country, the observation of the time, the observation of the lineage, and the observation of the woman. (1)
For what reason do Bodhisattvas perform the observation of their birth?
While residing in the Tuṣita heaven, the Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"In what kind of birth do Bodhisattvas take conception?"
He sees [it] either in a brahmin family or in a kṣatriya family; therein, sometimes the brahmins are regarded as being of high birth,
and sometimes the kṣatriyas.
But now, the Kṣatriyas are esteemed as being of high birth;
what if I were to take rebirth in a Kṣatriya family?
Lest others should say of me on this account: "The Bodhisattva has taken rebirth in a despised caste."
For it is thus: a bodhisattva has performed and accumulated karma that, though beginningless, does not lead to an unfavorable rebirth;
(for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are teachers whose dharma-instruction never fails to bear fruit);
for this reason, bodhisattvas perform the observation of their birth. (2)
For what reason do bodhisattvas perform the examination of a country?
This thought occurred to the Bodhisattva:
"In what kind of country do bodhisattvas take rebirth?"

He sees that region which is abundant in sugarcane, rice, garlands, cattle, and buffalo; crowded with hundreds of mendicants; devoid of bandit folk; and inhabited by noble people. To him it occurs: "This is the Middle Country, abundant in sugarcane, rice, garlands, cattle, and buffalo; crowded with hundreds of mendicants; devoid of bandit folk; and inhabited by noble people.
What if I were to take rebirth in the Middle Country?"
"Let there not be those who would say of me on this account: 'The Bodhisattva took rebirth in the outlying borderlands';
for the Bodhisattva has performed and accumulated karma that is from beginningless time and does not lead to such a rebirth."
For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are teachers of the Dharma whose fruit is never in vain;
for this reason, Bodhisattvas perform the observation of the place.
(3) For what reason do Bodhisattvas perform the observation of the time?
This thought occurred to the Bodhisattva:
"At what kind of time do Bodhisattvas take rebirth in Jambudvīpa?
They do not take rebirth when the lifespan of beings is eighty thousand years or more, while the population is in its period of increase."
During the period of decline, when the lifespan of humans is one hundred years, they do not take rebirth among them for any shorter duration.
For what reason do bodhisattvas not take rebirth among humans whose lifespan exceeds eighty thousand years?
For humans with a lifespan of eighty thousand years are difficult to stir from their complacency;
they are dull-witted, have weak faculties, are heedless, abound in pleasure, and are unfit vessels for the truths.
Even during the period of decline, when life spans fall below one hundred years, the five corruptions (pañcakaṣāya) become intensified:
namely, the corruption of lifespan, the corruption of afflictions, the corruption of sentient beings, the corruption of views, and the corruption of the eon.
[He thought: "Let there not be others who would say of me: 'The Bodhisattva took rebirth at a time when the five corruptions were intensified.'"
For thus, the Bodhisattva has performed and accumulated karma that is not subject to obstruction from beginningless time;
and the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are teachers of the Dharma whose fruit is never in vain.
For this reason, bodhisattvas observe the time. (4) For what reason do they observe the family?
It occurs to the bodhisattva as follows:
"What kind of family do Bodhisattvas take rebirth in?
He saw that it must be a family held in high esteem, whose conduct is irreproachable, reaching back through seven generations of maternal and paternal ancestors.

Then this thought occurred to him: "This Śākya lineage is held in high esteem, reaching back to Mahāsaṃmata, and its conduct is irreproachable; what if I were to take rebirth in the family of King Śuddhodana?"
"Let there not be those who would say of me on this account: 'The Bodhisattva has taken rebirth in an inferior family';
for indeed, the Bodhisattva has performed and accumulated karma that, from beginningless time, is conducive to non-rejection."
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are teachers of the Dharma whose fruit is never in vain;
for this reason, Bodhisattvas perform the examination of their lineage.
(5) For what reason do Bodhisattvas perform the examination of a woman?
The Bodhisattva reflects thus: "In what kind of woman's womb do Bodhisattvas take conception?

He sees that it is a woman who is beautiful, virtuous, of noble family, well-born, one who increases her lineage, and who has made a vow before former Buddhas, saying: "O, may I become the mother of a Buddha!"
She is able to carry a bodhisattva in her womb for ten months, yet she does not neglect her own welfare.

It occurs to her: "This Mahāmāyā, tracing back through seven generations of maternal and paternal ancestors, has been of unblemished conduct, beautiful, virtuous, of noble birth, and an enhancer of her family."
She is able to carry the Bodhisattva in her womb for ten months and does not neglect her own welfare;
for Mahāmāyā had previously made a vow and performed meritorious service toward former Buddhas, thinking, "O, may I become the mother of a Buddha."
And let there not be others who would say of me on this account: "The Bodhisattva took rebirth in the womb of a woman lacking auspicious marks";
for indeed, the Bodhisattva has performed and accumulated karma that is beginningless and conducive to non-rejection.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are teachers of the Dharma whose fruit is never in vain;
for this reason, Bodhisattvas perform the examination of a woman.
Then, having performed the five examinations, the Bodhisattva makes a proclamation three times to the gods of the six desire realms.
"Friends, having passed away from this Tuṣita host of gods, I shall take rebirth among humans in the womb of the chief queen of King Śuddhodana;
having attained the state of being his son, I shall realize the deathless."
"Whosoever among you desires the deathless, let him take rebirth among humans, specifically once more in the Middle Country.
When this was said, the gods of the Tuṣita host spoke thus to the Bodhisattva:

"Indeed, O Bodhisattva, you should know that at this time the world is defiled by strife, its people are of cruel disposition, and Jambudvīpa is thrown into confusion by the six logicians, the six traditionalists, and the six [heretical teachers]."
In that regard, who are the six philosophers? They are as follows: Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Maskarin Gośāliputra, Sañjayin Vairaṭṭīputra, Ajita Keśakambalin, Kakuda Kātyāyana, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra.
Who are the six who follow tradition? They are as follows: the brahmin Kūṭatāṇḍya, the brahmin Śroṇatāṇḍya, the brahmin Cogī, the brahmin Brāhmāyu, the brahmin Puṣkarasārin, and the brahmin Lohitya.
Who are the six practitioners? They are as follows: Udraka Rāmaputra, Arāḍa Kālāma, the wanderer Subhadra, the young brahmin Sañjayin, the seer Asita, and the matted-hair ascetic Urubilvākāśyapa.
But here, for the sake of hearing the Dharma from the Bodhisattva, seats are prepared over a distance of twelve yojanas; and we think:
"When the Bodhisattva, while staying in the Tuṣita heaven, teaches the Dharma to us, having heard that Dharma, we shall practice accordingly."
"Indeed, this will be for our long-term welfare, benefit, and happiness.
When this was said, the Bodhisattva spoke thus to the gods of the Tuṣita realm:
"In that case, friends, let all the musical instruments be struck!"
At the descent from Tuṣita,
all musical instruments were struck by the deities belonging to the Tuṣita realm; the Bodhisattva also blew his conch shell and said:
"Which among these, venerable sirs, is the coarse sound?
"The sound of the conch, Blessed One.
"Venerable sirs, just as this sound of the conch remains having overwhelmed all other musical instruments, even so shall I, having descended into Jambudvīpa, [overwhelm] the six philosophers."
Having overcome the six who follow what is heard and the six who practice [wrong] means, I shall attain the deathless;
with the deathless, I shall satisfy the world.
"Having resolved, 'I shall blow the conch of impermanence; I shall beat the drum of emptiness; I shall roar the lion's roar of selflessness,' he speaks this verse:"
A single lion overpowers many throngs of predatory beasts;
a single thunderbolt cleaves many horned mountains;
a single Śakra conquers many lords of the Dānavas.
The sun alone dispels manifold darkness.
O worthy ones, whoever among you seeks the deathless, let him take rebirth in the Middle Country;
we shall go to the six great cities.
This thought occurred to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"This Bodhisattva, the Blessed One, desires to take rebirth in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā;
what if I were to augment her vital energy and purify her womb? Having understood this, Śakra, the lord of the gods, augmented the vital energy of Queen Mahāmāyā.
And he purified her womb.
