Then the Bodhisattva, residing in the Tuṣita heaven, having performed the five observations and having announced himself three times to the gods of the six desire realms, entered the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā in the form of an elephant during the middle watch of the night. And it is said:
Having made a vow to protect the world and having taken leave of the gods,
he descended from there and entered the womb in the lineage of Ikṣvāku.
Like the young sun [dispelling] a streak of twilight clouds.
Conception; the auspicious signs in the dream:
thus indeed Mahāmāyā saw four dreams:
(1) a white elephant with six tusks entered her womb after breaking through her side; (2) ...
(1) I travel through the air above;
(2) I ascend a great rocky mountain;
(3) a great multitude of people pays homage to me; (4) [I think], "A great multitude of people pays homage to me."
She reported this to King Śuddhodana;
the king gave an order to his ministers:
"Sirs, let those Brahmins who are experts in the interpretation of dreams and those who are skilled in omens be summoned."
They summoned Brahmins who were experts in the study of dreams and skilled in interpreting omens;
then the king reported his dreams to them,
and they said:
"Your Majesty, as it is seen in the scriptures,
he will give birth to a son adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man;
if he should dwell at home in the household life,"

He will become a universal monarch (cakravartin); however, if he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on saffron-colored robes, and with perfect faith goes forth from the home to the homeless life, [he will become a Buddha].

"The Tathāgata will become an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, whose fame shall resound throughout the world. The intermediate summary verse says: "Death, the son of a god, the jewel, the eightfold path, and the mind weary of vows."

The Dharma-nature regarding the Buddha in his mother’s womb is as follows: at the time when the Bodhisattva, having passed away from the Tuṣita host of gods, descended into his mother’s womb, at that very moment a great earthquake occurred,
and this entire world was suffused with a sublime radiance.

Even those intermediate spaces between worlds— blind, shrouded in darkness, and enveloped in thick gloom, where even these two, the sun and the moon, despite such great supernatural power and such great majesty, do not experience their radiance with their light—
even those places were at that time suffused by a sublime radiance; and the beings born there, who previously could not even see their own outstretched arm, [now saw one another].

By that light, those beings, seeing one another, recognize each other, thinking, "Other beings, sirs, have also been reborn here; other beings, sirs, have also been reborn here," just as a vast, well-formed cloud, filled with much water and driven by the force of the wind.
In that same manner, the Sage, after a long time, entered her womb as the sun finally approaches a thick cloud.
Having illuminated all directions here,
as well as the world-antarīkṣas shrouded in darkness individually,
he of incomparable prowess entered the womb.
Thus it was; this is the natural law (*dharmatā*) here:

indeed, at the time when the Blessed Bodhisattva descended into his mother’s womb, Śakra, the lord of the gods, stationed four sons of the gods as protectors of the mother—each holding a spear, a javelin, and a lance.
"May no one— whether human or non-human— harass the Bodhisattva. Indeed,
it is the natural law that at the time when the Bodhisattva dwelt in his mother’s womb, he dwelt as if enclosed in a sheath, unsullied by the impurities of the womb or the impurities of the fetus.
by blood-stain, or by some other impurity that has defiled it;
just as when a precious gem is placed upon a Kāśī cloth, the precious gem is not at all stained by the Kāśī cloth.
Nor is a Kāśika jewel compared to a precious gem;
even so, at whatever time the Bodhisattva remained in his mother’s womb, he remained as if enclosed in a sheath, unsullied by the impurity of the womb or the impurity of birth.
It was defiled by blood, impurity, or some other kind of unclean substance—
just like a precious gem. Indeed,
it is the nature of things that at the time when the Blessed Bodhisattva dwelt in his mother’s womb, at that very moment his mother saw everything within her womb completely filled with him.
It is as if there were an eight-faceted beryl gem—pure, of noble origin, transparent, clear, and unclouded—which had been strung upon a five-colored thread:
blue, yellow, red, white, and madder-red.
A man with keen vision, seeing it, would know: "This is the thread; this is the gem."
In the Sūtra it is said that a jewel was placed [within];
in the very same way, at whatever time the Bodhisattva remained in his mother’s womb, at that time his mother saw him entirely within her womb, completely full.

Indeed, it is the natural law (dharmatā) that at whatever time the Blessed Bodhisattva remained in his mother’s womb, at that time his mother did not become weary of body or exhausted of body on account of the Bodhisattva.
It is indeed the nature of things that at the time when the Blessed Bodhisattva dwelt in his mother’s womb, at that time his mother undertook the five precepts for as long as she lived:
having abandoned the taking of life for as long as she lived, she abstained from taking life.

Having abandoned taking what is not given, unchaste conduct, false speech, and the occasion for negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, they abstain from the occasion for negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants.
She did not take what was not given, she did not harm living beings,
she did not speak falsehoods, and she was not addicted to intoxicants.
And Siddhārtha’s mother abstained from unchastity and sexual intercourse;
this is the natural law here:
indeed, it is the natural law that at the time when the Blessed Bodhisattva dwelt in his mother’s womb, his mother did not fix her mind upon men, namely, with thoughts associated with sensual desire.
She is not attached to the afflictions; her mind is not consumed by the cause of sensual desire;
nor does her mother fix her thoughts, associated with the qualities of desire, upon men.
Then a pregnancy longing arose in Mahāmāyā: "Oh, would that I might drink water from the four great oceans!
She informed King Śuddhodana of this.
King Śuddhodana informed the fortune-tellers:
"For what reason has such a longing as this arisen in the Queen? The fortune-tellers prophesied:
"O King, the queen will give birth to a son;

Asita, Nālada, and the yakṣa Śākyavardhana:
on Mount Kiṣkindha there dwells a seer named Asita, who is skilled in the process of cosmic dissolution and skilled in the process of cosmic evolution. He has a nephew named Nālada;
from time to time, the latter recounts to him the accounts of dissolution and evolution.
He went forth into homelessness in his presence;
at the birth of the Blessed One, the Bodhisattva, the entire world was suffused with a sublime radiance.

The Bodhisattva of great splendor will certainly emerge from the womb;

[Names of the Bodhisattvas]

"Let the prince's name be Sarvārthasiddha.

It is the custom of the Śākyas that whenever a son or a daughter is born to any Śākya, he or she is led to pay homage at the feet of the Śākyavardhana; the king then gave an order to his officers:

It is indeed the natural law that when a Bodhisattva has just been born, his parents present him to brahmins, fortune-tellers, and interpreters of signs.
"Friends, is the prince endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man,

There is no other [result]: if he remains a householder living at home,

He is righteous, a king of dharma, endowed with the seven treasures;

(1) the wheel-treasure, (2) the elephant-treasure, (3) the horse-treasure, (4) [the jewel-treasure]...

"If he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on saffron robes, and out of perfect faith goes forth from the home to the homeless life, he will become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, whose fame shall resound throughout the world. For a great man endowed with these, there are two destinies and no other:

A conqueror of the four quarters,

a righteous king of Dharma, as previously described, up until: he becomes a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, whose fame is proclaimed throughout the world, endowed with the marks of a Great Man.

What, sirs, are those thirty-two marks of a great man, endowed with which a great man has two possible destinies and no other— as previously described— until his fame resounds throughout the world? (1)
"O Lord, the prince has well-placed feet;
moreover, because his feet are so well-placed, he treads upon the earth evenly.
This is a mark of a Great Man belonging to the prince, a Great Man. (2)
And on the soles of his feet, there appeared wheels with a thousand spokes,
complete with hubs and rims,
perfect in every aspect.
"Your Majesty, this is a mark of a Great Man belonging to the Prince;
(3) the Prince has long fingers, (4) and he has broad heels. (5)
His hands and feet are soft and tender;
his hands and feet are so soft that they are like a tuft of silk-cotton or a tuft of cotton wool.
O King, this is a mark of a Great Man belonging to the Prince, a Great Man. (6)
O Lord, the prince has webbed hands and feet;

"Your Majesty, this is a mark of a Great Man belonging to the Prince:
(7) the Prince has ankles that are hidden; (8) he has calves like those of the eṇī deer; (9)"
With his body unbent, by not bending his body, he touches and strokes both kneecaps;

(10) The private parts of the Prince, O King, are withdrawn into a sheath.
The private organ is withdrawn into a sheath, just like that of a noble-bred elephant or a noble-bred horse;
this, O King, is a mark of a Great Man belonging to the Prince.
(11) The Prince, O King, is symmetrical in proportion like a banyan tree.
As long as his body is, so long is his outstretched armspan;
as long as his outstretched armspan is, so long is his body;
this, O King, is the mark of a Great Man belonging to the Prince, a Great Man. (12)
The divine youth has body hairs growing upward; he has a single hair per pore; each hair that grows on his body is blue.
His ears are adorned with earrings that curl to the right;
O King, this is a mark of a Great Man belonging to the Prince, the Great Man;
(14) O King, the Prince has a complexion resembling the color of gold.
He has a fathom-wide radiance and a skin resembling gold; his skin is fine,
and because of the fineness of his skin, even now dust and dirt do not remain upon his body.
“Your Majesty, this is a mark of a Great Man belonging to the Prince; (16) the Prince has a body with seven protuberances;
seven protuberances have arisen upon his body.”
Two on the hands, two on the feet, two on the shoulders, and one on the neck;
this, O Lord, is the mark of a Great Man belonging to the Prince, a Great Man. (17) The Prince has well-filled spaces between his shoulders, (18) O Lord.
(19) His upper body is like that of a lion; (20) his limbs are large and straight;

"Your Majesty, this is a mark of a Great Man belonging to the Prince;
Your Majesty, the Prince has the voice of Brahmā,
speaking as sweetly as the kalaviṅka bird, with a resonance like the sound of a drum."
"Your Majesty, this is a mark of a great man belonging to the prince:
(29) the prince has deep blue eyes, (30) and eyelashes like those of a cow. (31)
(32) He has a protuberance on his head;
and between his eyebrows there is a tuft of hair, white as a conch shell, which curls to the right.
O Lord, this is a mark of a Great Man belonging to the Prince, a Great Man.
"Your Majesty, these are those marks of a Great Man belonging to the Prince,
endowed with which there are only two possible destinies and no other."
As before, up until his fame resounded throughout the world: "If the prince does not go forth into homelessness, he will become a universal monarch (cakravartin).
[The following concerns] the beauty and other qualities of the Bodhisattva.
It is indeed the nature of things that the mother who gave birth to the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni passed away seven days after his birth;
immediately upon her passing, she was reborn in the sublime realm of the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
It is indeed the nature of things that the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni is handsome, beautiful to behold, and inspiring.
Having transcended human appearance yet not having attained divine appearance,
even now both men and women, gazing upon him, do not reach satiety;
they obtain joy.
Just as a golden ornament made of Jāmbūnada gold, polished by a smith and placed upon a white woolen cloth, shines, glows, and radiates intensely;
even so, the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni was handsome, beautiful to behold, and serene, surpassing human complexion yet not having fully attained divine complexion.
It is indeed the nature of things that the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni was dear and pleasing to the great multitude of people.
Even now, he passes his shoulder against the shoulder of the great multitude,
just as an autumnal lotus is dear and pleasing to a great multitude of people.
Now even the great body of people is warding off hand with hand;
thus, as before,
is the intermediate summary verse:
And the park is named Animisavipākadharma, Valgusvara, and Paṇḍita.
It is indeed the nature of things that as soon as he is born, the Bodhisattva does not blink;
beholding forms, he does not blink,
just like the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three.

It is indeed the nature of things that as soon as he is born, the Bodhisattva is endowed with a divine eye produced by the ripening of his former karma, by which he sees for a league in all directions, both by day and by night.
It is indeed the nature of things that as soon as he is born, the Bodhisattva possesses a voice that is lovely, sweet, and pleasing;
just like the Himalayan bird, which has a voice that is lovely, sweet, and pleasing.
In the same way, as soon as he was born, the Bodhisattva possessed a lovely voice, a sweet voice, and a pleasing voice.
It is indeed the natural law that as soon as he was born, the Bodhisattva was wise, discerning, and intelligent, endowed with analytical wisdom like a master of the scriptures;
even now, sitting in the council hall for the affairs of King Śuddhodana, he penetrates with his wisdom the profound meaning of words and syllables.
Upon the arrival of Asita and Nālada,
Nālada then said:
"Preceptor, the Bodhisattva has been brought into Kapilavastu."
And the three names were established;
"Now let us go to see the Bodhisattva," he said. He replied:
"We shall do so";
they set out,
but through the power of the Bodhisattva, they were deprived of their supernatural faculties.
Having entered the city of Kapilavastu on foot, they arrived at the gate of King Śuddhodana’s palace; then the sage Asita addressed the doorkeeper:
"Go, my good man, go to King Śuddhodana and say:"
"The seer Asita stands at the gate,
desiring to see the Lord";

It was reported to the king;
the king said, "Let him enter; who would stop you, O Asita?"
He entered;
he was honored by King Śuddhodana with hospitality, including water for the feet and an offering of honor, and having been offered a seat, he sat down.
After King Śuddhodana had greeted him with friendly conversation, he addressed him:
"Great Seer, what is the purpose of your visit?
He replied,
"Great King, we have come here to see your son."
"To see the Sage Vināyaka, the eldest in the world;
if it is so, wait for just a moment until the prince who is asleep awakens."
He said, "I see him while he is still asleep; do so.
He looked.
As long as the Bodhisattva is unblinking,
he beholds forms without blinking;
he then utters this verse:
"Like noble horses that do not sleep through the middle of the night,
sleep does not remain long in the eyes of those who have important tasks to perform.
Then, the Bodhisattva, having been born at that very moment, was taken by his nurse into her arms and presented to the seer.
The seer Asita received him with both hands;
having gazed at him for a moment, he said:
"Your Majesty, has the prince been shown to the brahmins, the diviners, and the interpreters?"
The king said, "He has been shown; what was predicted by them?
[They replied,] "He will become a universal monarch (cakravartin)."
As before, up until his fame was proclaimed throughout the world;
then the seer Asita, having seen the Bodhisattva, spoke this verse:
"The intellect of the logicians has fallen away, O King."
At the end of the age, there shall indeed be no universal monarch;
rather, he, having conquered all faults, will become a Buddha, a treasury of the supreme Dharma of merit.
With unmanifest characteristics, a lord of men becomes the sovereign ruler of the four continents;
with clearly manifest characteristics, he becomes a Lord of Sages.

"Having realized, 'He is the Perfectly Awakened One, the supreme among men, the Turner of the Wheel of Dharma,' he began to examine the extent of his own lifespan up until the time of the Bodhisattva’s full awakening;
he saw that the Bodhisattva, at twenty-nine years of age, would go forth from the household life."
He will practice austerities for six years;
thereafter he will attain the deathless;
yet he perceives his own death occurring even before that.
He stood there with his eyes clouded by tears;
King Śuddhodana, seeing this, his mind filled with terror, spoke this verse:
"Indeed, both men and women, upon beholding him..."
They do not reach satiety; they obtain joy upon seeing him here, who brings delight with his auspicious limbs.
Why, then, is the face of the Great Seer covered in tears?
I have no fear of anything, nor has the end of my life approached;
therefore, please tell me this quickly.
I am shaken by the falling of your tears.
The seer Asita also spoke this verse concerning him:
"Even if a fierce rain of thunderbolts were to be released from the sky and fall upon him..."
Not even all the bodies of the Great Sage combined would be capable of shaking even a single one of them.
Great fires driven by the force of the wind, sharp and most dreadful weapons,
virulent poison, and fierce, venomous serpents.
If they fall upon the prince, they would perish in an instant.
The giver of fearlessness to those afflicted by fear,
the ground of magnanimity, dwelling in compassion—
he destroys the fear of the entire world.
O lord of men, from what could fear arise for him?
The inhabitants of the heavens and others, including Brahmā, constantly provide protection for me,
who am devoted to the Dharma— the most excellent being in the world among those devoted to the Dharma.
O Lord of Men, from what source could fear arise for him?
But beholding my own misfortune, O King, I weep because I find no peace;
for this is that very treasury of the Dharma of the Supreme Being.
I, who am about to die, having failed to accomplish my purpose.
Blessed and meritorious are those who shall hear the Dharma of this peerless one, the Dharma from the best of speakers, and who have passed beyond all feverish distress.
And having heard it, they shall attain supreme peace.
Asita’s Departure:
The seer Asita, his mental continuum distressed, reflected:
"By the power of the Bodhisattva, I have fallen away from my supernatural powers."
Thinking, "If I go on foot,
the great multitude of people and the king will suspect me," he said:
"Your Majesty, for a long time he has harbored this aspiration: 'Oh,
may the ascetic Asita enter Kapilavastu on foot alone!'"
Thus, having entered Kapilavastu on foot,
I shall now depart on foot as well; you, therefore, should have the road beautified.
King Śuddhodana gave this command to his ministers:
"Go, sirs, and cause the city to be adorned and the road to be decorated. Let a proclamation be made by the ringing of bells at the thoroughfares, streets, crossroads, and junctions:
'The seer Asita is departing from the city of Kapilavastu on foot.'"
"Whatever task you have to perform or whatever duty must be done, do that.
Having thus promised the king, "So be it," the ministers cleared the city of Kapilavastu of pebbles and gravel.
Sprinkled with sandalwood water, hung with fragrant incense burners, and draped with clusters of garlands of fresh sprouts,
with banners and flags raised high;
a proclamation was made by the sounding of bells at the thoroughfares, streets, crossroads, and junctions:
"Listen, you Śākyas of Kapilavastu! The seer Asita is departing from the city of Kapilavastu;
whatever task or duty you have, perform it!
Then that man of afflicted intellect, having been honored by King Śuddhodana, who was surrounded by a host of ministers and many others...
Followed by the brahmins and householders of Kapilavastu, he departed from Kapilavastu through the very center of the city with supreme magnificence;
having sent the king back, he set out to travel wherever he pleased and in due course reached Mount Kiṣkindha.
Having mounted it, he wandered here and there, and while searching for a place according to his intention, he sat down in a certain spot; then,
having dispelled the fatigue of the journey, he produced the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and manifested supernormal power (ṛddhi).
Then, at another time, the seer Asita became ill;
he was attended with medicines consisting of roots, fragrances, leaves, flowers, and fruits, yet even so, he continued to decline.
Then Nālada, having discerned his physical condition, said to him:
"Preceptor, whatever we have become as renunciants, all that is for the sake of the Deathless, seeking the Deathless.
If the Preceptor has realized the Deathless, please share that Deathless with us."
He said:
"Young man, whatever I have gone forth to do, all that is for the sake of the Deathless, seeking the Deathless;
yet I have not attained the Deathless."
Moreover, this prince who has been born among the Śākyas will attain the deathless;
he will satisfy the world with the deathless.
Go forth into homelessness in his presence.
And having gone forth, he should not speak of birth, nor of lineage, nor of being a young brahmin student; rather, having gone forth, he should practice the holy life alone.
"Effort must be made for the attainment of the deathless;
then you will possess the deathless.
Having understood this, he spoke this verse.
Seek only those who have come before; thus you shall find the Tathāgata, for the sight of illustrious, perfectly awakened Buddhas is difficult to obtain.
Having said this:
"All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall; all unions end in separation; for life ends in death. (SBV I 57)
Having said this, he was joined with the law of time; then Nālada, having performed the funeral rites for his body,
went to Vārāṇasī and settled there.
There he taught the Vedic mantras to five hundred young Brahmins;
Nālada was his family name (gotra),
and thus the designation "Kātyāyana" came to be applied to him.

He will approach the Blessed One who has attained perfect awakening; the Blessed One, having awakened him through the instruction of Kātyāyana, will lead him out from the wilderness of saṃsāra and establish him in the ultimate, final security of nirvāṇa;
his name shall be Mahākātyāyana, Mahākātyāyana.
Siddhārtha, the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni, possessing the strength of a thousand nāgas, at another time, while in the care of his nurse, ate rice-meat porridge from a golden bowl;
he ate a great quantity.
Thinking that he would not remain [in the womb], the nurse began to pull him out,
but she was unable to extract him; she then informed King Śuddhodana.
The king, together with his harem, began to pull it out,
but he too was unable to do so.
Thereupon, the king employed his ministers and the multitude of people from Kapilavastu.
They were not able to pull it loose either;
then five hundred elephants were harnessed to it.
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"They will disparage my strength, saying 'Not me!';
what if I were to support the bowl with my curved finger?
Thinking thus, he drew the golden bowl toward him with his curved finger.
Those five hundred [oxen] were pulled backward,
but they did not pull the golden vessel;
King Śuddhodana reflected:
The Bodhisattva drew five hundred elephants with his left hand;
he will certainly draw a thousand elephants with both hands.
Therefore, let the name of the prince be "He of the Strength of a Thousand Elephants."
The intermediate summary:
The children, the playthings, the magic spell, and the palace; the swan, the battle, the excellent army, and the battle with the women of the inner apartments. (SBV I 58)
Regarding the deeds of Siddhārtha:

It is the very nature of things that the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, was presented to the writing master Kṛmivarman in order to learn the art of writing; the writing master Kṛmivarman wrote out a script for the Bodhisattva and gave it to him.
The Bodhisattva said, "I know this one";
then he [asked for] the second and the third,
and so on, until five hundred scripts had been written and given.
The Bodhisattva said: "I know even this; tell me another.
Kṛmivarman said:
"There are only this many scripts current in the world; I know no others," he said.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva himself wrote a script and gave it to Kṛmivarman.
And he was asked, "Tell me, what is the name of this script?
He replied, "I do not know.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Because two appear in the world, this script is known:
either that of a Bodhisattva or that of a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakravartin).
Then, Brahmā, standing in the vault of the sky, declared:
"It is even so, Kṛmivarman, as the Bodhisattva says:
this script is known to appear only upon the manifestation of two beings in the world— the Bodhisattva or a universal monarch (cakravartin)."
This script was read by the Bodhisattva with a Brahma-voice,
and Brahmā, standing in the expanse of the sky, gave his testimony;
thus it became known by the name "Brāhmī script, Brāhmī script."

When the Bodhisattva had reached the further shore of writing, he was instructed in the training on the neck of an elephant by his maternal uncle, the Bodhisattva named Bhāddāli; and by Sahadeva, a master of archery,
he was begun to be trained in cutting with a retinue of five hundred.
Bhaddāli was addressed by Sahadeva: "A compassionate bodhisattva must train in all the precepts."
The other princes were thus [innocent],
but this Devadatta was a man of cruel deeds; his vital organs must not be pierced, lest he should bring destruction upon the entire world.
When a bodhisattva has trained in all the precepts and has become accomplished in the five fields,
including long-distance shooting;
In hitting by sound, in hitting vital points,
and in hitting without missing the mark.

And when Dṛḍhaprahārin had been struck down, a report spread throughout the vicinity: "A prince has been born among the Śākyas," and so on, until it was proclaimed that his fame resounded throughout the world.
Now at that time, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī obtained an elephant endowed with all the auspicious marks.
They reflected:
"The son of King Śuddhodana was prophesied by the diviners, saying, 'He will become a universal monarch (cakravartin).
It is through his majesty that this precious elephant has appeared."
"It has been born! Let us go and present it to him.
Having adorned him with elephant ornaments, they set out with great magnificence and in due course reached Kapilavastu;
having stationed the elephant at the gate of the royal palace, they stood there.
By chance, Devadatta, a man of cruel deeds, came out;
he saw that elephant adorned with such ornaments,
whereupon a great envy arose within him.
Born of envy and jealousy, he asked, "Whose elephant is this?
They replied,
"The Śākyamuni prince has been prophesied by the diviners as a universal monarch (cakravartin)."
"This elephant-treasure has been sent by the Vaiśālī assembly.
Devadatta, becoming exceedingly incensed, said:
"As long as he is not a universal monarch (cakravartin), you have brought this elephant-treasure to him! Having said this, he deprived that elephant of its life with a blow of his palm.
When Nanda was passing by that place,
he saw him and asked:
"Sirs, who has killed this fine elephant? They replied,
"By Devadatta."
He reflected:
"Surely Devadatta has tested his strength here;
what if we too were to test our strength here?"
Having done so, he took it by the tail and placed it in a secluded spot, thinking, "Lest it should cause a foul odor";
meanwhile, the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni went out and saw it.
He asked,
"Where did this elephant come from? They explained to him exactly what had happened.
"By whom was he killed?
"By Devadatta.
"This is not good."
"Hospitality must be shown to guests.
In which place was he killed? In this very place. By whom was he brought here?"
Nanda reflected:

"Surely they have sought to test my strength here; what if I were also to test my strength here? Having realized this, he seized [the elephant] by the tail and hurled it over the wall, across seven walls.
Having leaped over the seven moats, he fell;
by his falling, a pit was made,
[which became known as] "Hastigarta, Hastigarta."
It became known as Saṃjñā;
there, faithful brahmins and householders established a shrine (caitya), which even today is venerated by monks who pay homage to shrines. And regarding this, it is said:
That lordly elephant who was killed by Devadatta and led away by Nanda for seven steps was [caught] far off by the Bodhisattva with his trunk.
Like a clod of earth thrown outside into the atmosphere. Thus it is said.
The princes said, "Let us go; let us perform the ritual cutting. Having departed, Śākyamuni Bodhisattva, having heard this, went out with a retinue of fifty to perform the ritual cutting.
The princes were performing a "rice-ear" cutting exercise;
as they cut them, the ears fell down one after another.
The Bodhisattva performed an "āḍhaka-measure" cutting exercise.
Severed by him, they did not fall;
they remained exactly as they were.
The princes said:
"Gentlemen, it is said that the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni is powerful and accomplished in the five fields of knowledge;
yet here he does not even know how to perform a simple cutting."
Nor is he stronger than we;
for while all the trees cut down by us have fallen,
those cut down by him remain standing just as they were.
Then, a certain deity who was devoted to the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni thought to herself:
"These Śākyas, not knowing the power of the Bodhisattva, will treat him with contempt for his skill in the arts and will disparage his strength."
"Therefore, a strategic arrangement must be made.
She released such a wind that all those trees fell down, making a rattling sound.
Seeing this, the Śākyas were struck with great amazement;
they began to practice archery,
and their targets there were made of iron.
Seven bronze palm-tree pillars and a drum (or gong) were installed;
Devadatta, having fixed his footing, discharged an iron arrow;
one palm tree was split,
and two by Nanda.
The Bodhisattva shot an iron arrow;
it pierced seven palm trees, a drum, and a gong,
and that iron arrow entered the underworld (pātāla).
He was pulled out by the nāgas;
sweet water appeared,
and a great multitude of people began to drink it.
Faithful brahmin householders established a caitya there;
even today, monks who pay homage to caityas continue to worship it. (SBV I 61) [This concludes] Śuddhodana’s efforts.
Regarding SBV I 61.18–63.3, cf. also GBM 10.3348–3349:
"The princes, mounted on chariots, were entering Kapilavastu; and the fortune-tellers were departing from the city."
As the young Śākyamuni was entering while mounted on a chariot, they prophesied:
"If he does not go forth into homelessness within twelve years, he will certainly become a universal monarch (cakravartin)."
King Śuddhodana heard that the prince had been prophesied by the diviners;
having heard this, filled once more with joy and gladness, he assembled the Śākyas and said:
"Gentlemen, I have heard that the prince has been prophesied by the diviners: if he does not go forth into the religious life within twelve years,"
"It is certain that he will become a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Therefore, if the prince does not go forth into homelessness within twelve years, he will become a universal monarch;
we, wandering through the expanse of the sky, shall travel across the four continents."
"Let him be settled in marriage," they said;
the ministers replied,
"Your Majesty, the prince has no desire for sensual pleasures."
King Śuddhodana said:
"Let us show all the maidens to the prince; whichever one he finds pleasing shall [be his bride]."
"We shall cause her to enter the inner apartments";
others said,
"Your Majesty, Prince Dānābhiruci [is devoted to giving]."
"Let ornaments for the maidens be provided; we shall admit into the inner apartments whichever one produces his satisfaction. King Śuddhodana replied, "Let it be done so."
The ministers presented a heap of various kinds of ornaments, variegated with jewels.

Then King Śuddhodana, having caused the beautification of the palace and the city, had a lion throne prepared in a pavilion at an auspicious constellation, lunar day, and moment, and seated the young Śākyamuni upon it.
And near the lion throne, a heap of various and wonderful ornaments was arranged.
The ministers and the rest of the principal citizens of Kapilavastu, who were highly esteemed by the populace, entered;
then all the maidens were ushered in, adorned with dress, ornaments, and finery appropriate to their respective family fortunes;
and because the Bodhisattva delighted in giving, he bestowed ornaments upon them.
Yaśodharā was the daughter of the Śākya Daṇḍapāṇi; she was endowed with beauty, youth, and the prime of her age. (For SBV I 61.18–63.3, cf. also GBM 10.3348–3349)
The Śākya Daṇḍapāṇi said,
"Daughter, the Bodhisattva is giving away his ornaments.
She replied:
"Father, do we have no ornaments?
"Daughter, it is not that we have none; however, he chooses whichever maiden is pleasing to the Bodhisattva."
"Father, whether he chooses me or not, he alone shall be my husband.
Daughter, if this is so, you must go by all means."
As they were going,
Yaśodharā— of youthful age, elegantly attired,
and captivating the minds and eyes of the great multitude, appearing like a celestial maiden among all those girls— entered with a peaceful deportment and stood before the Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva gave her all his ornaments; only his finger-ring remained,
and the Bodhisattva showed it to her.
Then, having ascended the steps of the lion throne by her, she drew [the hand] herself from the hand of the Bodhisattva—she who had been led forward through the long duration of beginningless time.
The ministers and the body of people from Kapilavastu, esteemed as leaders, said: "Sirs, among all maidens, this one is the most distinguished."
"She is able to capture the prince's heart;
let her be brought in.
Thereupon, King Śuddhodana had Yaśodharā, accompanied by a retinue of twenty thousand maidens, enter the inner apartments of Prince Śākyamuni.
The *Sārakalyāṇī* Tree,
the Goose, and Devadatta’s First Quarrel For SBV I 61.18–63.3, cf. also GBM 10.3348–3349.
It is indeed the nature of things that when the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, arise in the world, then a tree named Sārakalyāṇī is born;
it grows a hundred cubits in a single day,
and as long as the sun has not yet risen, it can even be cut with a fingernail.
But when the sun has risen, he cannot be cut even by a weapon;
he cannot be burned even by fire;
[between] Kapilavastu and Devadṛṣa—(SBV I 63).
In this interval there was a river named Rohaka;
he was born on its bank,
and from time to time, as the water rose, its root was washed away.
The dam, having fallen by the force of the wind, remained blocking the river;
consequently, the region of King Suprabuddha was being destroyed by a lack of water,
while that of Śuddhodana was being destroyed by an excess of water.
Suprabuddha sent word to King Śuddhodana:
"A most auspicious tree has fallen;
it remains standing, blocking the Rohaka River."
"The princes are heard to be powerful;
therefore, you ought to send them.
King Śuddhodana replied:
"I do not give orders to the princes," [the king replied].
Chanda said,
"Let the King simply grant his permission."
"I shall act in such a way that no command is given to the princes,
yet they go of their own accord";
King Śuddhodana consented.
On the bank of the river Rohaka, Chandaka caused individual gardens to be laid out for each of the princes;
he then said to the princes, "Let us go to the garden," and they replied:
"Let us go"; they each mounted their chariot and went to the park;
as a swan was flying over Devadatta's park, it was struck by Devadatta with an arrow.
He fell into the Bodhisattva’s garden; the Bodhisattva took him up, removed the arrowhead,
and provided him with offerings.
He became healthy again;
Devadatta sent word to the Bodhisattva:
"This swan was previously taken by me."
"Send him away";
the Bodhisattva replied:
"From the very moment I first conceived the thought of awakening (bodhicitta),..."
"Even at that time, all sentient beings were taken into my care";
therein, Devadatta first conceived hostility toward the Bodhisattva during his final existence,
though he had done so many times in other existences.
When Suprabuddha heard that the princes had gone out to the park grounds to remove the *sārakalyāṇī* tree, he dispatched a great multitude of people;
there, a loud clamor and a great noise arose from the roar of the vast crowd.
The Bodhisattva asked: "Sirs, what is this loud noise, this great clamor, and this roar of a vast multitude of people?
Chandaka related to him exactly what had occurred.
The Bodhisattva said,
"If that is so, let us go and remove it";
the Bodhisattva then set out together with the princes.
Just as the venomous serpent emerged from its hole facing the Bodhisattva,
Udāyin cut it in two with a sharp weapon, thinking, "Lest it bite the Bodhisattva.
By that very breath [of the serpent], Udāyin was consumed and turned black.
He became known by the name Kālodāyin (Kālodayin);
then the princes set about removing the Sārakalyāṇī tree,
and Devadatta, having girded his loins, moved it slightly.
Nanda tossed it up only slightly;
however, the Bodhisattva threw it entirely into the air, where it split into two pieces.
One fragment landed on one bank of the Rohaka River.
In the second [case], the second [person] spoke; the Bodhisattva said:
"Sirs, this Sārakalyāṇī tree has a cooling fruit."
It subdues bile;
apply it by making small circular patches;
you shall provide it as an ointment for eruptive boils and pustules.

The princes, having mounted their respective chariots, set out from the park grounds toward Kapilavastu. At the entrance of the city, the Bodhisattva, while mounted upon his chariot, was prophesied by the diviners:
"If he does not go forth into the homeless life within seven days,"
"He will become a universal monarch (cakravartin). [This was said] regarding Gopikā,
the daughter of the Śākya Ghāṭāgiri.
The Bodhisattva saw her as she stood upon the upper terrace of the palace;
at the mere sight of her, he pressed down on the chariot with his big toe so that it became motionless;
then the Bodhisattva began to gaze intently at Gopikā.
The cowherd girl was also a bodhisattva;
there was an iron arrow in the hand of the bodhisattva,
and as he looked at the cowherd girl, it shattered into pieces.
Even as Gopikā gazed at the Bodhisattva, she pierced the surface of the palace floor with her big toe.
A great multitude of people saw the Bodhisattva and Gopikā looking at one another, their profound intentions having been awakened.
Having seen her, they said:
"Such a maiden as this will indeed be able to capture the heart of the Bodhisattva.
King Śuddhodana heard this report.
He then introduced her into the Bodhisattva’s inner apartments, accompanied by a retinue of twenty thousand maidens.
[The sight of an old man]
It is indeed the nature of things that when a Bodhisattva desires to go out to the pleasure gardens, he addresses his charioteer:
"Come now, charioteer, quickly prepare an excellent vehicle so that, having mounted it, I may depart for the pleasure gardens.
Then the Bodhisattva addressed the charioteer:
"Come now, charioteer, quickly prepare the auspicious vehicle so that, having mounted it, I may go to the park grounds.
"So be it, Your Majesty," the charioteer replied to the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni, and having prepared the auspicious vehicle, he approached the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni;
having approached him, he said this to the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni:
"The auspicious vehicle of the Lord is ready; may the Lord now consider it the right time.
Then the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni, having mounted the auspicious vehicle, went out to the park grounds.
The Bodhisattva Śākyamuni saw a man who was aged, old, and decrepit, hunched like a roof-rafter, leaning upon a staff, walking with his body trembling before him.
And his hair was discolored, unlike that of other men;
and having seen this, he addressed the charioteer again:
"Charioteer, who is this man? He is worn out, aged, and decrepit; he is hunched and stooped, leaning on a staff as he moves forward with a trembling body;
and his hair is not like that of other men. "This one," [the charioteer replied].
"Your Majesty,
there is one called an 'old man';
what, O charioteer, is this that is called an 'old man'?"
"Your Majesty, this man must die before long;
he is what is called 'old. I too, charioteer, am subject to the nature of old age."
"And has he not transcended the nature of old age?
Even a god is subject to old age and has not transcended the nature of old age;
therefore, charioteer, turn back."
"Go to the inner apartments;
once I have entered the inner apartments, I shall consider this matter,
for it seems I have not yet transcended old age."
The charioteer turned the chariot back;
he went straight to the inner apartments. There, perhaps, the Śākyamuni Bodhisattva was present within the midst of the inner apartments.
Then, being dissatisfied, he meditated on compassion, thinking, "Alas, I have not yet transcended old age. And regarding this, he said:
"Indeed, having seen a man whose youth has passed away..."
"Seeing one who is decrepit, hunched, gray-haired, and holding a staff, he then meditates with compassion, being dissatisfied, thinking:
'Alas, I too have not transcended old age. Thus [it is said].
Then King Śuddhodana addressed the charioteer:
"Charioteer, did the prince go out to the park with a joyful heart, or did he take pleasure in the park?
"No, Your Majesty. And for what reason?"
O Lord, as the prince was going out to the park grounds, he saw a man who was aged, old, and decrepit; he was hunched, with a back curved like a rafter, walking while leaning on a staff,
his body trembling before him, and his hair discolored.
It was not as it is for other men;
and having seen me, he spoke this:
"Charioteer, who is this man? He is aged, old, advanced in years, hunchbacked, bent like a roof-rafter, and walking with his body trembling before him while leaning upon a staff."
"And his hair is discolored, unlike that of other men";
thus I speak of him, saying:
"O Lord, this one is called 'the aged'."
He spoke thus:
"Charioteer, who is this that is called 'old'?
To him I said this: "O Deva, by this man—"
"A man must soon die;
he is what is called 'old age'. He said this:
"O charioteer, I too am subject to the nature of old age."
And since he has not transcended the nature of aging,
I say this to him:
"Even a god is subject to aging."
"And he has not transcended the nature of old age. He spoke thus:
"In that case, charioteer, turn the chariot back;
go to the inner apartments alone."
While I was in the midst of the inner apartments, I was reflecting on this matter:
"Alas, I have not transcended old age!"
This very prince, having entered the midst of the inner apartments,
was then distressed and meditated with compassion, thinking: "Alas, I have indeed not transcended old age."
Then this thought occurred to King Śuddhodana:
"May it not be that the words of those brahmins— the interpreters of omens and the prognosticators— prove to be true and come to pass."
"Lest the prince, having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes, go forth from the home to the homeless life out of perfect faith;
what if I were now to bestow upon the prince the five strands of sensual pleasure with even greater abundance, so that, being delighted by them, he might not go forth?"

Then King Śuddhodana provided the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni with the five strands of sensual pleasure in even greater measure, thinking, "Perhaps, being thus delighted, he will not go forth. And regarding this, it is said: "For having heard these words of the one who seeks to restrain him..."
Śuddhodana was the father of Śākyamuni;
at that time, he offered him the five strands of sensual pleasure,
thinking, "Even though he may take further delight in them, he will not abandon me."
The sight of a sick man:
It is the nature of things that when a Bodhisattva desires to go out to the park grounds, he addresses his charioteer: "Well then, charioteer, quickly harness a fine carriage."
"Whereupon I shall mount and go forth to the park grounds";
then the Bodhisattva addressed the charioteer: "Now then, charioteer, quickly harness the noble vehicle."
"Whereupon I shall mount and go forth to the park grounds.
"Very well, O Lord," the charioteer replied to the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni, and having quickly harnessed the noble vehicle, he approached the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni;
having approached, he spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni:
"The auspicious vehicle of the Lord is ready;
now, O Lord, let the Lord do as he deems timely.
Then Śākyamuni, having mounted the auspicious vehicle, went out to the park grounds.

The Bodhisattva Śākyamuni saw a man who was extremely pale, emaciated, weak, with impaired faculties, and not fit to be looked upon by the eyes of many people. Having seen him, he addressed his charioteer:
"Charioteer, who is this man, so extremely pale, emaciated, weak, with impaired faculties, and not fit to be looked upon by the eyes of many people?"
"Your Majesty, this one is called 'afflicted. O charioteer, who is this one called 'afflicted'?
"Your Majesty, it is possible that this man will die from this very affliction."
"This is what is called being afflicted by disease;
am I also, O charioteer, subject to the nature of disease and not exempt from that state of being subject to disease?
Your Majesty too is subject to the nature of disease and not exempt from that state of being subject to disease."
"In that case, charioteer, turn the chariot back;
go to the inner apartments themselves, so that I, having entered the midst of the inner apartments, may reflect upon this matter."
Thinking, "I have indeed not transcended disease," the charioteer turns the chariot back;
he goes straight to the inner apartments.
In that regard, while the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni was in the midst of the inner apartments,
he became despondent and meditated with compassion, thinking, "Alas, I have not transcended disease. And regarding this, it is said:
Having seen here a man afflicted by disease, his form emaciated, pale, and lacking self-control,
he then becomes despondent and meditates with compassion.
"I have indeed not yet transcended disease," he said.
Then King Śuddhodana addressed the charioteer: "Charioteer, was the prince joyful and delighted when he went out to the park grounds, or did he take pleasure in the park?"
"No, O King. For what reason?
While going out to the park grounds, O King, the prince saw a man who was extremely pale, emaciated, weak, withered, and whose faculties were impaired."
"But he should not be kept so that many people may see him with their eyes.
And having seen him, he addressed me again:
"Charioteer, who is this man—so pale, yellowish-pale, emaciated, weak, withered, his faculties impaired, and not fit to be looked upon by the eyes of many people?"
I said this to him: "Sire, this one is called 'afflicted'. He replied: "Who is this, charioteer, who is called 'afflicted'?"
To him I say this:
"Your Majesty, it is possible that this man must die from this very affliction;
he, Your Majesty, is what is called 'one who is diseased'. He replied as follows:
"Charioteer, am I also subject to illness, not having transcended the nature of illness?
To him I say this:
"Your Majesty is also subject to illness, not having transcended the nature of illness. He says this:
"In that case, charioteer, turn the chariot back;
go to the inner apartments themselves, so that I, having entered the midst of the inner apartments, may reflect upon this matter."
"I am indeed not beyond illness";
thus, O King, this prince, having entered the midst of the inner apartments, broods with sorrow, thinking: "I am indeed not beyond illness."
Then this thought occurred to King Śuddhodana:
"May the words of those brahmins—the interpreters of omens and the prognosticators—not come true;
may it not be that the prince, having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes, will out of perfect faith go forth from the home to the homeless life."
"What if I were to provide the prince with an even greater abundance of the five strands of sensual pleasure?
Perhaps, being thus delighted, he will not go forth.

Then King Śuddhodana provided the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni with an even greater abundance of the five strands of sensual pleasure, thinking, "Perhaps, being thus delighted, he will not go forth. And regarding this, it is said:
Then he gave him the five strands of sensual pleasure: forms, sounds, and likewise fragrances, and indeed excellent, delightful objects of touch.
"Furthermore, even if he is delighted, may he not abandon me."

Regarding the dharma-nature of the sight of a dead man: indeed, when the Bodhisattva desired to go out to the pleasure grove, he addressed his charioteer: "Now then, charioteer, quickly prepare a fine carriage."
"Whereupon I shall mount and go forth to the park grounds";
thereupon the Bodhisattva addressed the charioteer: "Now then, charioteer, quickly harness a fine carriage."
"Whereupon I may mount and go to the park grounds.
"So be it, Your Majesty," the charioteer replied to the Śākya-muni Bodhisattva. Having quickly harnessed the noble vehicle, he approached the Śākya-muni Bodhisattva;
having approached him, he said this to the Śākya-muni Bodhisattva:
"It is fitting for the Lord’s auspicious vehicle, since the Lord now deems it the right time.
Then the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni, having mounted the auspicious vehicle, went out to the pleasure grove.
As he was departing for the pleasure grove, the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni saw a canopy spread out with cloths of various colors.
He saw the palanquin being carried,
a torch being led before him,
and a great multitude of people walking ahead.
Seeing them followed from behind by women with disheveled hair who were weeping,
he addressed the charioteer once more:
"What is this, charioteer, that a canopy of cloth is spread out with garments of various colors?"
Why is a palanquin being carried,
why is a torch being led in front,
and why is a great multitude of people walking ahead?
"And why are these women, with disheveled hair and weeping, following closely behind?
"Your Majesty, this one is said to be 'dead'.
"Charioteer, what is this that is called 'dead'?"
"Your Majesty, this man shall no longer behold his beloved mother and father, nor his wife and children, nor his female and male slaves, laborers, and servants."
They too shall no longer see him;
this, O King, is what is called "dead.
Am I also, O charioteer, subject to death and not beyond the nature of mortality?
Even a god is subject to death and has not transcended the nature of mortality; he spoke thus: "In that case, charioteer, turn back the chariot;
go to the inner apartments, so that I—"
"Having gone into the midst of the inner apartments, I shall reflect on this matter: 'I am indeed not exempt from death. The charioteer then turned the chariot back.
He went straight to the inner apartments;

there, the Śākyamuni Bodhisattva, having entered the midst of the inner apartments, was dejected and meditated with compassion, thinking, "Alas, I have not transcended death. And regarding this, it is said:
Seeing a man whose mind had departed, dead, unconscious, and whose life had reached its end,
he was then distressed and meditated with compassion.
"I have indeed not transcended death," he thought.
Then King Śuddhodana addressed the charioteer:
"How was it, charioteer, did the prince go out to the park with a joyful mind, or did he take delight in the park?
"No, Your Majesty. And for what reason?"
O Lord, as the prince was going out to the park grounds, he saw a canopy of cloth spread out with garments of various colors,
a palanquin being taken up,
and a torch being carried before him.
Seeing a great multitude of people walking ahead and women with disheveled hair weeping and following behind,
he addressed me again:
"Charioteer, what is this? Why is a canopy of cloth spread out with garments of various colors? Why has a palanquin been prepared? And why is a torch being carried before us?"
"Why is a great multitude of people walking ahead,
and why are noble women with disheveled hair, weeping, following closely behind?
To him, I speak thus:
"This, O Lord, is what is called 'dead'";
he said this:
"Who is this, charioteer, that is called 'dead'?"
To him I spoke thus:
"O King, this man shall no longer see his beloved parents, nor his wife and children."
"There will be no female or male slaves, laborers, or servants;
they too shall not see him again.
O King, he is what is called 'dead'. He spoke thus:
"O charioteer, am I also subject to death? Am I not beyond the nature of mortality?
To him, I speak thus:
"Even a god is subject to death and has not transcended the nature of mortality";
he spoke thus:
"In that case, charioteer, turn the chariot back."
"Go back to the inner apartments; there, having entered the midst of the harem, I shall contemplate this matter:
that indeed I have not transcended death."
This very prince, having entered the midst of the inner apartments,
was then distressed and meditated with compassion, thinking: "Alas, I have not yet transcended death."
Then this thought occurred to King Śuddhodana:
"May the words of those brahmins—the soothsayers and prognosticators—not come true;
may it not be that the prince, having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes, shall out of perfect faith go forth from the home into the homeless state."
"What if I were to provide the prince with an even greater abundance of the five strands of sensual pleasure?
Perhaps, being thus delighted, he will not go forth.
Then King Śuddhodana bestowed the five strands of sensual pleasure upon the Bodhisattva, the Śākya-muni.

"Perhaps one who delights in these [pleasures] would not go forth into homelessness"; and regarding this, it was said there in that most excellent, glorious, and beautiful city by the God beyond gods, the Youthful One, who is equal [to all]:
For he delights in the five strands of sensual pleasure, like the thousand-eyed Indra in the Nandana grove.
Upon seeing the mendicant, it then occurred to the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm:
"Although Bodhisattvas possess the power of causes, nevertheless, the provision of conditions [is required]."

It must be done, because the power of the cause depends upon the power of the conditions; by them, a man was created— shaven-headed, clothed in saffron robes, with a bowl in his hand, entering from house to house among the families.

It is indeed the nature of things that when a bodhisattva desires to go out to the pleasure groves, he addresses his charioteer: "Now then, charioteer, quickly harness a fine vehicle so that, having mounted it, I may go to the pleasure groves."
"I shall go forth.
Then the Bodhisattva addressed the charioteer: "Well then, charioteer, quickly prepare a fine vehicle so that, having mounted it, I may proceed to the park grounds."
"I am going out.
"Very well, Your Majesty," the charioteer replied to the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni, and having quickly harnessed the noble vehicle, he approached the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni.
Having approached, he said this to the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni:
"It is fitting for the Lord’s auspicious vehicle, if the Lord deems it now the right time.
Then the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni, having mounted the auspicious vehicle, went out to the park grounds.
There the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni saw a man with a shaven head, clothed in saffron-colored robes, with a bowl in his hand, approaching house after house from family to family.
And having seen him, he addressed the charioteer again:
"Charioteer, who is this man with a shaven head and a bowl in his hand, who goes from house to house among the families? And his garments are discolored."
"Is it not as with others?
"This one, Your Majesty, is called a renunciant.
"Who is this, charioteer, who is called a renunciant?"

"Your Majesty, this renunciant, having understood that he possesses excellent self-control, excellent restraint, excellent conduct for the sake of the goal, excellent conduct in virtue, and excellent conduct in goodness, has shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron robes, and out of right faith gone forth from the home to the homeless life."
"This is indeed one who has gone forth, O Lord;
therefore, charioteer, drive the chariot toward where this renunciant is.
"As you command, Your Majesty," the charioteer replied to the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni, and drove the chariot toward where that renunciant was.
Then the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni said this to that renunciant:
"Why, O man, do you go from house to house with a shaven head and a bowl in hand?
And why are your garments discolored, unlike those of others?"
He spoke thus: "I am, young man, one who is called 'one who has gone forth.
In what way, good sir, are you called 'one who has gone forth'?
"I am, young man, one who is well-restrained, well-disciplined, one who practices for the sake of the goal, and one who practices for the sake of the Dharma."

"Excellent is your practice of virtue, excellent is your practice of goodness," [he said]. Having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes, he has rightly gone forth from the home to the homeless life out of faith;
thus am I called "one who has gone forth. Excellent, O man, is your self-restraint, excellent is your discipline, excellent is your pursuit of the goal, and excellent is your practice of the Dharma.

"Excellent is his practice of virtue; excellent is his practice of goodness," [they said]. Then, having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes, he went forth from the home to the homeless life with perfect faith.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni addressed his charioteer:
"In that case, charioteer, turn the chariot back;
go to the inner apartments themselves,
so that I, having entered the midst of the inner apartments, may reflect upon this matter."
The charioteer turns the chariot back;
he goes straight to the inner apartments.

Thereupon, while staying in the midst of his harem, the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni reflected on this matter: "O, would that I might shave off my hair and beard, don saffron robes, and with perfect faith go forth from the home to the homeless life!
Then King Śuddhodana addressed the charioteer:
"Charioteer, was the prince joyful in mind as he went out to the park grounds, or did he take delight in the park?
"No, Your Majesty. And why is that?

While going out to the park grounds, Your Majesty, the prince saw a man with a shaven head, clad in saffron-colored robes, with a bowl in his hand, approaching house after house from family to family."
And having seen him, he addressed me again:
"Charioteer, this shaven-headed man with a bowl in his hand goes from house to house among the families;
and his garments are discolored, unlike those of others."
To him I spoke thus: "Your Majesty, this one is called a renunciant. He replied:
"Who is this, charioteer, who is called a renunciant?
To him I spoke thus: "Your Majesty, this is a renunciant who is well-restrained, well-disciplined, and well-practiced in the pursuit of the goal."

"Practicing the conduct of the virtuous, practicing the conduct of the wholesome, practicing the conduct of the auspicious," having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes, he has rightly gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith;
O King, such a person is called a "renunciant. He spoke thus:
"In that case, charioteer, drive the chariot to where that renunciant is.
"As you command, Your Majesty," the charioteer replied to the Śākya-muni Bodhisattva and drove the chariot toward where that renunciant was.
Then the Śākya-muni Bodhisattva said this to that renunciant:
"Why, O man, do you go from house to house with shaven head and bowl in hand? And why are your garments discolored,
unlike those of other men?"
He spoke thus: "I am,
O youth,
one who is called a renunciant."
The Bodhisattva asked: "How is it, O man, that you are called 'one who has gone forth'? He replied:
"O Prince, I am one who is well-restrained, well-disciplined, and well-practiced in the pursuit of the goal."
"Practicing the Dharma well,

practicing what is wholesome well, and practicing what is virtuous well," having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes, he went forth from the home to the homeless life with perfect faith;
thus am I known as one who has gone forth.

The Bodhisattva said: "Excellent, O man! Excellent is your self-control, excellent is your restraint, excellent is your practice for the sake of the goal (or: excellent is your practice of the Dharma)."

"He is one whose conduct is virtuous and good, whose conduct is excellent and auspicious," [the people said], "having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes, he has gone forth from the home to the homeless life out of perfect faith.
Then, O King, the prince addressed me:
"In that case, charioteer, turn the chariot back."
"Go back to the inner apartments; there, having entered the inner apartments, I shall consider this matter;
it was for that reason that I turned you back."
The chariot; the prince entered the inner apartments. Visit to a farming village.
The king reflected:
"May the words of those brahmins—the soothsayers and prognosticators—not prove true and come to pass;
may it not be that the prince, having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes, shall go forth from the home to the homeless life out of perfect faith."
Thinking, "What if I were to send the prince to Kārṣagrāmaka? Perhaps he might find diversion there," the Śākyan [king] addressed the prince Śākyamuni as follows:
"Come, prince, go to Kārṣagrāmaka."
"Examine the various occupations. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva, distressed by the sight of the old, the sick, and the dead, and with his mind intent upon the life of renunciation,
mounted his chariot in compliance with the words of his father, Śākya Śuddhodana, and set out for the village of Kārṣagrāmaka.
[He did this] with his body, but not with his mind;
on the way, five hundred openings of treasure-troves appeared before him,
and a voice was uttered:
"O Prince, we are your kinsmen and treasures; please accept us!
The Bodhisattva said:
"What have they done by first making such a deluded appropriation?"
"Go! We have no need for you," he said, and spoke this verse:
"Even those by whom the discourse of the Immortal was made have become, for us, nothing but talk of the dead."
We too, once dead, shall before long become mere stories for others.
They again uttered these words:
"If the prince does not accept us, we shall enter the great ocean.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Enter as you please," he said;
they entered the great ocean.
The Bodhisattva set out and saw farmers with their heads covered in dust, their hands and feet cracked, and their bodies covered in fine dust.
And he saw oxen whose bodies were wounded by goads, their backs and hips drenched in blood, their vital breaths oppressed by hunger, thirst, and exhaustion;
their hearts stifled by incessant panting,
and their wounds oozing pus and blood due to the bursting of their testicles under the pressure of the yoke.
Their vital breaths were being devoured by swarms of flies and worms;
their feet were furrowed by the yokes of plows;
and their mouths and nostrils were streaming with saliva and mucus.

Seeing them crowded with gadflies, mosquitoes, snakes, and other small creatures, his mind became agitated by compassion born from the accumulation of merit over beginningless time, and he said this to the farmers:
"Sirs, whose men are you?"
They said,
"To the King. He said, "Go, sirs."
"From this day forward, you are no longer slaves, nor servants, nor bondsmen; go wherever you wish and dwell in comfort.
And the oxen were told: "Go forth, and from this day forward, eat grass with uncut tips."
"Drink the waters that are untroubled, clear, and undisturbed;
and let cool breezes blow from the four quarters."— the shadow of the rose-apple tree.
Then, with that very same sense of spiritual urgency, the Bodhisattva, having observed the royal works of his father, Śākya Śuddhodana, approached the shade of a rose-apple tree (*jambū*);
having approached, he sat down in the shade of the rose-apple tree, secluded [from sensual desires].

Having entered the first dhyāna— which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, born of seclusion, characterized by joy and bliss, and resembling the untainted— he sat there; and the multitude of people, remaining at the roots of the remaining trees, did not depart, leaving the Bodhisattva behind.
King Śuddhodana reflected: "The Bodhisattva is taking a long time;
for indeed, the time for the midday meal has already passed."
"I am going,
I shall see";
having mounted his chariot, he went to the village of Kārṣakagrāmaka.
Searching for the Bodhisattva here and there, he arrived near the Jambu tree;
at that time, when midday had passed, the shadows of the other trees were slanting toward the east and inclining toward the east.
The shadows were slanting toward the east;
yet, by the power of the Bodhisattva, the shadow of the Jambu tree did not leave the body of the Bodhisattva.
King Śuddhodana saw that at the time when midday had passed, the shadows of the other trees were sloping toward the east.
Sloping toward the east,
inclining toward the east;
[this was] for the Bodhisattva.
But through his spiritual power, the shadow of the rose-apple tree did not leave the Bodhisattva’s body;
and having seen this, it occurred to him:

The prince is possessed of great supernatural power and great majesty, in that now, at the time when midday has passed, while the shadows of other trees lean toward the east, slope toward the east, and incline toward the east,
the shadow of the rose-apple tree does not leave the body of the Bodhisattva;
then, having performed an act of supreme faith, he fell at the feet of the Bodhisattva.
He spoke this verse as the second: "O you of vast growth, O you with all-seeing eyes, I bow at your feet."
And as soon as he was born, the earth trembled,
and the shadow of the Jambu tree did not leave his body.

Then, having performed the rites for propitiation, he raised the Bodhisattva from his cross-legged posture, placed him upon a chariot, and set out for Kapilavastu through the midst of the cremation ground.
As the Bodhisattva was traveling through the midst of the cremation ground, he beheld corpses that were bluish-black and those that were festering.
He saw bodies bloated with gas;
thereupon, becoming even more deeply agitated, he remained seated cross-legged while still mounted on his chariot;
then the king raised him up from that cross-legged posture.
He set out;
as he was entering the city of Kapilavastu, the fortune-tellers prophesied: "If the prince does not go forth into homelessness on the seventh day, he will become a universal monarch.
Having learned this, they said this to the king: (SBV I 78)
O King, there is no doubt that the seven jewels will appear at the rising of the sun;
therefore, indeed, provide protection for seven nights.
If you wish to behold the splendor of the Sūtra.
A son shall be born to you who will become a king, a lord of the seven jewels;
he shall rule the earth bounded by the oceans without the use of punishment.
Or else, having abandoned the earth, he will go to the forest fearlessly;
and having attained omniscience, he will deliver the world.
The meeting with Mṛgajā:
Kālakṣema the Śākyan had a daughter named Mṛgajā;
while standing at the window, she saw the Bodhisattva and spoke this verse.
Happy indeed is that mother, and happy too is his father;
truly blessed is that woman who shall become his wife.
Upon hearing the word "nirvāṇa," that supreme person, being meditative,
understood the tranquility in nirvāṇa and set his heart upon it.
Then the Bodhisattva threw a pearl necklace as a token of his good wishes;
through the power of the Bodhisattva, it entered through the window and became fastened around her neck.
As it was entering, it was seen by the great multitude of people.
They related this in detail to King Śuddhodana;
King Śuddhodana then introduced Mṛgajā, accompanied by a retinue of twenty thousand women, into the Bodhisattva’s inner apartments.
Thus, there came to be sixty thousand women in the Bodhisattva’s harem, headed by Gopikā, Mṛgajā, and Yaśodharā.
Then King Śuddhodana, together with his brothers, including Droṇodana, took precautions.
Together with Śuklodana and Amṛtodana, he gathered in one place and began to converse:
The Brahmins, the prognosticators, and the interpreters of signs had prophesied that if the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni did not go forth into the religious life on the seventh day,
he would become a universal monarch, a Cakravartin king.
Therefore, we must diligently protect the Bodhisattva for seven days and nights;
let us cause the city to be well-guarded.
Then they surrounded the city of Kapilavastu with seven walls and seven moats.
Iron door-panels were set at the city gates,
and resonant bells were fastened to those panels,
the sound of which vibrates for a league in every direction when the gates are being opened.

And the Bodhisattva was stationed on the palace roof, being attended by women who were beautiful and captivating with dance, song, and instrumental music; meanwhile, the ministers, together with a body of cavalry, were stationed in outposts all around outside the ramparts,
and a search for spies was carried out.
A gate for the inner apartments was constructed such that it was operated by five hundred men;

when it was being opened, the palace of King Śuddhodana resounded with the noise, and upon hearing it, the people of the inner apartments, those stationed at the city gates, the ministers stationed outside the city, and the citizens and countryfolk all remained vigilant.

Then the Bodhisattva, having ascended to the upper terrace of the palace, remained there being serenaded by a great display of splendor and by instrumental music performed by women, consisting of lutes, flutes, drums, sweet-sounding instruments, and the like.
At night, outside the palace, Śuddhodana stood stationed at the eastern gate with a fourfold army;
Droṇodana was at the southern gate, and Śuklodana at the western.
In the north was Amṛtodana;
in the center of the city was Mahānāman, a Śākya who provided alms-food;
he went to the eastern gate and said:
"Who is awake? Who is awake?
the king asked.
"I am awake;
wake up, O Lord! For one who is awake, there is what is better."
Having understood this, he spoke this verse:
"The world is asleep, like one who is dead; it is asleep, having fallen under the power of Māra.
The virtuous are always awake here; therefore, wake up, wake up! Thus he said.
Having gone to the southern gate, he asked: "Who is awake?
Who is awake?
Droṇodana replied:
"I am awake;
may the Lord wake, for it is better for you while you are awake.
Having understood this, he spoke this verse: (SBV I 79)
"The world is asleep like one who is dead; asleep, it has fallen under the power of Māra;
asleep, it has come under the power of death. Therefore, wake up! Wake up! Having said this, he went to the western gate and spoke:
"Who is awake? Who is awake?
Śuklodana replied, "I am awake."
"Wake up, O Lord! For one who is awake, there is excellence.
Having understood this, he spoke the verse:
"Truly, he who is always intoxicated is asleep; having drunk an āḍhaka of liquor, he is asleep in the wildernesses and forests. Therefore, wake up! Wake up!
Having said this, he went to the northern gate and spoke:
"Who is awake? Who is awake?
Amṛtodana replied, "I am awake."
"Be awake, O Lord;
for one who is awake, there is what is better. Having understood this, he speaks a verse.
I have slept on mountains, I have slept in caves,
and I have even slept upon the waters of the ocean;
I have also slept upon the tops of trees.
"Therefore, wake up! Wake up!
Having gone to the center of the crossroads, he calls out:
"Who is awake? Who is awake?"
The appointed guards said: "We are awake;
stay awake, for there is welfare for those who remain awake."
Having understood this, he spoke this verse:
"Practice the Dharma, do not practice what is unrighteous; speak the truth, do not speak falsehood.
One must enter into great darkness; therefore, be awake, be awake! Thus he said.
Then, when the night had turned to dawn, the Śākya Mahānāman announced to King Śuddhodana:
"Your Majesty, the night has dawned;
one full day and night of the seven days and nights has passed."
"Six days and nights remain," [the astrologers said].
King Śuddhodana replied, "Excellent! With the passing of six days and nights, the prince will become a universal monarch (cakravartin)."
"We shall travel through the four continents, moving across the expanse of the sky";
thus they spoke until only one night and day remained.
At that time, Śakra, the lord of the gods, exercised his knowledge and vision from below.
He spoke this verse:
"That sage, born from the womb of the Śākya king, that great-souled one who has fulfilled the six perfections,"
"Desiring to go to the forest beloved by the noble ones, to that penance grove which brings joy to the sages. Thus [he spoke].
(The loathsome sight in the harem)

Then, while the Bodhisattva was sporting, enjoying himself, and being entertained together with his harem to the sound of music performed by women alone, this thought occurred to him: "On account of this, others will say of me: 'The prince Śākyamuni is not a man.'"
"By whom Yaśodharā, Gopikā, Mṛgajā, and others—sixty thousand women in total—were abandoned and he went forth into homelessness;
what if I were to enjoy myself with Yaśodharā?
Thinking thus, he enjoyed himself with Yaśodharā.
Yaśodharā became pregnant;
it occurred to her:
"When the night has turned to dawn, I shall inform the Bodhisattva."
Then, at that moment, the Bodhisattva, through his mastery of dependent origination, spoke this verse: "This is my final bed in a house with women;
I shall never again dwell in a home together with a young woman."

Then the Bodhisattva saw those women, exhausted by dancing, singing, and instrumental music, their faces streaming with saliva, their hair disheveled, their arms and garments cast about, prattling various indecent words, fallen into sleep. Seeing them with their faces streaming, their hair disheveled, their arms and garments cast about, prattling various indecent words, and overcome by sleep, there arose within him the perception of his inner apartments as a cemetery.
He spoke this verse:
"Like a cluster of lotuses struck down by the wind, he lies cast away upon this earth with his arms and feet scattered."
Even upon seeing him with his hair disheveled and his private parts and hips exposed, I am terrified by the very nature of the Śākya prince.

I see these multitudes of young women, devoid of beauty, whose natures are distorted like cremation grounds; O sir, why are you thus possessed by a mind lacking consciousness, intelligence, and mindfulness?
That which a foolish being, following his own conduct, might delight in regarding sense objects.
Fie upon these desires, which are like arrows, spears, poison, and fire; they are like dreams and like drinking salt water mixed with poison!
I renounce these things that resemble lordly serpents and lead to an endless end.
"Desires, which have become the cause of misfortune, strife, and sin"— thus [it was said].
This is from the *Mahāprajāpatī-Yaśodharā-Siddhārtha-svapna*.
In the meantime, Mahāprajāpatī saw four dreams:
the moon being eclipsed by Rāhu,
and the sun rising in the eastern direction.
Right there he saw himself setting [into the earth], a great multitude of people bowing down to him, and himself laughing.
Yaśodharā saw eight dreams: her own maternal lineage broken,
and the auspicious couch broken.
Her bangles were broken, her rows of teeth shattered,
and her braided hair hanging down.
Fortune departed from her home;
the moon was seized by Rāhu;
and the sun rose in the eastern quarter only to set in that very same place.
The Bodhisattva also saw five dreams: the great earth as his own vast couch, and Sumeru, the king of mountains, as its pillow.
His left arm reached into the eastern great ocean;
his right arm reached into the western great ocean;
both his feet reached into the southern great ocean.
A mass of grass rising from his navel and extending up to the sky remained fixed there;
all-white birds with black heads flew down to his feet and rose as far as his knees;
and birds of various colors [flew] in the four directions.
Having approached, he saw those of a single caste standing before him,
and himself walking back and forth upon a mountain of impurities.
Having seen this, he was further gladdened in mind and reflected:
"Since such dreams as these have been seen by me, before long I shall attain unsurpassed knowledge."
Then Yaśodharā reported the dreams to the Bodhisattva:
"O Lord, today eight dreams were seen by me:
the lineage of my mother was broken;..."
The glorious couch was broken;
the bangle-adorned arms were shattered;
the ivory railing was shattered to pieces.
The braid has slipped;
she has departed from the house of fortune;
the moon has been seized by Rāhu.
"The sun has risen in the eastern direction and has set in that very same place";
thus the Bodhisattva, dispelling Yaśodharā's distress, revealed his dreams:
"As for what you said—that my maternal lineage is broken—"
Indeed, he remains here;
as for what you say regarding the broken throne of glory,
even that is not broken.
He stands here.
As for what you say regarding his arms being broken like bracelets,
examine it yourself to see whether they are broken or not.
As for what you say regarding the decay of the row of teeth,
this is something to be personally experienced by yourself;
examine for yourself whether it has decayed or not.
As for what you say, that "the braid has slipped," this is something you must know for yourself;
examine it and see whether it has slipped or not.
As for what you say— that Fortune has departed from my house— women are Fortune, and since I am here, she is indeed present.
As for what you say— that the moon has been swallowed by Rāhu—
is it not this very moon that stands right before us?
And as for what you say— that the sun, having risen in the eastern direction, has set in that very same place— [is that not so?]
