Thus, it is now midnight; the sun has not yet risen,
so how could it set?
Thus addressed, Yaśodharā remained silent;
the Bodhisattva reflected:
"From the kind of dreams Yaśodharā has seen, it is certain that I must depart this very day."
"Therefore, tell me even a small portion of it";
he told him a small portion of it;
Yaśodharā said:
"O Lord, wherever you go, you shall take me with you.
The Bodhisattva, intending Nirvāṇa, replied, "So be it; wherever I go, there I shall take you. (SBV I 84)
Then Śakra, Brahmā, and the other gods, having understood the thought in the Bodhisattva’s mind with their own minds, approached the Bodhisattva;
[he who was] like a spirited young colt.
It is like the mind of a wild forest monkey;
if you turn your mind away from the qualities of sensual desire, then you will behold the light, the irreproachable state.
Arise, arise, O one of noble mind! Leaving this earth, go forth;
having attained omniscience, you shall deliver the world.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Do you not see, Kauśika, that I am like a lord of beasts ensnared in a net?"
Kapilavastu was surrounded on all sides by powerful throngs of men bearing bows, arrows, and swords, and by a vast multitude of troops consisting of horses, elephants, and chariots.
Indeed, this Śākya assembly, headed by Śuddhodana,
having mounted elephants, horses, and vehicles with their bodies well-armored,
stands within the palaces, gateways, and the interiors of the celestial mansions.
With various kinds of weapons held in their hands that were repulsive to behold.
The door of the inner apartments and likewise the outer gate.
It is bound, restrained, and likewise protected on all sides.
Amidst the sounds of drums, conchs, and kettledrums, and the resonance of large drums,
[the city] was filled with elephants, horses, and warriors stationed within the interiors of palaces, archways, and celestial mansions, remaining ever vigilant and undistracted.
For the multitude of people protects me, thinking, "Let him not go."
Śakra said,
"O gentle one, remember your former vow and the prophecy of Dīpaṃkara."
Furthermore, having abandoned this world afflicted by suffering, go forth from the home.
"We, including Brahmā and the other celestial dwellers, shall act in such a way that you,
free from obstacles, may reside in the forest this very day. Thus [they spoke].
The Bodhisattva, saying "Excellent," became joyful in mind;
then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having cast a sleep-inducing spell, gave an order to Pāñcika, the Great General of the Yakṣas:
"Friend, bring the staircase."
"The Bodhisattva is descending from the palace roof";
he brought a ladder forward,
and the Bodhisattva descended.

Then, having made an appointment with Śakra, he approached where his attendant Chandaka was; there he saw Chandaka overcome by a deep sleep. The Bodhisattva, exerting effort, awakened him and spoke to him with verses and song: "Arise, O Chandaka, bring me [my horse]."
"Quickly [bring] Kanthaka, the jewel among horses, from the house;
I shall go to the forest of asceticism enjoyed by the former Victors, which brings satisfaction to the sages."
Chandaka, his eyes opening as if waking from sleep, said: "O Lord, the time for the garden has not yet arrived; you have no enmity with anyone, O gentle one."
Moreover, you have no enemy whatsoever;
for what business with horses do you have at midnight?
The Bodhisattva said:
"Never before have you disregarded my word;
do not disregard this word of mine now, at the final hour."
Chanda said:
"Prince, this night is terrifying and fearsome;
I will not bring the horse."
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"Surely, from one person to the next, the people will gradually come to understand;
I shall go there myself."
"I shall prepare Kanthaka, the king of horses.
Then, having opened the city gate himself, he began to take hold of Kanthaka, the king of horses;
[the horse], as if inflamed by the fire of anger, threw out its foot.
He turns his face away, shifts from place to place,
and does not remain still.

Then the Bodhisattva, with his hand—which was marked with the wheel, the auspicious sign, and the swastika; which was produced from hundreds of various merits; and which brings comfort to all beings—stroked [the horse's] head and said:
"O Kaṇṭhaka, bear this final burden; carry me without delay to the forest of asceticism."
"Having attained enlightenment, I shall before long satisfy the entire world with rains of meditative concentration and liberation.
Now, it is the very nature of things that even animals, when being pacified, do not resort to hostility.
The horse-king Kaṇṭhaka stood motionless;
then the Bodhisattva, seeing the horse-king Kaṇṭhaka standing ready and filled with joy, arose.
The gods, headed by Śakra and Brahmā, instructed four sons of the gods— Kūla and Upakūla— to expel the Bodhisattva, and they were stationed there.
Parṇa and Śabara were there; they were addressed by the Bodhisattva: "Sirs, who will lead me?"
They said:
"We shall take him away;
what strength do you possess?"
One said:
"Prince, I shall go taking all the earth upon my shoulders as far as it extends.
The second said:
"The water that is in the four great oceans, as well as in rivers, ponds, and wells—all that I shall carry on my shoulder and go," said the third; the fourth said:
"As many mountains as there are on the earth, those I shall carry on my shoulder and go."
The fourth said:
"I shall go taking upon my shoulder all that grass, wood, leaves, and moss upon the earth";
thereupon, the Bodhisattva placed his foot upon the ground.
They were not even able to shake him;
filled with wonder, they said:
"Prince, we did not know that such strength as this existed."
"Of the bodhisattvas";
thinking, "If this were known, we would not remain," Chandaka, having heard those words, approached the presence of the Bodhisattva, following the example of previous Buddhas.
Then the Bodhisattva mounted Kanthaka, the king of horses; as Chandaka held onto the horse's back, Kanthaka, the king of horses, rose up into the air above,
through the power of the Bodhisattva’s bodhisattva-majesty and the power of the deities.
The deities dwelling in the inner apartments began to weep at the separation from the Bodhisattva;
as they wept, drops of their tears began to fall upon their own bodies and upon the earth.
Chandaka said:
"Prince, drops of water are falling; is it raining?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"The god is not raining;
rather, the deities residing in the inner apartments have begun to weep because of their separation from me;
as they weep, drops of tears are falling upon their bodies."
Then Chandaka, his eyes clouded with tears, sighed long and hot and remained silent;
the Bodhisattva looked back with the gaze of an elephant, surveying with his entire body turned toward the right, and he thought:
And this is my final night when I shall lie down in the same dwelling together with women.
Again he reflected:
"If I were to leave by another gate, bypassing the eastern one, it would cause distress to the King; for at the final moment, I was not looked upon by the Prince."
Thus);
he saw King Śuddhodana overcome by a deep sleep;
having circumambulated him, he said:
"Father, it is not out of lack of respect for you, nor due to a lack of desire to serve you that I am going;
rather, it is so that I might liberate this world, which is crushed by old age and death, from the fear of the suffering of old age and death."
When the Śākya Mahānāma, while inspecting the watchmen, arrived at that place,
he saw the Bodhisattva intent on departing; then, with a throat choked by sobs and eyes clouded with tears, he said:
"What is this that has been undertaken? "Mahānāman, it is being understood. "Prince, this is not appropriate."
"Mahānāman, by me, for the sake of sentient beings, enlightenment has been fully acquired through three incalculable eons and many hundreds of thousands of difficult deeds;
how could I possibly live at home? This is my resolve."
"I have gone to the forest of asceticism.
Then the Śākya Mahānāma, struck down by these pitiless words and conduct, began to cry out: "Alas, what a tragedy!
Today for all the Śākyas and for King Śuddhodana!"
The hope that has been contemplated again and again will become fruitless.
Today King Śuddhodana, overwhelmed by grief for his son and deeply distressed,
will raise his arms and utter a terrible cry.
"Having deprived Siddhārtha of Gopikā, Mṛgajā, Yaśodharā, and his vast harem, they will become deeply distressed.
Realizing this, he rose in agitation and, raising Yaśodharā up, said:
"Here goes Siddhārtha; restrain your dear husband!
You will weep, afflicted by sorrow and overwhelmed by grief for your husband."
Your husband departs; behold today this final sight of your husband, so difficult to see again.
Alas! Not even one person gives heed to my words.
"I cry out in distress at night; herein there is no fault of mine. Even as he lamented thus, not a single person in the inner apartments woke up...
"Or like a forest without a protector, so it was presided over by the gods."
Then Mahānāma, overcome with suffering and dejection, went in haste to King Śuddhodana and, awakening the king, said:
"Siddhārtha is departing; restrain him by force!"
"Do not weep, afflicted by suffering and overwhelmed by grief for your son.
But by the power of destiny, he did not wake up.
Then Śakra, Brahmā, and the other gods, surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of deities, approached the place where the Bodhisattva was.
Having approached and surrounded the Bodhisattva, they set forth;

on the right side were the gods of the form realm, maintaining a peaceful and composed demeanor, while on the left were the gods of the desire realm with raised banners and flags, accompanied by various divine musical instruments.

In front [of him were] Śakra, Brahmā, and others, each with their own respective conduct and deportment; and in the expanse of the sky stood many hundreds of thousands of deities, [holding] divine blue lotuses, red lotuses, and white water lilies above the Bodhisattva.
They scattered white lotuses,
as well as powdered aloe-wood and powdered tagara.
They scattered powdered *tāmalapatra* and divine *māndāraka* flowers,
and they played various kinds of divine musical instruments.
They waved their garments, and regarding this it is said:
"The inhabitants of heaven, with joyful minds, fill the sky with a tumultuous sound of clapping and wave their robes."
Some stupefy the Bodhisattva, while others lash out at him with hundreds of fingers toward the sky.
Some open the gates,
others scatter mandāra flowers;
some grasp the horse's hooves.
Gazing upon the Sugata, they proceed.
Some follow him as he goes on the left, while others walk on the right;
Kubera himself shows him the way.
Śakra likewise, together with Brahmā.
Honored by the hosts of gods like the full moon by the clusters of stars, the Great-Souled One proceeds joyfully to the forest beloved by the Noble Ones.
The penance grove, which brings joy to the sages.
Then the Bodhisattva departed from the city of Kapilavastu;
Śakra, Brahmā, and the other gods, with joyful minds, encouraged him, saying:
"O Noble One, that long-standing aspiration of yours, 'When indeed, freed from obstacles, might I go to the forest of asceticism?'—that has been fulfilled for you today."
"When you have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then you should also take us into your consideration.
Having promised "So be it," the Bodhisattva looked back with the gaze of a nāga, turning his entire body to the right, and said:
"Until I have attained the supreme path practiced by all the Buddhas..."
"I shall not enter the city of Kapilavastu again.
Then the Bodhisattva, having traveled twelve yojanas in two watches of the night, dismounted from his horse, removed his ornaments, and addressed Chandaka:
"Chandaka, turn back, taking with you the horse and the ornaments."
And he said in this regard:
"O charioteer, give this horse and these very ornaments to my kinsmen."
For I shall now renounce extensive sensual pleasures and undergo initiation right here and now.
Then Chandaka, his face clouded with tears, said to the Bodhisattva:
"O Noble One, how will you fare alone and deprived of your kin in this forest teeming with lions and tigers and covered with thorns?"
The Bodhisattva said:
"For this one is born alone when being born; likewise, this one dies alone when dying."
In this world, a living being experiences sufferings alone;
there exists no friend for one wandering in saṃsāra.
Chandaka said:
"O Prince, you who have never known suffering, whose feet are so delicate, and who were accustomed to riding on elephants, horses, and litters!"
How will you wander in the forest, treading upon this hard ground strewn with darbha grass and stones?
The Bodhisattva said: "Neither my delicacy, nor my being accustomed to comfort, nor having a protector, nor my noble birth [is the reason]."
Neither valor nor heroism, nor popularity among the people, ever disregards the fear of death.
Or perhaps he will come after having experienced the fear of old age and death; or else, failing to achieve his purpose and remaining without any undertaking, he will go to his destruction.
Chandaka said:

"Your Majesty, the aged king will pass away out of grief for his son. Thus, because the Bodhisattva had already accumulated the provisions for enlightenment, he did not take Chandaka’s words to heart.
Then the Bodhisattva, having drawn his sword—which was like a blue lotus—from its scabbard and removed the topknot (*cūḍā*), cast it high into the air.
Śakra, the lord of the gods, caught it and, with great honor, took it to the Trāyastriṃśa gods, where he established the festival of the topknot (*cūḍāmaha*).
Faithful brahmins and householders also established a shrine called Keśagrahaṇa at that spot, which even today is venerated by monks who come to pay homage to the shrine.
The Bodhisattva said: "What do you think, Chandaka?
Would one who possesses such a resolve ever again dwell as a householder in a home?"
"No, O Deva"; Chandaka reflected:
"The prince is full of Kṣatriya pride;
it is not possible for him to be turned back."
The Return of Kaṇṭhaka and Chandaka:
Then Kaṇṭhaka, the king of horses, licked the feet of the Bodhisattva with his tongue;
the Bodhisattva, having stroked him with his hand marked with wheels, svastikas, and nandyāvartas, addressed him:
"Go, Kaṇṭhaka! Once I have attained perfect awakening, I shall be grateful for what you have done.
Chandaka was also told: "You must not bring Kaṇṭhaka into the inner apartments."
When this had been said, Chandaka, his throat choked with tears and his eyes clouded with weeping, took Kanthaka, the king of horses, and set out while looking back again at the Bodhisattva.
They returned in seven nights to the place they had reached after two watches of the night.
Then Chandaka reflected:
"If we enter all at once, I shall not be able to sustain myself amidst the great clamor;
therefore, staying in the garden, Kanthaka was sent forth."
He neighed;
hearing that sound, the people of the inner apartments and the rest of the populace rushed out in great agitation, but they did not see the Bodhisattva.
Embracing Kaṇṭhaka around his neck, they began to weep;
for this is the natural law: even other ordinary beings born as animals possess conventional knowledge, let alone Kaṇṭhaka, the king of horses.
Hearing the distress of the great multitude of people, he passed away with tears welling up within him;
he then took rebirth in a certain brahmin family, renowned for its devotion to the six duties.

When the Bodhisattva shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then, having awakened him by means of the harsh speech of a wild horse, he will lead him out from the wilderness of saṃsāra and establish him in the ultimate, final security of nirvāṇa. The Taking of the Yellow Robes.
The Bodhisattva had need of saffron robes.

In the city of Anupama, there was a certain householder who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-ranging property; he was as prosperous as Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa.
He brought home a wife from a family of equal status.
He played, took pleasure, and amused himself with her;
while he was thus playing, taking pleasure, and amusing himself,
a son was born to him.
In this way, ten sons were born;
they all went forth into homelessness and realized pratyekabodhi.
Their mother was old.
She gave them hempen robes;
they said to her,
"Mother, we shall pass into final nirvāṇa."
"We have no need for these;
however, King Śuddhodana has a son, a prince named Śākyamuni, who will attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. You shall give them to him."
"Then you will obtain a great reward," he said;
having spoken thus, and having performed the miracles of blazing, heating, raining, and flashing light, they passed away into the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Then that old woman gave those robes to her daughter at the time of her death.
He reported exactly what had occurred; her daughter also became ill, and she too,
discerning that the end was near, placed [the offerings] upon a tree.
"The deity who dwells in that tree was requested by you, saying, 'These must be given to the son of King Śuddhodana';
for Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, possesses a range of knowledge and vision extending downward [to this world]. Having taken them, he has brought them here."
Then, having magically transformed himself into the appearance of an old hunter, and having put on those garments with bow and arrow in hand, he stood in the path of the Bodhisattva.
And the Bodhisattva, proceeding gradually along that road, saw the hunter clad in saffron-colored robes with bow and arrow in hand.
Having seen that man, he addressed him again:
"O man, these hempen garments are suitable for one who has gone forth;
take these fine Kāśī cloths,
and give those to me."
He said:
"Prince, I will not give these to you;
lest others should speak against me on this account."
"By depriving the prince of his life, you have taken these fine garments of Kāśī," [he said].
The Bodhisattva replied:
"O man, the whole world knows me as one endowed with such power; who is able to deprive me of life?"
"Who would believe that I have been deprived of life by you?
Give it back without hesitation.
Thereupon Śakra, Lord of the Devas, prostrated at the feet of the Bodhisattva and returned the hempen garments.
He took the Kāśika garments;
those hempen robes of the Bodhisattva were not the right size for his body,
and this thought occurred to him:
"O, would that these hempen robes of mine were the size of my body!
Immediately upon the utterance of these words, those hempen robes became the size of the Bodhisattva’s body,
through the power of the Bodhisattva and the power of the deities.
The Bodhisattva reflected: "Now that I have gone forth,
I shall bring benefit to the world."
Then, having accepted those Kāśī garments of the Bodhisattva,
Śakra established the Kāśī festival among the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Faithful brahmin householders established a shrine named Kāṣāyapratigrahaṇa in that region, which even today is venerated by monks who pay homage to shrines;
then the Bodhisattva, shaven-headed and clad in saffron robes, wandering here and there, arrived at the hermitage of the seer Bhārgava. The seer Bhārgava.
And at that time, the seer Bhārgava sat with his cheek resting on his hand, absorbed in thought;
he was seen by the Bodhisattva in such a state, and addressed as follows:
"Great Seer, for what reason do you stand here, lost in thought with your cheek resting on your hand?
He replied,
"In this hermitage of mine, the palmyra trees once had flowers and fruits made of gold."
"They have become as they were before.
The Bodhisattva said:

"Great Seer, it was through his power that the palm trees in this hermitage bore golden flowers and fruits; yet, distressed by the sight of the old, the sick, and the dead, he has fled to the forest."
"If he had not become despondent upon seeing the old man, the sick man, and the dead man, and had not departed for the forest of asceticism, this would have been his pleasure grove.
Having spoken thus, the seer Bhārgava began to gaze intently at the Bodhisattva.
Then, having seen his beauty of form and his peaceful attire,
and having gazed at him for a long time, he was filled with curiosity and said:
"O renunciant, could you really be that very person?"
The Bodhisattva said,
"Great Seer, this is evident.
Then Bhārgava, his eyes wide with wonder, first invited the Bodhisattva to take a seat and offered him flowers and fruits.
Having been thus greeted and having waited for a moment, he said:
"Great Seer, how far is the city of Kapilavastu from here?
He replied:
"It is twelve yojanas [from Kapilavastu].
The Bodhisattva reflected: "The city of Kapilavastu is near; it is not wise to remain here."
"The Śākya citizens will cause a commotion;
what if I were to cross the Ganges? Thus [he thought].
[Then follows] his arrival at Rājagṛha and his meeting with Bimbisāra.
Having crossed the Ganges and traveling by stages on his alms-round, he arrived at Rājagṛha.
Being skillful in various arts and crafts, the Bodhisattva made a bowl from a *karavīra* leaf and entered Rājagṛha for alms with a tranquil deportment.
At that time, King Bimbisāra was situated upon the upper terrace of his palace.

He saw him walking for alms with a graceful gait in advancing and retreating, with a composed manner of looking forward and looking around, with his arms neither too extended nor too drawn in, and carrying his outer robe, inner robe, and bowl properly;
and having seen him, this thought occurred to him:
"As many as there are who have gone forth and dwell in Rājagṛha..."
No one possesses such a mode of conduct as this renunciant; yet, in this context, I shall proclaim the excellence of renunciation— how the One with Vision went forth,
and how, through deep reflection, he took delight in the life of renunciation.
"This household life is a confinement; it is an abode of dusts. Renunciation is an open space. Having understood this, he went forth into homelessness accordingly.
Having gone forth, he then abandoned evil action with the body,
renounced sinful speech, and purified his livelihood.
Then, having gone to Rājagṛha, the Protector, the supreme city of the Magadhas,
wandered for alms, fully conscious and mindful.
Standing in his palace, Śreṇika, the lord of Magadha, saw him;
and having seen him with a serene mind, he then spoke thus to his ministers:
"Sirs, behold this one, adorned with the excellent marks,
endowed with perfect proportions, and looking only a yoke’s length ahead."
"The wise man with downcast eyes is not born of a low family;
let the king’s messengers follow him, for where will he go to take up residence?"
Then, thus urged on, the messengers followed after him, thinking, "Where will this monk go? Where will he take up residence?"
He wanders for alms with his six sense-doors well-restrained;
being clearly comprehending and mindful, he quickly fills his bowl.
Then, having wandered for alms and departed from the city, the Sage proceeded toward Pāṇḍava; there he will stay.
Having learned that he had arrived at his lodging, one messenger sat down;
others, arriving quickly thereafter, reported this to the king.
"O Great King, this monk stands upon the Pāṇḍava mountain like a tiger cub or a lion sitting in a mountain cave."
Having heard the words of the messengers, the king mounted his chariot and set out immediately, surrounded by his ministers.
Having emerged from the road and descended from his vehicle,
he approached on foot and beheld the Tathāgata in that manner.
The king, having sat down and exchanged pleasantries, and having engaged in friendly conversation, spoke these words— neither arrogant nor harsh— to this purpose:
O monk, when youth has first arisen and is present,
and when one is thus endowed with the quality of splendor, the life of wandering for alms does not shine.
"I give you delightful dwellings and well-adorned women; I grant you excellent enjoyments. Tell me your own birth when asked."
O King, there are provinces on the slopes of the Himalaya mountains,
renowned as Kosalā, which are abundant in wealth and grain.
The Ikṣvākus are of the solar lineage; the Śākyas dwell there.
O King, my family is of the Kṣatriya caste; I do not seek sensual pleasures.
For even after ruling this earth with its mountains and oceans, filled with every kind of prosperous jewel,
a person never attains satisfaction.
Just as a fire blazes with wood in the summer heat.
But they say, O Lord of Men, that sensual desires lead to enmity and are like a difficult-to-cross torrent,
the source of suffering, grief, and fear.
The root is supreme, yet it is served by those with ordinary intellects.
O King, as soon as I had gone forth, I no longer conceived a desire for sensual pleasures; how could I ever take back those things I have already vomited up?
Terrifying, they have become like enemies to the Dharma.
Even if Mount Meru and the Himavat, with their many peaks, were to tremble from the winds,
the force of desire could never shake my resolve.
They are capable of shaking those who have taken refuge in liberation.
For this world, its course submerged in desire, wanders incessantly upon the wheel of saṃsāra;
O Lord of Men, I am its protector, and no other.
I shall liberate him from great fears.
Having understood the danger in sensual pleasures and having seen the peace of Nirvana,
I shall go forth for the sake of abandonment, where my mind will find delight.
King Bimbisāra said:
"O renunciant, what do you seek by means of this vow? He replied: "Unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
The king said:
"O renunciant, when you have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, then please remember us as well.
The Bodhisattva replied:
"So be it; I shall attend to you.
Having said this, he departed from Rājagṛha for the Hermitage of the Sages.
Not far from Vulture Peak was a hermitage of sages;
he approached it and,
remaining devoted to meditation, settled there in a state of wandering and dwelling.
When they stand on one leg for one watch of the day,
the Bodhisattva stands for two; if they stand for one watch of the day by means of the practice of the five fires, [the Bodhisattva does likewise].
The Bodhisattva remained there even by that means;
then they were filled with wonder and began to converse among themselves, saying,
"This ascetic is great indeed."
The designation "Great Śramaṇa, Great Śramaṇa" came into being.
The Bodhisattva asked them: "Sirs, what do you seek by means of this vow?"
In that regard, some said,
"The state of Śakra"; others said, "The state of Brahmā."
Others say, "It is the state of Māra";
the Bodhisattva reflects:
"For these seers are subject to rebirth and have entered upon a wrong path."
Considering that path to be insufficient, Ārāḍa Kālāma approached where Ārāḍa Kālāma was;
having approached, he said this to Ārāḍa Kālāma:
"If it is not troublesome for you, Ārāḍa, I would practice the holy life in your presence.
He replied,
"It is not troublesome for me, venerable Gautama."
"Stay as you please," he said. The Bodhisattva asked:
"How many dharmas have been realized by you, Ārāḍa?"
He replied:
"Venerable Gautama, it is only as far as the sphere of nothingness.
Then this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva:
Ārāḍa Kālāma had faith, and I too have faith; Ārāḍa Kālāma had energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, and I too have them.
"I too possess energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
Ārāḍa Kālāma has realized these very same dharmas, as far as the sphere of nothingness;
why then should I not realize these dharmas?"

Then the Bodhisattva, for the sake of attaining those very dharmas not yet attained, for the sake of realizing those not yet realized, and for the sake of manifesting those not yet manifested, dwelt alone, withdrawn, heedful, ardent, and resolute;
dwelling alone, withdrawn, heedful, ardent, and resolute, he soon manifested those dharmas directly.
Having personally realized those dharmas, he approached Ārāḍa Kālāma;

having approached him, he said this to Ārāḍa Kālāma: "Has not this dharma, up to the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcanyāyatana), been personally realized by you, venerable Ārāḍa, through your own direct knowledge? He replied thus:
"It is true, Gautama, that these dharmas have been realized by me, up to and including the sphere of nothingness.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Venerable Ārāḍa, these dharmas have also been realized by me through my own direct higher knowledge, up to and including the sphere of nothingness."
"In that case, venerable Gautama, as much as is yours is mine, and as much as is mine is yours;
come, let us both lead this group together."
In this matter, we two were exactly equal and attained the same status;
nevertheless, although Ārāḍa Kālāma was formerly the teacher of the Bodhisattva, he honored the Bodhisattva with the highest honor and worshiped him with the highest worship.
And he was delighted and satisfied with those supreme conditions;
then this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva: "This path is not sufficient for knowledge."
Udraka Rāmaputra is not capable of seeing [the truth], nor is he capable of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
Then the Bodhisattva, realizing that this path was not sufficient, approached where Udraka Rāmaputra was; having approached, he said this to Udraka Rāmaputra:
"If it is not troublesome for you, O Udraka, I would practice the holy life in your presence."
"I have no concern for you, venerable Gautama; dwell as you please.
How many dharmas have been realized by you, Udraka?"
"Venerable Gautama, it is as far as the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception";
this was the thought that occurred to the Bodhisattva: "Udraka Rāmaputra has faith."
I too have faith;
Udraka Rāmaputra has energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom;
I too have energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
"By Udraka Rāmaputra, these dharmas have been realized up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
why then should I not realize these dharmas?

Then, for the sake of attaining those very dharmas not yet attained, for the realization of those not yet realized, and for the direct realization of those not yet directly realized, the Bodhisattva dwelt alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute.
With self exerted, he spoke:
"Living alone, withdrawn, heedful, ardent, and with self exerted, I soon realized those dharmas through direct experience.
Having realized them, I then approached where Udraka Rāmaputra was."

Having approached Udraka Rāmaputra, he said this to him: "Has not these dharmas, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, been personally realized through direct knowledge by you, venerable Udraka?
"It is so, Venerable Gautama; these dharmas, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, have been realized by me."
The Bodhisattva said:

"Venerable Udraka, these dharmas, up to and including the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, have been realized by me as well through my own direct knowledge. Therefore, Venerable Gautama, as far as you have attained, so far have I."
"As much as is mine, so much is yours;
come, let us both lead this group together;
and in this matter, we two are exactly equal, having attained an equal status."
Then Udraka Rāmaputra, being a former teacher of the Bodhisattva, honored him with the highest honor and worshiped him with the highest worship;
and he was both delighted and gratified by his [the Bodhisattva’s] excellent requisites.
Then this occurred to the Bodhisattva:
"This path, too, is not sufficient for knowledge, not sufficient for vision, and not sufficient for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."

Then the Bodhisattva, considering even that path to be insufficient, departed. King Śuddhodana, overcome by grief for his son, constantly dispatched messengers in search of the Bodhisattva. The river Nairañjanā—[the messengers searched there].
King Śuddhodana, overcome by grief for his son, constantly dispatched messengers in search of the Bodhisattva.
He heard that Prince Siddhārtha, having lived together with Udraka, the son of Rāma, had departed from Rājagṛha and was wandering about without an attendant.
Upon hearing this, he sent three hundred attendants.
In the city of Devadṛśa, Suprabuddha the Śākyan heard exactly the same thing.
He too sent two hundred attendants;
there, the Bodhisattva wandered through the forest of austerities surrounded by five hundred attendants.
He reflected:
"Dwelling in a forest of asceticism and living in a crowded place are not sufficient for the attainment of the Deathless."
"What if I were to take five attendants and send the rest away?
He then took two from his mother's side and three from his father's side.
They performed service for him;
then the Bodhisattva, surrounded by five attendants, set out on a journey toward the village of Senāyanī at Uruvilvā by way of the south of Gayā.
As he wandered here and there, he beheld a delightful region of the earth.

He saw a beautiful grove of trees and the river Nairañjanā, flowing with cool water, possessing sandy banks and excellent landing-places, its wide shores covered with green grass and adorned with various kinds of trees;
and having seen it, this thought occurred to him:
"How delightful indeed is this region of the earth! And how pleasing is this grove of trees!
And the river Nairañjanā is lovely—cool-flowing, sandy, with easy fords, its banks broad with lush green grass, and adorned with various kinds of trees."
"Ah! It is indeed fitting for a son of good family seeking abandonment to rely upon this forest grove and resolve upon abandonment;
and I, too, am one who seeks abandonment."
"What if I were to rely on this forest grove and apply myself to strenuous effort?
Then the Bodhisattva, having entered that forest grove, leaned against the foot of a certain tree and set his teeth against his teeth.
Having placed the tip of the tongue against the palate,
he restrains, presses down upon, and torments the mind with the mind;
as he thus restrains, presses down upon, and torments the mind with the mind, sweat is released from all his pores.
Just as a strong man might seize a much weaker man by the arms, press him down, and torment him until sweat is released from the pores of his hair;
even so, at that time, the Bodhisattva, having set his teeth against his teeth and placed the tip of his tongue against the palate...
As he restrains, suppresses, and torments the mind with the mind, sweat is released from all his pores;
his energy becomes exerted and unshrinking,
and his body becomes pliant and unagitated.
Mindfulness becomes present and undeluded,
and the mind becomes concentrated and one-pointed;
even as the bodhisattva experiences such painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and unpleasant sensations, his mind does not remain overwhelmed by them.
Because his body had been cultivated in such a way, this thought occurred to him:
"What if I were now, to a still greater degree, [to contemplate] bloated corpses?"
"May I meditate on the meditations of the bloated";
with even greater intensity, he began to meditate on the meditations of the bloated.
Practicing the meditations on the bloated corpse,
he restrains the inhalation and exhalation through his mouth and nose;
when the inhalation and exhalation are thus restrained through his mouth and nose, at that time there arise in his head extremely intense headaches.
Just as a strong man might give a tight headband of leather thongs to a much weaker man,
causing him to experience extreme pain in his head;
even so, for a bodhisattva practicing the meditations on the bloated corpses, there arise extreme pains in the head.
His energy becomes aroused and unshrinking;
his body becomes tranquil and free from agitation;
his mindfulness becomes established and undeluded.
The mind becomes concentrated and one-pointed;
even as the Bodhisattva experiences such painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable sensations, his mind does not remain overwhelmed by them.
Because his body had been cultivated in such a way, this thought occurred to him:
"What if I were to further [meditate] upon bloated corpses?"
"May I meditate on the meditations of the bloated corpse"; with even greater intensity, he began to meditate on the meditations of the bloated corpse;
while meditating on the meditations of the bloated corpse, he suppressed the inhalations and exhalations through his mouth and nose.

When his inhalation and exhalation were completely obstructed in the mouth and the nose, at that very time— [here follows the Tibetan translation of the missing portion as an appendix] — at that very time, he experienced an extreme [sensation].
Pains in the belly arise within the womb; just as when a butcher or a butcher’s apprentice might slit open a cow’s belly with a sharp cow-slicer,
such that there would be exceedingly intense pains in the belly.
In the same way, at that time, as the bodhisattva meditates on the bloated meditations, there arise at that time exceedingly intense pains in his belly;
yet his vigor becomes exerted and unshrinking,
and his body becomes tranquil and unagitated.
Mindfulness becomes present and undeluded,
and the mind becomes concentrated and one-pointed;
even as the Bodhisattva experiences such painful, intense, bitter, sharp, and unpleasant sensations, his mind does not remain overwhelmed, because of his having cultivated the body in this way.
The thought occurred to him:
"What if I were to meditate even more intensely on the meditations of bloated corpses?
He then began to meditate on the meditations of bloated corpses with even greater intensity.
Meditating on the "inflated" meditations, he restrains the inhalations and exhalations through the mouth and the nose.
When the inhalations and exhalations have been restrained through the mouth and the nose, at that time there arise in his body extreme bodily torments,
just as if two very strong men were to seize a much weaker man by his outstretched arms and lead him toward a pit of glowing coals.
In his body there would arise extreme bodily torments;
in the very same way, for a bodhisattva meditating on the bloated meditations, at that time extreme bodily torments arise in his body,
and his vigor becomes exerted and unremitting.
The body becomes pliant and unagitated; mindfulness is established and undeluded;
and the mind becomes concentrated and one-pointed.
Even as the Bodhisattva experienced such painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable sensations, his mind did not remain overwhelmed, because of the cultivation of his body.
Then this thought occurred to him:
"What if I were to practice total abstinence from food?
Then, many deities, having understood the Bodhisattva's thought with their own minds, approached the place where the Bodhisattva was.
Having approached, they said this to the Bodhisattva:
"If you, noble sir, are distressed by, feel ashamed of, loathe, or feel revulsion toward human food,
we shall infuse divine vitality into your body through all the pores of your skin."
"Go, therefore, and obtain it.
Then this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva:
"If I were to declare that humans have no food at all,"
And may the deities infuse divine vitality into my body through all my pores,
and may I then take that into myself.
If that were mine, it would be false; if that were mine, it would be a wrong view.
Furthermore, conditioned by wrong view, some beings here, upon the breakup of the body after death, are reborn in states of deprivation, in miserable destinies, in perdition, in the hells.
"What if I were to entirely reject the words of the deities and take only a small, slight, few, and limited amount of food—
whether it be mung-bean soup, or lentil soup, or pea soup? Thus he made a new effort.

Then, at that time, while the Bodhisattva was completely rejecting the words of the deities and consuming only a small, meager, few, and trifling amount of food, all his limbs and members became withered;
they were utterly shriveled, emaciated, and possessed of little flesh.
Just as the joints of an *asītakā* plant or a *kālakā* plant become withered,
completely shriveled, emaciated, and depleted of flesh—
even so it was in him.
At that time, as the Bodhisattva was consuming food that was meager, scant, limited, and small, the skin on his head became withered;
it became shriveled, contracted, and covered in wrinkles,
just like a bottle-gourd that has been severed from its stalk and remains withered.
It was withered, shriveled, and covered in blisters; even so, at that time, as the Bodhisattva took food that was meager, scant, limited, and small, the skin on his head became withered,
shriveled, and covered in blisters.
His vigor is initiated and becomes unshrinking;
his body is tranquil and free from agitation;
his mindfulness is established and undeluded.
The mind becomes concentrated and one-pointed;

even while the Bodhisattva at that time experiences such painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable sensations resulting from his own self-inflicted approach, his mind does not remain overwhelmed,
because of the way his body has been cultivated.
As he consumes food that is meager, scant, limited, and small, the pupils of his eyes recede, becoming deep, deeply set, far-sunken, and far-receded;
they appear as if they have been drawn out,
just like the reflections of stars disappear from a well of deep water when it has run dry.

Having become exceedingly remote, profound, deep-reaching, and far-penetrating, they were now heard only through traditional accounts; even so, at that time, as the Bodhisattva was consuming food that was meager, slight, limited, and small, the pupils of his eyes became sunken—
exceedingly remote, profound, deep-reaching, and far-penetrated.
Even now, they appear as if drawn out;
his energy has begun and is not slackened;
his body is tranquil and not agitated.
Mindfulness becomes present and undeluded;
the mind becomes concentrated and one-pointed.

Even when the Bodhisattva at that time experiences such painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable sensations resulting from his own self-inflicted exertion, his mind does not remain overwhelmed by them.
This was because of his cultivated body;
at that time, as he took food that was meager, slight, scant, and limited, the spaces between his ribs became sunken and uneven.
Just as the rafters of a grass hut that has been covered for two or three years become uneven,

rising and falling, even so at that time, as the Bodhisattva was taking food that was meager, slight, scant, and small, the spaces between his ribs became uneven, rising and falling; yet his vigor was aroused.
It becomes uncontracted;
the body becomes pliant and free from agitation;
mindfulness becomes established and undeluded.
The mind becomes concentrated and one-pointed.
Even as the Bodhisattva at that time experiences such self-inflicted feelings—painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable—his mind does not remain overwhelmed by them.
Then, because the Bodhisattva was consuming food that was meager, scant, limited, and small, his backbone became like a cord of twisted reeds.
He was like a cripple, resembling the footprint of a camel;
at one time, thinking "I shall rise," he falls face downwards; at another time, thinking "I shall sit down," he falls face upwards.
He draws up the upper part of his body and settles the lower part; he draws up the lower part of his body and settles the upper part; with both hands he rubs his body.
He stroked it; as he rubbed and smoothed his body with both hands, even now the hairs on his body fell away to the ground by their very roots.
Then this thought occurred to him:
"This path, too, is not sufficient for knowledge, not sufficient for vision, and not sufficient for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Then three deities approached the Bodhisattva; there, one of them spoke thus:
"The ascetic Gautama is black."
The second spoke thus:
"He is not black, but rather dark-complexioned";
the third spoke thus:
"He is neither black nor dark-blue, but rather the color of a madgura fish";
that beautiful, radiant complexion of the Bodhisattva had completely vanished.
The three similes.

Then, at that time, three similes never heard before occurred to the Bodhisattva: 1) Suppose there were a piece of moist wood, full of sap, placed in water far from dry land; then a man might come seeking fire, searching for fire.

Just as one who, having placed the upper fire-drill upon the lower fire-drill there, rubs it, would not be able to produce fire or manifest heat— this is exactly what happens when [the wood] is wet and full of sap from a moist tree.
In the same way, whatever ascetics or brahmins dwell neither physically nor mentally withdrawn from sensual pleasures,

the desire for sensual pleasures, the affection for sensual pleasures, the love for sensual pleasures, the attachment to sensual pleasures, the fetter of sensual pleasures, and the obsession with sensual pleasures remain, having completely taken possession of their minds.
In this very way it happens to those who dwell neither withdrawn from body nor withdrawn from mind:
even though they experience such painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable sensations resulting from their own self-inflicted violence.
And yet, moreover, they are not capable of knowledge, not capable of vision,
and not capable of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
At that time, this first simile, never heard before, occurred to the Bodhisattva there:
"Suppose, for example, there were a piece of moist wood, full of sap, placed on dry land far from water.
(Then...)
Suppose a man were to come seeking fire, searching for fire;
yet, having placed the upper fire-drill upon the lower fire-drill there, he were unable to produce fire by rubbing it.
In order to manifest his splendor;
it happens thus, just as from moist wood that is still wet;
even so, whatever ascetics or brahmins dwell with their bodies withdrawn from sensual pleasures...

Yet, it is not by means of their minds that the sensual desire for sense-pleasures, the affection for sense-pleasures, the attachment to sense-pleasures, the obsession with sense-pleasures, and the fixation upon sense-pleasures— which they have there— remain having completely taken possession of their minds;
even though they experience such painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable sensations resulting from self-inflicted violence.
And yet, furthermore, they are not capable of knowledge, not capable of vision,
and not capable of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, this second simile, never heard before, occurred to the Bodhisattva:
"Suppose there were a piece of dry wood, hollow and sapless, lying on dry land far from water;
then a man might come seeking fire."
One seeking fire:
having placed the upper fire-drill upon the lower fire-drill there and rubbing it, he is capable of generating fire and manifesting its brilliance;
it happens just as this occurs from dry wood, from the hollow of a tree.

In the same way, whatever recluses or brahmins dwell withdrawn in body and mind, their sensual desire for sense-pleasures, their affection for sense-pleasures, their love for sense-pleasures, their attachment to sense-pleasures, their infatuation with sense-pleasures, and their obsession with sense-pleasures do not persist by taking possession of their minds;
even though they do not experience such painful, intense, harsh, and unpleasant sensations as those resulting from self-inflicted violence.
And yet, moreover, they are sufficient for knowledge, sufficient for vision,
and sufficient for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening;
this was the third simile, never heard before, that occurred to the Bodhisattva at that time.
"What if I were to take a single sesame seed as my food?
He took a single sesame seed as his food;
he did not take a second until that vitality had departed from his body.
As he took a single sesame seed as his food, his limbs and minor members became even more emaciated, just like that single sesame seed or a single grain of rice.
one kola, one kulattha, one māṣa,
A Single Mung Bean:
The Reaction of Śuddhodana and Others.
Having heard of that state of his practice of austerities, King Śuddhodana dispatched two hundred and fifty messengers.
King Suprabuddha also had two and a half [thousand];
they reported news of those two to him every day, again and again: "The Bodhisattva is practicing such austerities."
He takes a single sesame seed as food;
a single grain of rice,
a single jujube fruit.
one horse gram, one black gram, and one mung bean;
And he prepares his bed upon a layer of *darbha* grass;
having heard this, King Śuddhodana, overwhelmed by grief for his son, with a heart further tormented by tears and eyes clouded by weeping,
suffers in deep distress and prepares his bed upon a layer of *darbha* grass.

Having heard of her husband’s condition, Queen Yaśodharā, together with the women of the inner apartments, was overwhelmed by grief for her husband; her face wet with tears, her garlands and ornaments cast aside, she was despondent and practiced austerities,
taking only a single sesame seed as food.
one grain of rice, one jujube fruit, one horse-gram,
She ate a single mung bean and prepared her bed upon a layer of grass;
consequently, that fetus of hers perished.
King Śuddhodana heard this;
he reflected:
"If Yaśodharā hears news of the Bodhisattva every day, it is possible that, struck by grief for her husband, she will not carry the fetus because of these difficult practices."
"Or he will be parted from his life-breaths.

Having understood that a strategic arrangement must be made so that no one tells Yaśodharā news of the Bodhisattva, King Śuddhodana caused all the people of the inner apartments to take a formal oath that none of them should speak of the Bodhisattva's news.
"It must be made known to Yaśodharā";
and the messengers were thus instructed.
"Except for me, you must not report any news concerning the Bodhisattva to anyone.

Having heard this, Yaśodharā—out of consideration for him, though harboring a hidden anguish within herself even upon hearing the news—deceived the women of the inner apartments by saying otherwise, so that having heard it, Queen Yaśodharā might continue to cling to her life. (SBV I 107)
Regarding unpalatable food, then this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva:
"This path, too, is not sufficient for knowledge."
"It is not sufficient for vision, nor is it sufficient for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
what if I were to take food that is extremely repulsive?"
He partakes of food that is most repulsive;
in this regard, "most repulsive food" refers to the excrement and urine of those recently born calves who are sustained by their mother’s milk.
And he does not take a second meal until that vital energy has departed from his body; but when it has [departed] on the second [occasion],...
Having departed [from that], he takes his second meal;

and having gone to the great cemetery, he places a corpse upon his head and makes his bed on his right side, with one foot placed upon the other, perceiving light, mindful, clearly comprehending, and maintaining the perception of rising.
While he was reflecting thus,
even the village boys and girls now came and, with their fingers, pushed in and pulled out the cotton-tips from both his ear canals.
From both ear canals they said thus:
"Alas, we see a dust-demon! Alas, we see a dust-demon!"
Now they even throw dust at them, clods of earth, and pebbles as well.
The Bodhisattva does not recall ever having conceived a malicious thought toward those village boys or village girls, nor ever having uttered an evil word in their presence;
as the Bodhisattva was practicing such difficult deeds, this thought occurred to him:
Whoever dwells devoted to the practice for the abandonment of suffering, all of them do so to this extent and not beyond it;
even more than that, such a path is not sufficient for knowledge, nor is it sufficient for vision.
"It is not sufficient for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment";
thus his vigor becomes initiated and unshrinking,
and his body becomes tranquil and free from agitation.
Mindfulness became established and undeluded;
his mind became concentrated and one-pointed. Then this occurred to him:
What is that path which is sufficient for knowledge, sufficient for vision, and sufficient for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?

This thought occurred to him: "I recall that in my father Śuddhodana’s residence, while observing the various works, I sat in the shade of a rose-apple tree and, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, entered upon the first *dhyāna*, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, born of seclusion, and filled with rapture and pleasure."
Having attained and dwelt in the first dhyāna,
there may be that path,
there may be that way, sufficient for knowledge.
"It is enough for seeing,
enough for unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; yet it is not easy for me to generate that [mind] while being so emaciated, weak, and lacking in vigor."
"What if I were to breathe in at ease and breathe out at ease, and were to take substantial food at my pleasure— rice and boiled grain— and were to anoint my limbs with ghee and oil?"
"May I sprinkle my body with pleasant water";
thus he breathes in at ease,
and he breathes out at ease.
He partakes of gross food, such as boiled rice and sour gruel; he anoints his limbs with ghee and oil,
and he bathes his body with warm water.
The five attendants deserted him; then this thought occurred to those five attendants:
"Sirs, this ascetic Gautama has become lax."
He is one who indulges in abundance and lives a life of luxury, having strayed from the practice of abandonment; he now partakes of coarse food such as boiled rice and sour gruel,
and anoints his limbs with clarified butter and oil.
They sprinkled their bodies with warm water;
perceiving that "he is now unable to achieve anything," they abandoned the Bodhisattva and departed.

Having gone to Vārāṇasī by stages, they went forth under those who were arhats in the world; being five in number, living together in harmony, in agreement, and without dispute, they dwelt at Ṛṣivadana in the Deer Park, and thus the designation "the Group-of-Five" came to be. [Also mentioned are] Nandā and Nandabalā.
The Bodhisattva, too, having gradually generated physical stamina, strength, and vigor, proceeded in due course to the village of Senāyanī.
There lived a village headman named Sena,
who had two daughters, Nandā and Nandabalā.
They heard:
"A prince has been born among the Śākyas on the slopes of the Himalayas, on the bank of the river Bhāgīrathī, not far from the hermitage of the seer Kapila.
He has been prophesied by Brahmins, diviners, and interpreters of omens, that he will become a universal monarch (cakravartin)."
And he was handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, endowed with all the [auspicious] marks, and captivating to the minds of all people;
it was said that whichever woman observes this very vow for twelve years,
he shall become her husband.
The woman was the man's intention;
by them both, the twelve-year vow was performed.

Upon its completion, it was heard that sixteenfold honeyed milk-rice (*madhupāyasa*) was to be presented to a visiting seer who had been exhausted by his ascetic penances. Having heard this, they again caused a thousand cows to be milked.
That very thousand cows was made to drink [the milk];
then, having milked that same thousand cows, five hundred were given to drink;
then, having milked those five hundred, those very [five hundred]...
Five hundred [of them] were given to drink;
(then those...)
Having milked five hundred cows, two hundred and fifty were fed [the milk]; then, having milked those same two hundred and fifty, those very two hundred and fifty were fed [that milk].
Then, having caused those two hundred and fifty [cows] to be milked, he had one hundred and twenty-five [cows] fed with that [milk];
then, having caused those one hundred and twenty-five [cows] to be milked...
That same [cow] was made to drink one hundred and twenty-five [measures];
then, having caused that [cow] which had been milked after drinking one hundred and twenty-five [measures] to be milked, sixty-three [cows] were made to drink.
Then, having milked those sixty-three, those same sixty-three were made to drink [the milk]; then, having milked those sixty-three, thirty-two were made to drink;
then, having milked those thirty-two, those same thirty-two were made to drink.
Then, having milked those thirty-two, sixteen were given to drink;
then, having milked those sixteen, those same sixteen were given to drink; then, having milked those sixteen, eight were given to drink.
Then, having milked those eight [cows], they were made to drink those same eight [measures of milk];
then, having milked those eight, they began to prepare sixteenfold honey-milk-rice (*madhupāyasa*) in a vessel made of crystal;
the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm perceived this.

"The Bodhisattva, having eaten this milk-rice, will attain unsurpassed knowledge this very day; therefore, we must withdraw its potency. Thinking thus, they threw in medicinal herbs of instantaneous power.
And as that milk boiled, signs such as wheels, svastikas, and nandyāvartas appeared upon it.
And there, an Ājīvika named Upaga, while wandering about, arrived at that place;
he saw that milk-rice and reflected:
"He who eats this milk-rice will attain unsurpassed knowledge; what if I were to request it? Having thought thus, he went aside for a moment and stood there until [the food] had been served.
Having approached him, he said:
"I am afflicted by hunger, thirst, and fatigue;
give this to me."
They said,
"We will not give it";
he then departed in silence.
Then, having placed it in a crystal vessel and a jewel-encrusted bowl by those two,
Śakra, the lord of the gods, exercised his supernatural vision from below; at that moment, having manifested himself in the guise of a brahmin, he stood before them.
Brahmā also descended and stood not far from him; when he began to give them to Śakra, he said:
"Do you give it to me, or rather to one who is more distinguished than I?
"We shall give it to him who is more distinguished than you.
"This Brahmā is more distinguished than I."
"Therefore, give it to him. When they began to give it to him, he said:
"Do you grant it to me, or rather to him who is most distinguished from me? To him who is most distinguished from you?
These are the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa realm."
"Give these to them"; when they began to give them to those people, the latter said:
"Do you bestow this upon us, or rather upon him who is most distinguished among us—
he who is most distinguished among you?
They replied:
"This Bodhisattva, the Blessed One, having descended into the Nairañjanā river and bathed his limbs, is unable to emerge because of his lack of strength;
he is far superior to us.
Give him [the fruit]!"
They set out toward him;

then, by the power of the deities, branches of an *arjuna* tree were bent down, and by leaning upon them, the Bodhisattva crossed the Nairañjanā River, put on his robes, and sat down on the bank of the Nairañjanā.
Then, with great reverence and intense devotion, they offered that honey-milk porridge to him.
The Bodhisattva also accepted them for the sake of favoring those two;
having accepted them, he said:
"Has even this bowl been renounced?"
They said:
"Blessed One, even this has been cast away.
Then the Bodhisattva, having consumed the honeyed milk-rice, washed that bowl and threw it into the Nairañjanā River.
She was received by the nāgas;
the vision of knowledge operates for the gods from below;
Śakra, the lord of the gods, having manifested himself in the guise of a garuḍa, agitated the Nairañjanā River.
Having terrified the nāgas and seized that bowl,
the Festival of the Bowl was established among the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Then Nandā and Nandabalā were asked by the Bodhisattva:
"What do you pray for with this gift?
They replied:
"Blessed One, that Śākyan prince who was born on the slopes of the Himavat,
on the bank of the river Bhāgīrathī, not far from the hermitage of the seer Kapila, has been prophesied by Brahmins, diviners, and astrologers: 'He will become a universal monarch (cakravartin).'"
"May he become our husband through this root of merit, this production of the thought of awakening, and this renunciation of food.
The Bodhisattva said,
"He has gone forth into homelessness and has no desire for sensual pleasures."
They said:
"Blessed One, if one is not desirous of sensual pleasures,
whatever merit there may be from the gift of what is excellent,"
May there be the complete accomplishment of all goals for that illustrious one,
the supreme among men, Sarvārthasiddha, who possesses the foremost intelligence.
Having said, "So be it," the Bodhisattva partook of the honeyed milk-rice; being fully satisfied, he attained the strength and power of the six sense-faculties.
Sitting here and there on the bank of the Nairañjanā River, he searched for a site, until he saw a great mountain, a massive peak endowed with various flowers and fruits.
Having mounted it, he sat down cross-legged on a secluded spot of ground;
immediately upon his sitting down, that mountain crumbled away.
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"Surely I must have committed defiled deeds, since this mountain has crumbled.
The deities, perceiving the mind of the Bodhisattva with their own minds, said:
"Blessed One, you have not committed any evil deeds."
Moreover, this is indeed the nature of things:
that even the entire earth is unable to support both one whose roots of merit are severed and one whose roots of merit are fervent;
and you, sir, are one whose roots of merit are fervent.
"Lord, this is not the place for bodhisattvas.
Rather, having crossed the river Nairañjanā, go to that spot where the Vajrāsana is;
there all bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present have sat and attained unsurpassed gnosis."
"And they shall attain [it].
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva set out upon the path pointed out by the deity;
as his feet fell, lotuses appeared.
Water comes from the four great oceans;
a lotus pond appears;
and as his foot falls, this great earth, being pressed down, begins to resound like a bronze vessel.
Blue jays and deer circumambulated the Bodhisattva clockwise;
even the Vātabalāhaka gods began to blow very gently,
and the Varṣabalāhaka gods also began to let fall a light rain.
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"From the kind of omens that appear to me, it will be this very day that I shall attain unsurpassed knowledge.
[Thus spoke] Kālika, the Nāga King.
On the Nairañjanā River, a dwelling produced by the ripening of the former karma of the nāga king Kālika had come into existence;
at each appearance of a Buddha, he regained his two eyes,
and he emerged from his dwelling at the sound of the earth quaking.
He saw the Bodhisattva from afar, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his body radiant with the eighty secondary characteristics,
and graced by a fathom-wide halo of light.
With a radiance exceeding that of a thousand suns,
like a moving mountain of jewels,
he was auspicious on all sides.
And upon seeing the Bodhisattva, he began to praise him with verses and song:
"Having heard the earth resounding and the river filled with noise,
the Naga rose up from his abode and looked out toward all directions."
The best of serpents, the Naga King of great supernatural power,
saw the Leader of the World approaching along the bank of the Nairañjanā River.
And through the power of the Buddha’s appearance in the world, having regained his sight, the serpent,
with a joyful heart and a serene mind, spoke these words:
For those Buddhas of great supernatural power were seen by me in the past; O Sage, I perceive no difference between them and you.
"O Sage, since you first lift up your right foot today,
you shall become a Buddha for this world that is worthy of offerings."
Just as your robe is fluttering and just as you are plunging into the cool waters of the Nairañjanā, today you shall become a Buddha.
O you of most firm prowess, you stride with the gait of a playful bull;
O bull among men, best among the upholders of the Dharma!
Today you shall become the supreme Buddha here.
Just as hundreds of blue jays flying through the sky perform this circumambulation from left to right,
so too does your body, O you of noble and sublime deeds.
Today you shall become a supreme Buddha among inferior Buddhas.
Fragrant breezes blow,
yet the flocks of beasts and birds do not tremble, nor do the trees sway when stirred by the wind.
Today you shall become the most excellent of all Buddhas.
O Venerable One, just as your stainless radiance possesses a luster equal to the brilliance of blazing gold,
so too does this face of yours shine with exquisite color.
Today you shall become a supreme Buddha among inferior Buddhas.
The intermediate summary verse: They cried out;
he saw; and the Buddha.
Former, feet, robes, very firm.
Cāṣa and Anilāśa— having thus made these ten for you.
Svastika and the Bodhisattva’s Resolve:
Then the Bodhisattva, being praised by the naga king Kālika, set out toward the Vajrāsana;
he reflected:

"I shall prepare a seat upon a layer of grass," he thought. Perceiving with his own mind the thought in the Bodhisattva's mind that he had need of grass, Śakra, the lord of the gods, took from Mount Gandhamādana a bundle of grass as soft to the touch as cotton and, appearing in the guise of a Svastika grass-seller, approached him.
Having manifested himself, he stood before the Bodhisattva;
the Bodhisattva said:
"Good sir, let these grasses be given to me."
Śakra, the lord of the gods, prostrated at the feet of the Bodhisattva and respectfully offered them [the grass];
then the Bodhisattva, taking the grass from Svastika the grass-cutter, proceeded by the path pointed out by the deities toward the foot of the tree of awakening.
Having arrived there, he began to prepare a seat of grass, spreading it out without confusion or disorder.
Then those blades of grass began to fall in a clockwise direction;
the Bodhisattva reflected:
"Since these blades of grass fall in a clockwise direction,"
"Today, I must certainly attain unsurpassed knowledge.
Having understood this, he ascended the diamond throne (*vajrāsana*), sat down having assumed the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*) with his body coiled like the hoods of a sleeping serpent-king,
set his body upright, established mindfulness before him, and generated the thought [of awakening].
And he makes this declaration:
"I shall not break this cross-legged posture until the destruction of the outflows has been attained.
He does not break that cross-legged posture until the destruction of the outflows has been attained.
Māra the Evil One has two banners: one that causes joy and one that causes grief;
even the banner that causes grief began to tremble.
Māra the Evil One, having exerted himself, reflected:
"Since this banner is trembling, there must surely be some misfortune."
He began to reflect and saw the Bodhisattva seated upon the diamond throne (vajrāsana).
This thought occurred to him:
"This son of Śuddhodana is seated upon the diamond throne; as long as he does not invade my domain," [he will remain there].
"An obstacle must be created for him";
having realized this, with his head disheveled and wearing a garment of hemp,
he transformed himself into the appearance of a messenger.
He approached the Bodhisattva;
having approached, he said with agitation:
"For what reason do you remain seated?"
"The city of Kapilavastu has been seized by Devadatta;
the inner apartments have been destroyed; and the Śākyas have been slaughtered."
In that regard, three evil and unwholesome thoughts arose in the Bodhisattva; namely, the thought of sensual desire, the thought of ill will, and...
And there is the thought of cruelty;
therein, there is the thought of sensual desire regarding Yaśodharā, Mṛgajā, and Gopikā,
and the thought of malice regarding Devadatta.
Among the Śākyas who were his dependents, there arose a thought of malice;
this occurred to the Bodhisattva:
"For what reason have these three sinful, unwholesome thoughts arisen in me?"
As soon as he saw that Māra, the Evil One, had approached with the intent of causing distraction,
three wholesome thoughts arose in the Bodhisattva.
Namely: the thought of renunciation, the thought of non-ill will,
and the thought of non-harming.
Again Māra said:
"For what purpose have you sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"I shall attain unsurpassed knowledge";
Māra said,
"Prince, from where will you obtain unsurpassed knowledge?"
The Bodhisattva said:
"O Evil One, it was only after you had performed a single sacrifice that you attained sovereignty over the realm of desire;
how much more so for me, who throughout three incalculable aeons have performed many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sacrifices?"
"For the sake of sentient beings, I have renounced my head, hands, feet, eyes, flesh, blood, children, wife, gold, silver, and so forth, for the attainment of unsurpassed knowledge.
How could it be that I shall not attain that unsurpassed knowledge?
When he had spoken thus, Māra replied:
"You yourself are the witness that by means of a single sacrifice, sovereignty over the realm of desire was attained by me;
who is your witness that throughout three incalculable eons, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sacrifices were performed by you?"
"Is it for the sake of sentient beings that you have renounced your head, hands, feet, eyes, flesh, blood, sons, wife, silver, gold, and so forth, for the purpose of attaining unsurpassed knowledge?

Thereupon, with his hand—which was marked with wheels, svastikas, and nandyāvartas, webbed, produced from hundreds of merits, and capable of providing comfort to the frightened—the Blessed One touched the earth, saying: "The earth is my witness how by me..."
"Throughout three incalculable eons, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sacrifices have been performed;
and for the sake of sentient beings, heads, hands, feet, eyes, flesh, blood, sons, wives, gold, silver, and so forth have been renounced.
Then the Earth Deity, having split open the earth, raised her joined palms and uttered these words:
"It is even so, O Evil One, as the Blessed One says.
When this was said, Māra the Evil One became silent, crestfallen, with shoulders slumped and head bowed; lacking any retort, he remained lost in deep reflection.
Sorrowful and dejected, he reflected:
"Even though I act in this way, I find no opportunity against the Śākya, the son of Śuddhodana; what if I were to create an even greater obstacle for him? Having said this, he departed.
Then, he sent his three daughters—Tṛṣṇā, Ratā, and Rati.

Intoxicated by the pride of their beauty and youth, and adorned with divine garments and ornaments, they began to display before the Bodhisattva those feminine wiles by which women exert their influence.
Then, through his skill in means, the Bodhisattva exercised such a supernatural power that they were transformed into old women.
They then approached Māra.
Seeing them in such a state, Māra became despondent; resting his cheek upon his hand, he remained lost in thought:
"What means might there be by which I could create an obstacle to the asceticism of this Śākyan, the son of Śuddhodana?

Taking with him a supreme force of thirty-six *koṭis* of spirits, who assumed the forms of elephants, horses, camels, deer, buffaloes, boars, crows, owls, mongooses, monkeys, and other creatures, and who were armed with black spears, javelins, slings, discuses, lances, bows, nooses, axes, *bhusuṇḍī*-missiles, and other weapons, [he approached].
He himself drew his bow back to his ear and stood surrounding the Bodhisattva;
then, seeing them in their many forms, equipped with various and manifold weapons, the Bodhisattva reflected: "If one begins a conflict even with an ordinary man..."
He applied himself to the antidote;
indeed, even though he was the lord of the desire realm, he thought, "I shall apply myself to the antidote," and having understood this, he began to contemplate the means for its pacification.
And Māra, accompanied by thirty-six koṭis of spirits, began to hurl spears, discuses, javelins, slings, arrows, and other weapons at the Bodhisattva;
then the Bodhisattva entered into the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*maitrī*),
and those weapons of his, having become divine blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses, began to fall all around the Bodhisattva.
Then Māra, having ascended into the sky above, began to rain down a shower of dust;
even that, however, began to fall upon the Bodhisattva as divine māndārava flowers.
Then Māra released a poisonous wind and a rain of stones.
Then the deities belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm fashioned a leaf-hut over the Bodhisattva;
yet, even with the rain of stones accompanied by poisonous winds, nothing was done to the Bodhisattva.
Māra reflected:
How long must I remain standing, surrounding him?
Meditative concentrations have sounds as their thorns;
I shall go after having miraculously created a Bodhi tree made of crystal.
"His leaves will constantly make noise,
and because of that, he will not achieve one-pointedness of mind.
Having understood this, he manifested the Bodhi tree as being made of crystal and remained there, intent on listening with his ears.
The Bodhi leaves,
made of crystal, began to tinkle repeatedly;
because sound is a thorn to meditative absorptions, the Bodhisattva could not attain one-pointedness of mind.
The gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm reflected:
"The Bodhisattva does not attain one-pointedness of mind due to the sound of the crystal Bodhi-leaf;
a strategic device must be employed."
Then they held up a leaf;
nevertheless, Māra’s army remained just as it was.
The gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm reflected:

"Thinking, 'This Māra, the Evil One, will harass the Bodhisattva for a long time,' [the Bodhisattva], having understood this, cast that army of Māra above the Cakravāḍa mountain range. This is the experience of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).

There, the Blessed One, the Bodhisattva, was dwelling at Uruvilvā on the bank of the river Nairañjanā at the foot of the Bodhi tree; he dwelt devoted to the application of cultivation regarding the factors of awakening, with constancy and discernment.
During the first watch of the night, he directed his mind toward the supernormal knowledge that consists in the realization of the sphere of psychic power.
He experiences various kinds of supernormal power:
having been one, he becomes many;
having been many, he becomes one.
He experiences the manifestation and disappearance of knowledge and vision;
he passes through walls, through mountains, and through ramparts with an unimpeded body,
just as if through space.
He performs the act of emerging from and sinking into the earth as if in water;
he walks upon water without breaking the surface, as if upon the earth.
He traverses the sky while sitting cross-legged, just like a winged bird;
moreover, he touches and strokes with his hand these very sun and moon, so powerful and so majestic; and finally, he exercises mastery with his body as far as the Brahma-world.
Again Māra reflected:
"Meditations have sound as their thorn;
what if I were to make a noise while remaining at a distance?"
Accompanied by his retinue of thirty-six million spirits, he let out a great, terrifying, and fearsome roar.
To block it, the Bodhisattva then manifested a grove of plantain trees extending twelve yojanas, by which that sound was muffled so that it could no longer be heard.
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"What if I were to direct my mind toward the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the divine ear, by means of which I may hear whatever sounds I desire to hear— both divine and human?"
Having understood this, he directs his mind toward the supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) that consists in the realization of the cognition of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā*).
With the divine ear, purified and surpassing that of humans, he hears both kinds of sounds— both human and non-human— even those that are far away.
Those who are near to reasoning within and to enlightenment.
Then the Bodhisattva reflected: [of Māra], who has an entourage of thirty-six billion spirits...
"By whom has my mind been corrupted, and by whom not? How is this to be known?
Then this occurred to him:
“By means of the superknowledge consisting in the realization of the knowledge of the movements of the minds of others”;

during the middle watch of the night, he directs his mind toward the superknowledge consisting in the realization of the knowledge of the movements of the minds of others; [he knows] the discursive thoughts of other beings, of other persons.
Having investigated with the mind, one understands the mental state as it truly is;
one understands a mind with lust as "a mind with lust" as it truly is;
one understands a mind free from lust as "a mind free from lust" as it truly is.
With hatred, free from hatred; with delusion, free from delusion; contracted, distracted.
Laxity and over-exertion; agitation and non-agitation; lack of tranquility and tranquility.
The unconcentrated mind as concentrated, the uncultivated mind as cultivated, and the unliberated mind.
He understands as it really is: "the mind is unliberated"; [he understands as it really is:
"the mind is liberated."
Thus he understood it as it truly is.
Then this thought occurred to him:
"Among these servants of Māra, who has a connection with my mother or a connection with my father in another birth?"
Who, indeed, is the executioner, the adversary, or the enemy?
"How is this known?
It occurred to him:
"By means of the supernormal knowledge (abhijñā) that consists in the realization of the knowledge of recollecting past lives."
During the middle watch of the night, he directs his mind toward the supernormal knowledge that realizes the recollection of former abodes;
he recollects his manifold former abodes,
such as one birth, two [births], and so forth.
three, four, five, six;
Seven, eight,
nine, ten, twenty,
thirty.
Forty,
fifty,
or even a thousand births.
Even many hundreds of births, even many thousands of births, even hundreds of thousands of births.
Even a kalpa of dissolution, even a kalpa of evolution,
even a kalpa of both dissolution and evolution.
He recollects many eons of dissolution, many eons of evolution, and many eons of both dissolution and evolution.
"These indeed were those beings where I was, having such a name, such a birth, and such a clan."
Such was his food,
such was his experience of pleasure and pain,
and such was his lifespan.
Such was my duration of stay, such was the limit of my lifespan; having passed away from that state, I was reborn there, and passing away from there as well, I was reborn elsewhere.
"Having passed away from there, I have been reborn here";
thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their modes and details.
Then this occurred to him:
