"Among these servants of Māra, which ones are destined for the states of woe and which are not? How is this to be known?
This thought occurred to him:
Regarding the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the knowledge of death and rebirth:
during the middle watch of the night, he directs his mind toward the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the knowledge of death and rebirth;
with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he beholds sentient beings.
those passing away, those being reborn,
those of beautiful complexion, and those of ugly complexion;
Whether they be lowly or exalted, or those going to a happy rebirth,
He knows truly, as they really are, beings who go even to an evil destiny, according to their karma:
"These worthy beings, having been possessed of misconduct of body and possessed of misconduct of speech and mind, being revilers of the noble ones and holders of wrong views..."

Due to the cause of adopting actions and dharmas based on wrong view, with that as their cause and that as their condition, after the breakup of the body, following death, they fall into the states of woe, the evil destinations, and ruin, being reborn in the hells. Furthermore, these beings, endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech and mind, not reviling the noble ones, and possessing right view— due to the cause of adopting actions and dharmas based on right view, with that as their cause and that as their condition, after the breakup of the body, following death, they are reborn in a happy destination, in the heavenly world among the gods.
This thought occurred to him:
"These venerable beings wander in saṃsāra due to the influx of sensual desire, the influx of existence, and the influx of ignorance."
Those are the influx of desire, the influx of existence, and the influx of ignorance;
how is it known how they are abandoned?
This occurred to him:

Regarding the direct realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows through higher knowledge—[the phrase] "in the direct realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows" [is used].

And being disciplined in constancy and thoroughness, dwelling engaged in the yoga of cultivation regarding the factors conducive to awakening, he directs his mind toward the higher knowledge of the direct realization of the destruction of the outflows.
He understands, as it truly is, "This is the noble truth of suffering."
He understands, as it truly is: "This is the origin of suffering, this is the cessation of suffering, and this is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering."
As he thus knows and thus sees, his mind is liberated from the influx of sensual desire;
his mind is liberated from the influx of existence.
The mind is liberated from the outflow of ignorance;
for one who is liberated, there arises the knowledge and vision of liberation:
"Birth is exhausted for me."
"The holy life has been lived,
what was to be done has been accomplished,
and I know no further state of existence beyond this."
Thus, having fully awakened to enlightenment therein, the Blessed One had accomplished what was to be done, completed his task,
and entered the fire-element concentration.
The defeat of Māra and the malicious rumor:
when the Bodhisattva, having utterly conquered Māra— who was accompanied by a retinue of thirty-six billion beings— by means of the weapon of loving-kindness, attained unsurpassed knowledge.
Then the bow slipped from the hand of Māra, the Evil One,
his banner fell,
and his abode shook.
Then Māra, the Evil One, accompanied by a retinue of thirty-six koṭis of spirits, was miserable, dejected, and full of remorse.
Having vanished right there,
he was announced by the deities belonging to Māra’s host in the city of Kapilavastu:
"The Bodhisattva Śākyamuni, having practiced austerities and ascended the diamond throne, has passed away upon a bed of grass."

Upon hearing this, King Śuddhodana, together with the women of the inner apartments, the princes, and the assembly of ministers, was consumed by great suffering and dejection; and the multitude of people in Kapilavastu likewise suffered.
Gopikā, Mṛgajā, and Yaśodharā, through the recollection of the Bodhisattva’s virtues, fainted and fell to the ground.

Their lives restored by the sprinkling of water, they remained there being consoled by the women of the inner apartments; with eyes clouded by tears and voices faltering due to the obstruction of sobbing, they stood lamenting.
Seeing that state of distress, deities who were devoted to the Buddha announced:
"The Bodhisattva Śākyamuni has not passed away."
Moreover, hearing that he had attained unsurpassed knowledge, Rāhula and Ānanda, as well as King Śuddhodana with his retinue and the multitude of people from Kapilavastu, experienced supreme joy.
And upon the Blessed One’s attainment of unsurpassed knowledge, Yaśodharā gave birth to a son,
Amṛtodana also gave birth to a son,
and the moon was eclipsed by Rāhu.
Then King Śuddhodana, seeing that prosperity, became thrilled, satisfied, and joyful, filled with an exalted sense of gladness and well-being.
He had the city of Kapilavastu cleared of stones, pebbles, and gravel;

it was sprinkled with sandalwood water, perfumed with fragrant incense, draped with bundles of silk ribbons and garlands, with banners and flags raised aloft, strewn with various flowers, and made beautiful.
Alms-houses were established at the four city gates and in the center of the crossroads;

then, at the eastern city gate, gifts were bestowed upon ascetics, brahmins, wandering mendicants, peripatetics, and others— upon the destitute, the pitiable, the wretched, the beggars, and those seeking alms— and likewise at the southern, western, northern, and central crossroads.
Gifts were being given;
meritorious deeds were being performed;
and the name of Yaśodharā’s son was being established.
The people of the inner apartments said:
"At the birth of this child, the moon was eclipsed by Rāhu; therefore, let the boy's name be Rāhula."
Amṛtodana likewise gave gifts and performed meritorious deeds, and then the naming of his son was determined.
"What shall be the name of the boy? his kinsmen asked. They said:
"Since the entire city was filled with joy at his birth, let the boy's name be Ānanda. King Śuddhodana said:
Hearing it said, "This son who has been born to Yaśodharā is not the son of Śākyamuni," Yaśodharā was distressed.
Thereupon, having placed the Bodhisattva upon the exercise stone, she stood by the edge of the pleasure pond and made a vow of truth:
"If this [child] was born as a bodhisattva, he shall float in this lotus pond along with the stone; if not, he shall sink.
Having said this, he was thrown into the water.
He began to float together with the stone like a tuft of cotton;
King Śuddhodana, having heard of that great marvel...
Surrounded by a great multitude of people, he went to the Bodhisattva’s pleasure pond and saw Rāhulabhadra sitting upon a stone, floating in the water like a tuft of cotton-wool.

Upon seeing this, filled with joy, satisfaction, and delight, his heart overflowing with exultation and gladness, he suddenly descended into the pond, took the young prince Rāhulabhadra upon his shoulder, and emerged.
This occurred when the Blessed One, having conquered Māra—who was accompanied by an entourage of thirty-six million spirits—with the weapon of loving-kindness, attained unsurpassed knowledge.
At that time, there was a great earthquake of the earth;

and this entire world was suffused with a sublime radiance— even those intermediate spaces between worlds, which are blind, shrouded in darkness, and enveloped in thick gloom, where even these two, the sun and the moon, despite their such great supernatural power and such great majesty, do not experience their own light with their brilliance.
At that time, they too were suffused with a sublime radiance;
and those beings who had been reborn there did not even see their own outstretched arms.
By means of that light, those beings, seeing one another, recognized each other, saying:
"Other beings, sirs, have also been reborn here; other beings, sirs, have also been reborn here."
The intermediate summary verse:
The assembly of the fourfold congregation, the youth, the meeting of father and son, the going forth of the Śākyas, Gaṅgāpāla— homage be to you!
Then two deities belonging to the Brahma-body (deities dwelling in the Brahma-world).
This thought occurred to him:

"This Buddha, the Blessed One, is staying at Urubilvā on the bank of the river Nairañjanā at the foot of the Bodhi tree; having recently attained awakening, he has entered the fire-element concentration and is passing seven days in a single cross-legged posture."
"And no one provides him with alms-food;
what if we were to go to him and each praise him individually with verses?
Then two deities of the Brahma-realm, just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm, [vanished from there and appeared before the Blessed One].
Or as one would extend what was contracted,
even so two deities of the Brahma-body, having vanished from the Brahma-world, stood before the Blessed One;
the two deities of the Brahma-body stood to one side.
She spoke this single verse:
"Arise, O victor in battle, caravan leader free from affliction; wander through the world!"
O Sugata, teach the sublime Dharma;
there will be those who become knowers of the jewel of the Dharma.
The second recites this verse:
"Arise, O conqueror of battle!
Wander through the world, O you who are free from the affliction of leaf-falling."
"For your mind is utterly pure,
like the moon on the fifteenth day, full.
Having said this, he vanished right there.
Then the Blessed One, having emerged from that meditative absorption, at that time spoke this verse:
Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever heavenly pleasure there is—
this does not equal even a sixteenth part of the bliss of the exhaustion of craving.
Having indeed laid down the heavy burden, one should not take up another again;
the taking up of a burden is suffering, while the laying down of the burden is happiness.
Having abandoned all craving through the exhaustion of all conditioned formations,
and through the complete understanding of all states of existence, one does not go to further becoming.
Trapuṣa and Bhallika,
the Buddha, the Blessed One, experiencing the joy and bliss of liberation, spent seven days in a single cross-legged posture;
yet no one offered him any almsfood.
Now at that time, the two merchants Trapuṣa and Bhallika, while traveling for trade together with about five hundred wagons,
had set out on that very same road. Then,
it occurred to a certain deity who was an old friend, minister, kinsman, and blood relative of the two merchants Trapuṣa and Bhallika:

This Buddha, the Blessed One, is dwelling at Uruvilvā on the bank of the river Nairañjanā at the foot of the Bodhi tree; having recently attained full enlightenment, he is experiencing the joy and bliss of liberation and passes seven days in a single cross-legged posture. Yet no one has offered him almsfood.
Let the two merchants Trapuṣa and Bhallika be the first to offer it to him.

"That would be for the long-term welfare, benefit, and happiness of the merchants Trapuṣa and Bhallika if I were myself to take up the initiative for the purpose of offering alms-food to the Blessed One.
Then that deity, having illuminated the entire Karvaṭaka region with a sublime radiance, spoke thus to the merchants Trapuṣa and Bhallika:

"Merchants, merchants! This Buddha, the Blessed One, is staying at Uruvilvā on the bank of the Nairañjanā River at the foot of the Bodhi tree. Having recently attained full enlightenment, he is experiencing the joy and bliss of liberation;
he spends seven days in a single cross-legged posture, and no one has yet offered him almsfood."
"Therefore, you two should first provide him with almsfood;
that will lead to your long-term welfare, benefit, and happiness.
Having said this, that deity vanished right there.
Then this thought occurred to the two merchants Trapuṣa and Bhallika:
"Surely the Buddha is no inferior being; surely the proclamation of the Dharma is no inferior teaching."

Knowing that even the deities were now filled with eagerness for the sake of providing almsfood to the Blessed One, they took a great quantity of honey and parched grain and approached the place where the Blessed One was. Having approached,
they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
As they stood to one side, the two merchants Trapuṣa and Bhallika said this:
"Venerable sir, we have brought here a great quantity of honey and flour-cakes for the sake of the Blessed One;
may the Blessed One accept them out of compassion."
Then this occurred to the Blessed One:
"It would not be fitting for me to receive almsfood with my hand, as do the followers of other sects."
"What if I were to reflect upon where the previous perfectly awakened ones accepted almsfood for the benefit of living beings?
The deities informed the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, the previous perfectly awakened ones accepted almsfood in a bowl for the benefit of living beings."
The Blessed One’s knowledge and vision also turned toward him, [perceiving]: "In the past, alms-food was accepted in the bowl by former Perfectly Awakened Ones for the benefit of living beings";
thus, a need for a bowl arose for the Blessed One.
Then, the Four Great Kings, knowing that a need for a bowl had arisen for the Blessed One, [went] from one [place]...
Taking four stone bowls from the Stone Mountain— made of rock, not made by humans, not fashioned by humans, clear, pure, and free from odor— they approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the four Great Kings said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, we perceived here that a need for a bowl had arisen for the Blessed One, and [we thought] from among [ourselves]..."
"From the Stone Mountain, four stone bowls— unmade by humans, finished by non-humans, transparent, pure, and free from odor— have been brought here;
may the Blessed One accept them out of compassion."
Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "If I were to accept a single bowl from one of the great kings,
there would be a change of heart in the other three."
If it were between two, there would be a change of mind in both;
if it were among three, there would be a change of mind in one.
"It would be a transformation if I were to receive four bowls from the four Great Kings and resolve them into a single bowl.
Then the Blessed One, having received four bowls from the four Great Kings, resolved them into a single bowl.
There, the Blessed One accepted alms-food from the two merchants Trapuṣa and Bhallika for the welfare of living beings.
Then the Blessed One said this to the two merchants Trapuṣa and Bhallika:
"May you two merchants go for refuge to the Buddha."
Go for refuge to the Dharma;
and whatever is that which will be known as the Saṅgha in the future time, go for refuge to that as well.
Venerable Sir, we two go for refuge to the Buddha.
"We go for refuge to the Dharma,
and we also go for refuge to that which will be known as the Saṅgha in the future time.
Then the Blessed One expressed his approval of that gift from the merchants Trapuṣa and Bhallika with this expression of appreciation:
For whatever purpose a gift is given, it will serve that purpose;
a gift is given for the sake of happiness, and it will result in happiness.
The maturation of meritorious deeds is pleasant, one's intentions are fulfilled,
and one swiftly attains supreme peace and liberation.
Whatever external calamities there may be, whether from deities or the hosts of Māra, they are truly unable to create an obstacle for one who has performed meritorious deeds.
For if that person, being generous, exerts himself with noble wisdom for the sake of making an end to suffering, he attains the touch of realization as he clearly perceives.

Then the two merchants Trapuṣa and Bhallika, having rejoiced and delighted in the words spoken by the Blessed One, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from his presence. (SBV I 125) The Buddha’s ailment,
and Māra’s mischief once more.
Then the Blessed One, having accepted almsfood from the merchants Trapuṣa and Bhallika, went to where the river Nairañjanā was;
having arrived, he sat down on the bank of the river Nairañjanā and performed his meal.
There, even the honey was wind-disorder-inducing.
Even the churns were made of wood;
because of that, a wind-related illness arose in the Blessed One.
Then Māra the Evil One, having learned that a wind-related illness had arisen in the Blessed One, [approached].
He approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
"May the Blessed One pass into final nirvana."
"It is the time for my final nirvāṇa.
Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One:
"This is surely Māra, the Evil One, who has approached with the intent of causing distraction."
Having understood this, he said this to Māra the Evil One:
"Evil One, I shall not enter final nirvāṇa until my disciples have become wise, discerning, and intelligent."

"They are capable of suppressing, in accordance with the Dharma, whatever opposing disputants may arise; they are capable of purifying their own doctrine—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—and my holy life will become widespread, popular, extensive, and perfectly proclaimed among gods and humans.
Then, this thought occurred to Māra, the Evil One:
"Alas, the śramaṇa Gautama will not attain parinirvāṇa! Having realized this, he became sorrowful, dejected, and full of regret, and vanished right there.
[Thus ends the section on] the *harītakī* brought by Śakra.

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, perceiving that the Blessed One had fallen ill with a wind-disorder, took from a great grove of *harītakī* trees not far from the Jambu tree after which Jambudvīpa is named— *harītakī* fruits endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and taste— and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Śakra, lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, having learned that a wind-related illness had arisen in the Blessed One here, [I have come] from the Jambu tree named after which..."
Jambudvīpa is known to be not very far from there, where there is a great grove of harītakī trees; from there, I have brought harītakīs endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and taste;
may the Blessed One partake of them.
"Having been consumed by the Blessed One, they will harmonize the bodily humors and pacify the illness caused by wind";
the Blessed One then consumed them.
The Blessed One digested it, and his wind was set in proper motion; the illness caused by the disorder of wind was pacified,
whereby the Blessed One became more comfortable and better able to sustain himself.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at the foot of the Bodhi tree as long as he pleased in that delightful place, approached the abode of the Naga King Mucilinda.
Having approached, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him.
Now at that time, an unseasonable storm lasting for seven days had arrived at the abode of Mucilinda, the king of the nāgas.
Then Mucilinda, the king of the nāgas, perceiving that an unseasonable storm lasting for seven days had arrived, emerged from his abode and coiled his body around [the Buddha's] body seven times.
Having formed a great hood above him, he stood there, thinking:
"May it not be cold for the Blessed One during these seven days; may it not be hot; and may the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping reptiles not cause his body distress."

The Naga King Mucilinda, perceiving that the seven-day period had passed, uncoiled his body from the body of the Blessed One; having adorned himself with armlets, earrings, variegated garlands, ornaments, and ointments, he extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One and addressed him thus:
May it not be cold for the Blessed One during these seven days, nor hot;
may the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping reptiles not afflict his body.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
"For one who is content, who has heard the Dharma, and who sees clearly, solitude is bliss;
in this world, restraint toward living beings is the bliss of harmlessness."
Bliss is detachment from the world, the transcending of sensual desires;
the subduing of the conceit "I am"—this indeed is the supreme bliss.
(SBV I 127) [The Comprehension of Dependent Origination]
Then the Blessed One, having stayed for as long as he pleased in the abode of the naga king Mucilinda,
approached the foot of the Bodhi tree;
having approached, he sat down upon the prepared seat of grass.
Having sat down cross-legged, having set his body straight, and having established mindfulness before him, he spent seven days in a single cross-legged posture,
contemplating this very twelvefold dependent origination in both forward and reverse order,
namely: "When this exists, that comes to be."
With the arising of this, that arises;
namely, conditioned by ignorance are the volitional formations;
conditioned by the volitional formations is consciousness.
With consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise;
with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises.
With contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises;
with craving as condition, clinging arises.
With clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises;
with birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair come into being.
Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering;
that is to say: when this is not, that does not come to be;
from the cessation of this, that ceases.
That is to say: from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations;
from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness;
from the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form.
From the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases;
from the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact;
from the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling.
From the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving;
from the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging;
from the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence.
From the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth; from the cessation of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
Thus occurs the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.

Then, at the end of those very seven days, the Blessed One arose from that meditative absorption and at that time spoke these verses: "When these phenomena appear to the ardent, meditating brahmin..."
Then all his doubts vanish when he understands the Dharma together with its cause.
When these phenomena appear to the ardent, meditating brahmin,
then all his doubts depart.
When one understands that suffering has a cause.
When these phenomena appear to the ardent, meditating brahmin,
then all his doubts vanish away.
When one attains the destruction of the sensations.
"When these phenomena become manifest to the ardent, meditating brahmin,
then all his doubts depart."
When the conditions reach their exhaustion.
When these phenomena become manifest to the ardent, meditating brahmin,
then all his doubts depart.
When one attains the destruction of the outflows.
When these phenomena appear to the ardent, meditating brahmin,
they remain illuminating the entire world.
Just as the sun has risen in the sky.
When these phenomena appear to the ardent, meditating brahmin,
he stands dispelling the army of Māra.
For the Buddha is completely liberated from the fetters.
Then this occurred to the Blessed One:
"The Dharma realized by me is profound, appearing profound, difficult to see, difficult to understand;
it is beyond reasoning, outside the sphere of reasoning, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise who are skilled and discerning."
If I were to announce this to others, and they did not understand it,
that would be a source of vexation for me.
There might be this delusion:
"Let there simply be no arising of the mind; what if I were to dwell alone in the forest, on a slope, devoted to the practice of dwelling in happiness in this very life?"
There, the Blessed One’s mind inclined toward dwelling in a state of little concern, not toward teaching the Dharma;
then, this thought occurred to Brahmā, the Lord of the Assembly:
"Alas, this world is perishing! Alas, this world is being destroyed,
since at this time, at some point, somewhere, Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas [appear]."
They arise in the world as rarely as the flower of the udumbara tree;
and today the Blessed One’s mind inclines toward dwelling in a state of few concerns.
"It is not right for him to remain silent regarding the teaching of the Dharma;
what if I were to go to him and entreat him?
Then Brahmā, the Lord of the Assembly, [approached].
Just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm,
even so did Brahmā Sabhāpati vanish from the Brahma-world.
He stood before the Blessed One;
then Brahmā, the Lord of the Assembly, at that moment spoke this verse:
"In the past, he appeared among the Magadhans."
For the Dharma is impure and bound by defilement;
open the door to the deathless and teach the Dharma that is free from passion.
The Blessed One said:
"O Brahmin, having indeed torn asunder [all obstacles], this entire [Dharma] was attained by me with great difficulty;
for this Dharma is not easily awakened to by those who are limited by passion for existence."
Those who are stained by passion and shrouded by a mass of darkness will not see the path that flows against the current— profound and exceedingly difficult to perceive.
Brahmā’s Request for the Teaching of the Dharma:
"Venerable Sir, there are beings born in the world, grown up in the world, who possess sharp faculties."
Those of middling faculties, those of dull faculties, and those of good character;
They are easy to discipline,
possessing little dust and being of a nature with little dust,
yet they fall away because of not hearing the true Dharma.
It is just as, venerable sir, blue lotuses, or red lotuses, or white water lilies,
or white lotuses, which are born in the water, [and yet remain unsullied by it].
Those grown in water remain with some parts emerging above the water and others submerged level with the water.
Some remain with their sheaths submerged in water;
even so, Venerable Sir, there are beings born in the world and grown up in the world who possess sharp faculties.
Those of medium faculties, those of dull faculties, and those of good character;
There are those who are easy to discipline,
possessing little dust and belonging to a nature with little dust, yet who fall away because they have not heard the true Dharma;
may the Blessed One teach the Dharma!
"May the Sugata teach the Dharma;
there will be those who understand the essence of the Dharma.
Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One:
And [he thought], "May I myself survey the world with the eye of a Buddha";
then the Blessed One himself surveyed the world with the eye of a Buddha.
While surveying the world with his Buddha-eye, the Blessed One himself saw that there are beings born in the world,
grown up in the world,
who possess sharp faculties.
Those of medium faculties, those of dull faculties, and those of good character;
They are easy to discipline,
possessing little dust and being of a nature with little dust,
yet they fall away because they have not heard the true Dharma.
And having seen this, great compassion arose within him for all sentient beings;
then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
"I shall open the door of the Deathless."
May those who are givers of ears dispel their doubts;
O Brahmā, seeing that there would be much hostility, I do not speak extensively of the sublime Dharma among men.
Then, this thought occurred to Brahmā Sahāmpati:
"The Blessed One will indeed teach the Dharma! The Sugata will indeed teach the Dharma!"

Having understood this, thrilled, satisfied, and delighted, filled with exultation, joy, and gladness, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and vanished right there.
Then, this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "Ārāḍa Kālāma has died."
"To whom indeed should I first teach the Dharma?
Then this occurred to the Blessed One:
"What if I were to first teach the Dharma to Ārāḍa Kālāma?"
He who, being my very own former teacher, honored me with the highest honor, worshipped me with the highest worship, and was filled with joy and satisfaction regarding the supreme teachings;
The deities informed the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, Ārāḍa Kālāma has been dead for seven days";
and as soon as the Blessed One directed his attention, his knowledge and vision were activated.
Ārāḍa Kālāma had passed away seven days ago; then this thought occurred to the Blessed One:
"Alas, what a great loss!"
"At the passing away of Ārāḍa Kālāma,
alas, this is indeed a very great loss for Ārāḍa Kālāma, that he did not hear this Dharma and Vinaya."
"If he had heard it, he would have understood this Dharma and Vinaya.
Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One:
"To whom, indeed, should I first teach the Dharma?"
Upon the death of Udraka Rāmaputra, this thought occurred to the Blessed One:
"What if I were to teach the Dharma first of all to Udraka Rāmaputra?"
He who, being my very own former teacher, honored me with the highest honor, worshipped me with the highest worship, and was filled with joy in the highest forms of confidence;
And having been satisfied,
the deities informed the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, Udraka Rāmaputra has passed away during the night."
The Blessed One’s knowledge and vision also proceeded after he had directed his attention:
"Udraka Rāmaputra has died this very night.
Then this occurred to the Blessed One:
"Alas, what a great loss this is for Udraka Rāmaputra at his passing! Alas, what a very great loss this is for Udraka Rāmaputra at his passing, he who did not hear this Dharma and Vinaya from me!"
"If he had heard this Dharma and Vinaya, he would have understood this Dharma and Vinaya. Then, at Benares, it occurred to the Blessed One:
"To whom indeed should I first teach the Dharma?
Then this occurred to him:
"What if I were to first teach the Dharma to the group of five monks?"
Those who formerly attended upon me with honor, affection, and reverence while I dwelt devoted to the practice of abandoning suffering—
then this occurred to the Blessed One:
"Where are the group of five monks dwelling now?"

With his pure divine eye, which surpasses that of humans, the Blessed One saw the five monks staying at the Deer Park in Ṛṣivadana near Vārāṇasī. Having seen them, and having dwelt as long as he pleased at the foot of the Bodhi tree, he set out on a wandering tour toward Vārāṇasī, the market town of the Kāśīs.
At that time, Upaga the Ājīvika was traveling along that very same road.
Upagu the Ājīvaka saw the Blessed One proceeding along the road; having seen him, he spoke thus:
"Venerable Gautama, your faculties are perfectly serene."
Your complexion is perfectly pure and the color of your skin is radiant;
who, venerable Gautama, is your teacher? Or for whose sake have you gone forth?
"Or whose Dharma do you favor?
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"I have no teacher; there is no one equal to me."
I am the one fully awakened one in the world, having attained supreme enlightenment.
I am the conqueror of all, the knower of all in this world, and I am not defiled here by any phenomena; having abandoned everything, free from craving, I am liberated.
Having realized it for myself, whom should I point to as my teacher?
Whom should I point out, for I am peerless and incomparable;
having myself realized awakening, the Tathāgata, the teacher of gods and humans, speaks by himself?
And he is endowed with all the powers of an omniscient one.
In all the worlds, including those of the gods, I am the Victor who has overcome Māra.
"Venerable Gautama, whom do you call a 'Jina' (Victor)?
For those like me, who have attained the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), should be known as Jinas."
— “Because I have destroyed the outflows and conquered all evil states, O Upaga, I am indeed a Victor.”
"Where will you go, venerable Gautama?
"I shall go to Vārāṇasī to beat the drum of the Dharma,
to set in motion the wheel of Dharma which has not been set in motion in the worlds."

For the virtuous do not manifest themselves once they have understood the course of the world; those Buddhas, whose intellects are extinguished through perfect knowledge, have crossed over the attachment to the world.
"Excellent, venerable Gautama! You are a Jina!
Having said this, Upagu the Ājīvaka stepped aside from the path. The five bhikṣus.
Then the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the Kāśī country, arrived at Vārāṇasī.
At that time, the group of five monks were staying at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana;
the group of five monks saw the Blessed One from afar.
Having seen one another, they stood together and made an agreement:
"Sirs, here comes that ascetic Gautama— he who is lax, indulgent, living in abundance, and fallen away from his exertion."
Now he partakes of solid food— rice and boiled grain—
and anoints his limbs with ghee and oil,
and bathes his body with warm water.
When he has approached us, he is not to be greeted, nor saluted, nor is he to be risen for.
He should not be invited to sit by rising from his seat; rather, having already prepared seats beforehand, he should be addressed thus:
"Venerable Gautama, there are seats available."
"If you so desire, sit down. As the Blessed One approached the five monks to see them, the five monks,
unable to endure his brilliance, splendor, and majesty, rose from their seats, some making way for the Blessed One.
They prepare a seat;
some set out water for washing the feet and a footstool in a secluded spot.
Some went out to meet him and received his robes; they spoke thus: "Come, venerable Gautama;
welcome to you, venerable Gautama."
"May the venerable Gautama sit on this very seat prepared for him.
Then this occurred to the Blessed One:
"Alas, these foolish men have fallen away from their own agreement."
Having understood this, he sat down on the very seat that had been prepared.
Thereupon, the group of five monks addressed the Blessed One excessively with appellations of name, appellations of clan, and the address "Venerable One.
Then the Blessed One addressed the group of five monks:
“Monks, do not address the Tathāgata excessively by his name, by his clan name, or by the term ‘venerable’; lest it lead to your misfortune, harm, and suffering for a long time.”
For what reason?

Monks, if anyone addresses the Tathāgata excessively by name, by clan, or by the title "Venerable One," that leads to the long-term misfortune, harm, and suffering of that deluded man. Thus it was said. (SBV I 134)
They said: "Venerable Gautama, did you, by means of that former mode of conduct, behavior, and practice of austerities, attain anything superior to human conditions— a noble distinction,
or knowledge, or vision?"
Or [how could you have attained] a state of dwelling in comfort?

For how much less so now, when you are lax, living in abundance, and have strayed from abandonment— that you now take coarse food such as boiled rice and sour gruel, and that you anoint your limbs with ghee and oil?
And you sprinkle your bodies with pleasant water;
do you not, O monks, perceive the difference between the Tathāgata’s former and later countenance, or the clarity of his sense faculties?
"What is the distinction?
They replied thus:
"It is so, venerable Gautama."
Regarding the middle way of conduct,
the Blessed One addressed the group of five monks:
"Monks, these two extremes should not be pursued by one who has gone forth."
They should not be spoken to, nor should they be attended upon;
which two?

That which is devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasure among desires— lowly, vulgar, common, and belonging to ordinary worldlings— and that which is devotion to self-mortification— painful, ignoble, and leading to no good: having avoided both these extremes, there is a middle way that brings about vision, brings about knowledge, leads to peace, and conduces to higher knowledge, to full awakening, and to Nirvana.
What is the middle way? It is the noble eightfold path; its first factor is right view.
right intention, right speech, and right action;
right livelihood,
right effort,
and right mindfulness.
Right concentration;
the Blessed One was able to instruct the five monks with this exhortation;
and the Blessed One instructed two of the five monks before the morning meal.
Three enter the village for alms;
what the group of three acquires, by that the group of six is sustained;
and after the meal, the Blessed One instructs the group of five monks.
Two [monks] enter the village for alms; whatever the pair of them procures, by that the group of five is sustained;
the Tathāgata, however, eats only at the proper time.
The Four Noble Truths:
Therein the Blessed One addressed the group of five monks:
"1) Monks, regarding these dharmas unheard of before, as I applied my mind thoroughly, the vision arose: 'This is the noble truth of suffering.'"
Knowledge, vision, and awakening arose:
"This is the origin of suffering; this is the cessation of suffering."

"This is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering"— thus, monks, as I applied my mind thoroughly to these phenomena unheard of before, there arose in me the eye, the knowledge, the wisdom, and the insight.

"That noble truth of suffering must be fully understood through direct knowledge by me"— thus, monks, as I applied my mind thoroughly to these phenomena unheard of before, there arose in me the eye, the knowledge, the wisdom, and the insight.

"Monks, regarding that noble truth of the origin of suffering, the thought 'this must be abandoned by me through direct knowledge' arose in me when I applied systematic attention to things unheard of before; thus, vision arose,
knowledge arose, wisdom arose, and awakening arose."

"Monks, regarding that noble truth of the cessation of suffering, 'this must be realized by me through direct knowledge'— as I applied systematic attention to these teachings unheard of before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, and awakening arose.

Regarding that noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering, 'this must be cultivated by me through direct knowledge'— as I applied systematic attention to these teachings unheard of before..."
"Vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, and awakening arose:
'That noble truth of suffering has indeed been fully understood through direct higher knowledge by me. Monks, as I was attending wisely to these teachings unheard of before, vision arose."
Knowledge, vision, and wisdom arose:

"Indeed, this noble truth of the origin of suffering has been abandoned by me through direct knowledge. Monks, as I applied my mind thoroughly to these phenomena unheard of before, vision arose, knowledge arose, vision arose, knowledge arose, and wisdom arose.

"Monks, regarding that noble truth of the cessation of suffering: 'This has been realized by me through direct knowledge,' as I applied proper attention to things unheard of before, there arose in me the eye, knowledge, wisdom, and insight. Regarding that noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering: 'This has been cultivated by me through direct knowledge,' as I applied proper attention to things unheard of before, there arose in me the eye..."
Knowledge, vision, and wisdom arose.
Monks, as long as this threefold revolution and twelvefold aspect regarding these four noble truths had not yet produced vision for me, nor knowledge... [nor wisdom].
O monks, as long as this knowledge and insight had not arisen in me regarding this world with its gods, its Māras, and its...

"O monks, as long as I did not dwell extensively with a mind free from perversion— liberated, emerged, detached, and completely released from the world including the Brahmās, from the generation of recluses and brahmins, and from gods and humans— I did not claim, 'I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.'"

And because, monks, regarding these four noble truths, the eye arose in me in this way— three turns and twelve aspects— and knowledge, wisdom, and insight arose, therefore, from this world with its gods, its Māras, and its Brahmās...
I dwelt extensively with a mind free from perversion—liberated, emerged, detached, and completely released from the generation of beings including śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, as well as gods and humans;
O monks, I knew for certain: "I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
[The name of Ājñātakauṇḍinya]
While this Dharma discourse was being spoken, the dust-free and stainless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose in the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya and in eighty thousand deities.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Kauṇḍinya:
“Kauṇḍinya, have you understood the Dharma? “I have understood it, Blessed One; I have understood it. “Kauṇḍinya, have you understood the Dharma?”
"It has been understood, Sugata; it has been understood.
"The Dharma has been understood by the Venerable Kauṇḍinya"; therefore, "Ājñātakauṇḍinya" is the designation for the Venerable Kauṇḍinya.
"The Dharma has been understood by the Venerable Kauṇḍinya!"—
thus did the terrestrial yakṣas raise their voices in proclamation of the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
They proclaimed the sound:
"Friends, this Dharma wheel—having three turnings and twelve aspects—has been set in motion by the Blessed One at Ṛṣivadana, the Deer Park in Vārāṇasī;
it is not to be turned back by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else whatsoever."
"In the world, through conformity with the Dharma—

for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the welfare and happiness of gods and humans— the divine hosts will increase and the demonic hosts will diminish."
Having heard the sound of the terrestrial yakṣas, the yakṣas who roam the atmosphere [re-echo it],
as do the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods.
At that moment, at that instant, at that second,
In that very instant, moment, and second,
the sound reached as far as the Brahma-world;
the gods of the Brahma-realm raised their voices.

They proclaimed this cry: "Friends, at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana, the Blessed One has set in motion the Wheel of Dharma— which is righteous, having three revolutions and twelve aspects— a wheel that cannot be turned back by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, or Māra."
Whether by Brahmā or by someone else in the world, it was spoken in accordance with the Dharma for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world,
and for the sake, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans: "The divine hosts will increase,
and the demonic hosts will diminish."
"The Wheel of Dharma, consisting of three revolutions and twelve aspects, has been set in motion by the Blessed One at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana.
Therefore, "Setting in Motion the Wheel of Dharma" is the designation for this Dharma discourse. [The Buddha explains the Four Noble Truths.]
There, the Blessed One addressed the group of five monks a second time:
"Monks, there are these four noble truths. Which four?"
The noble truth of suffering,

the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. 1) What is the noble truth of suffering?
Birth is suffering, aging is suffering,
and illness is suffering.
Death is suffering; separation from the beloved is suffering;
association with the unbeloved is suffering.
Not obtaining what one desires and seeks after is also suffering;
in brief, these five aggregates of clinging are suffering;
for the full comprehension of this, the Noble Eightfold Path is to be cultivated. 2)
What is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?
It is craving, which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and passion, finding delight here and there; for its abandonment, the noble eightfold path is to be cultivated. 3)
What is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?

It is the complete abandonment, relinquishment, vomiting out, destruction, fading away, cessation, pacification, and disappearance of this very craving— which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and passion, and finds delight here and there.
For the direct realization of that, the noble eightfold path is to be cultivated. 4) What is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering?
It is the noble eightfold path; namely:
Right view, right intention; right speech, right action;
right livelihood;
right effort; right mindfulness;
Right concentration;
that too is to be cultivated.
While this Dharma discourse was being spoken, the mind of the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya was liberated from the outflows through non-clinging.
But for the remaining five monks, the dustless, stainless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose;
at that very time, there was one [in the world].
The Blessed One was the second Arhat;
there, the Blessed One addressed the remaining five monks:
"Form, monks, is not the self."
Monks, if form were the self, form would not lead to affliction and suffering;
and one could obtain regarding form: "Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus."
Therefore, monks, because form is not-self, form leads to affliction and suffering;
and it is not possible regarding form to say, "Let it be thus for me," or "Let it not be thus."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, monks, are not the self. Monks,
if consciousness were the self, then consciousness would not lead to affliction (suffering).
It would undergo transformation;
and one could obtain for consciousness [the wish]: "Let my consciousness be thus," or "Let it not be thus."
Therefore, monks, because consciousness is not-self,
consciousness leads to affliction and suffering.
And yet, regarding consciousness, it cannot be obtained such that one could say, "Let my consciousness be thus," or "Let it not be thus.
What do you think, monks?
Is form permanent or impermanent?
"Venerable sir, this is impermanent.
And that which is impermanent, is it suffering or not suffering?
"Venerable sir, this is suffering."
Furthermore, that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change— would a learned noble disciple regard it as a self, thinking, "This is mine,
this I am"?
"Is this my self?
"No, venerable sir.
"What do you think, monks: are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent?"
"Venerable sir, this is impermanent;
and that which is impermanent,
is it [suffering]?"
Or is it not suffering?
This is suffering, venerable sir;
for that which is impermanent—
[It is] suffering and subject to change;
would a learned noble disciple regard that as a self, thinking, "This is mine"?
"Am I this? Is this my self?
"No, venerable sir. (SBV I 139)
Therefore, monks, whatever form there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external;
gross or subtle; inferior or superior; whether far or near—all that is not mine, I am not this, and this is not my self.
"This is not my self"—
thus should this be seen as it really is with correct wisdom;
likewise, whatever feeling, whatever perception, whatever formations, and whatever consciousness there may be— whether past, future, or present.
Whether internal or external, coarse or subtle, inferior or superior, whether far or near— all that is not mine, I am not this, and this is not my self.
"This is not my self"—
thus, this should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.
And because, monks, the learned noble disciple does not regard these five aggregates of clinging as self or as belonging to a self;
Observing in this way, he does not grasp at anything in the world; not grasping, he is not troubled; being untroubled, he personally attains parinirvāṇa:
"Birth is exhausted for me."
"The holy life has been lived;
what was to be done has been accomplished;
I know no further state of existence beyond this."
While this Dharma discourse was being spoken, the minds of the remaining five monks were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging;
at that time, there were five Arhats in the world,
and the Blessed One was the sixth.
The Conversion of Yaśas, the Son of a Headman: There the Blessed One was staying at Vārāṇasī, on the bank of the river Vārakā.
Now at that time, Yaśas, the son of a prominent family, was living in Vārāṇasī.

Having played, enjoyed himself, and amused himself day after day with music consisting entirely of women, his body became exhausted, weary, and overcome by fatigue; he fell right there into a state of sleep.
Those women also, their bodies exhausted, weary, and overcome by fatigue, fell right there into a state of sleep.

Yaśas, the son of the head of the clan, having awakened from sleep in the middle of the night, saw all those women— some rolling about, some naked, some with disheveled hair, some with their arms flung out, and others wailing piteously. Upon seeing this, the perception of his own inner apartments as a cemetery entered his mind.
Then Yaśas, the son of the head of the guild, descended from his great couch, put on a pair of jeweled sandals worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold],
and approached the gate of the inner apartments; having approached it, he raised a cry of distress:
"I am beset, friends! I am afflicted, friends!"—
at this, non-human beings open his door and cause the sound to vanish.
Then Yaśas, the son of the head of the guild, approached the gate of the residence;
having approached it, he raised a cry of distress: "I am beset, sirs! I am afflicted, sirs!"
Non-human beings opened the gate for him and caused the sound to vanish;
then Yaśas, the son of a prominent family, approached the city gate.
Having approached, he raised a cry:
"I am beset, friends! I am afflicted, friends!"
Non-human beings opened the door for him and made the sound vanish;
then Yaśas, the son of a prominent family, approached the river Vārakā.

At that time, the Blessed One was walking back and forth on a walkway in the open air outside the monastery on the bank of the river Vārakā, for the most part waiting for Yaśas, the son of a preeminent family.
Yaśas, the son of a preeminent family, saw the Blessed One from afar as he was walking back and forth on the walkway on the bank of the river Vārakā;
having seen him, he cried out in a loud voice:
"I am beset, O Śramaṇa! I am afflicted, O Śramaṇa! Then the Blessed One said this to Yaśas, the son of a prominent family:
"Come, young man; this place is free from danger for you; this is uninhabited.
Then Yaśas, the son of a preeminent family, cast down a pair of jeweled sandals worth a hundred thousand [pieces] on the bank of the river Vārakā.
Having crossed back over the Vārakā River, he approached the Blessed One;
having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Then the Blessed One, taking Yaśas, the son of a prominent family, went to his own monastery.
Having approached, he sat down on the very seat that had been prepared;
having sat down, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened Yaśas, the son of a leading family, with a discourse on the Dharma.

He inspires and gladdens them; that which is the Dharma discourse to be delivered by the Blessed Buddhas at the outset— namely, the discourse on giving, the discourse on ethical discipline, and so forth.

He spoke at length on the discourse of heaven, and extensively elucidated the dharmas pertaining to the side of purification— namely, the gratification, the danger, and the defilement of sensual pleasures, as well as the benefit, seclusion, renunciation, and purification of transcendence.
And when the Blessed One saw that his mind was uplifted, pliable, joyful, free from hindrances, and capable and competent to understand the most excellent teaching of the Dharma, [he taught it].
Then he extensively proclaimed that preeminent teaching of the Dharma of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— namely, the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Just as a clean cloth, free from stains and ready for dyeing, takes the dye perfectly when placed in it;
even so, while seated on that very seat, Yaśas, the son of a leading family, realized the four noble truths— namely, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Then Yaśas, the son of a prominent family, having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, known the Dharma,

and plunged deeply into the Dharma— having crossed beyond doubt, crossed beyond uncertainty, no longer dependent on others, not led by another, and having attained confidence regarding the teachings in the Teacher’s instruction—
rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
I have transcended, O Venerable One; I have transcended!
I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks.
"And consider me a lay follower from this day forward for as long as life lasts, one who has gone for refuge and is full of faith.
Yaśas’s father became a lay disciple, and Yaśas became an arhat.
Then a certain female attendant, having woken up during the night while still asleep, saw that the young man Yaśas was not to be seen upon his great couch.
Having seen him, she approached the householder of the foremost family;
having approached, she said this to the householder of the foremost family:
"Venerable sir, you should know that Prince Yaśas is not to be seen upon his own great couch."
Thus it was; then this thought occurred to the householder Agrakulika:
"Could it be that the prince has been sent outside by thieves or rogues for the sake of his wealth?
Having understood this, he dispatched horse-messengers in the four directions.
Accompanied by men carrying torches in their hands, he approached the river Vārakā.
On the bank of the river Vārakā, the headman of the household saw a pair of jeweled sandals worth a hundred thousand [pieces] cast away.
Upon seeing them, this thought occurred to him: "Could it not be... (SBV I 142)
The prince must have been led away by thieves or rogues;
for indeed, a pair of jeweled sandals worth a hundred thousand [pieces] has been left behind on the bank of the river Vārakā.
Surely the prince must have crossed the river Vārakā by way of this very ford!
For he had learned that a pair of jeweled sandals worth a hundred thousand [pieces] had been cast away on the bank of the river Vārakā;
having understood this, he crossed the river Vārakā by that very same ford and approached the place where the Blessed One was.
The Blessed One saw the householder Agrakulika from afar;
having seen him, this thought occurred to him:
"Suppose I were to perform such a feat of supernatural power (*ṛddhyabhisaṃskāra*) that the householder Agrakulika, while seated right here on this very seat, would not see Prince Yaśas."
Then the Blessed One performed such a feat of supernatural power that the householder Agrikulika, while seated on that very seat, could no longer see the youth Yaśas.
Then the householder Agrikulika approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Has the Blessed One seen Prince Yaśas?
"In that case, householder, sit down; it is possible that while seated on this very seat, you will see Prince Yaśas."
Then this thought occurred to the householder Agrakulika:
"Surely the Blessed One must have seen Prince Yaśas, for the Blessed One has spoken thus."
"In that case, householder, sit down; it is possible that while seated on this very seat, you shall see the youth Yaśas.

Having understood this, the householder of the foremost family—elated, satisfied, joyful, uplifted, and filled with gladness and happiness—bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he sat to one side, the Blessed One instructed, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma.
He encourages, inspires, and gladdens them;
that which is the Dharma-discourse to be delivered at the proper time by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones—

Namely, a discourse on giving, a discourse on ethical conduct, and a discourse on heaven; and, in detail, the teachings pertaining to the side of purification—concerning the gratification, the danger, and the defilement of sensual pleasures, as well as the benefit of renunciation, seclusion, and purification.
And when the Blessed One saw that his mind was uplifted, prepared, joyful, free from hindrances, and capable of understanding the most excellent teaching of the Dharma, [he taught it].

Then, that most excellent Dharma teaching of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones—namely, the detailed proclamation of the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—was revealed to him.
Just as a clean cloth, free from stains and ready for dyeing, when placed in a dye-vat, perfectly absorbs the color; so too did he receive it.
In the very same way, the householder Agrakulika, seated on that very seat, realized the four noble truths:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
While this Dharma discourse was being spoken, the dust-free and stainless eye of Dharma regarding all phenomena arose in the householder Agrakulika;
and the mind of the venerable Yaśas, though adorned with every ornament, was liberated from the outflows through non-clinging.
Then the Blessed One, having withdrawn those miraculous feats, at that time spoke these verses:
Even if adorned, one should practice the Dharma— self-controlled, tranquil, restrained, and living a life of celibacy—
having laid aside the rod of punishment toward all beings.
He is a brahmin, he is a śramaṇa, he is a bhikṣu.
At that time, there were six Arhats in the world,
and the Blessed One was the seventh; the householder Yaśas, of a preeminent family, saw the youth Yaśas seated on that very same seat.
And having seen the youth Yaśas, he said this to him:
"Come, youth, let us go to the house; your mother is exhausted in body, weary in body, and has been lamenting.
Then the Blessed One said this to the householder Agrakulika:

"What do you think, householder? By means of which knowledge of one beyond training and vision of one beyond training were the four noble truths realized— namely, suffering, its origin, [its cessation, and the path]?"
Cessation and the Path—
would such a person ever again dwell as a householder in a home?
"Or would you enjoy sensual pleasures by means of hoarding them?
"No, Venerable Sir.
Just as, householder, the four noble truths have been realized by you with the knowledge of a learner and the vision of a learner,"
suffering,
its origin, and its cessation;
the path; in this very way, by means of the knowledge of one beyond training and the vision of one beyond training, the four noble truths were fully realized by the prince, namely:
suffering, its origin, [cessation, and the path].

"Cessation, the Path"— Venerable Sir, it is a great gain for Prince Yaśas, a true acquisition, that by means of the knowledge of one beyond training and the vision of one beyond training, he has realized the Four Noble Truths, namely: suffering, [its origin, its cessation, and the path]."
The origin, the cessation,
and the path; it would be well, Blessed One, if out of compassion you were to approach the head of the family with the youth Yaśas as your attendant monk.
The Blessed One consented to the request of the householder Agrakulika by remaining silent;
then, the householder Agrakulika, understanding the Blessed One’s consent through his silence, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet and departed from the Blessed One’s presence.
Yaśas’s mother and wife became lay-disciples.

Then, at the end of that very night, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and with the Venerable Yaśas following behind him as an attendant, approached the residence of the householder Agra-kulika.
At that time, the Venerable Yaśas’s mother-in-law and his former second wife were standing in the middle of the gate-hall, waiting primarily for the arrival of the Blessed One.
The two elderly women, Yaśodharā and her former companion, saw the Blessed One from afar; having seen him, they prepared a seat for the Blessed One and said:
"May the Blessed One come!"
"Welcome to the Blessed One;
let the Blessed One sit upon the seat already prepared.
The Blessed One sat down upon the seat already prepared.
Then the elder wife and the former second wife of the venerable Yaśas bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As they sat to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the elder wife and the former second wife of the venerable Yaśas with a discourse on the Dharma.
He inspires and gladdens them;
that which is the Dharma discourse to be delivered at the proper time by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones—

Namely, a discourse on giving, a discourse on ethical conduct, and a discourse on heaven; and he spoke in detail on the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, their danger, their defilement, and the benefits of renunciation, seclusion, and purification—those dharmas belonging to the side of purification.

And when the Blessed One saw that their minds were uplifted, well-disposed, joyful, free from hindrances, and capable of understanding the preeminent teaching of the Dharma, then he [proceeded with] that preeminent teaching of the Dharma of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
Namely, he elucidates in detail the four noble truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Just as a clean cloth, free from stains and ready for dyeing, takes the dye perfectly when placed in the dye-vat,
even so, while seated on that very same seat, the elder wife and the former second wife of the venerable Yaśas realized the four noble truths—
namely, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Then the elder sister and former wife of the venerable Yaśas— having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, known the Dharma,

and plunged into the Dharma; having crossed over doubt and transcended perplexity, being independent of others and not led by others, having attained fearlessness regarding the teachings in the Dharma of the Teacher’s instruction—
rose from her seat, draped her upper robe over one shoulder, and extending her joined palms toward the Blessed One, she addressed the Blessed One as follows:
We have come forward, venerable sir; we have come forward.
"We two go for refuge to the Blessed One,
and to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikṣus;
please accept us as lay followers from this day forward, for as long as life lasts, having gone for refuge with our lives and being full of faith."
"In that case, Venerable Sir, let the meal be prepared right here.

The Blessed One consented to the request of the venerable Yaśas’s elder mother and his former wife by remaining silent. Then, the venerable Yaśas’s elder mother and his former wife, understanding the Blessed One’s consent through his silence, served the Blessed One—who was seated comfortably—with pure and excellent solid and soft foods.
Satisfying him with his own hand and serving him with his own hand,
having satisfied and served him in many ways with pure and exquisite foods, both solid and soft, with his own hand.
Knowing that the Blessed One had finished his meal, had washed his hands, and had set aside his bowl, he took a very low seat and sat down before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the venerable Yaśas’s mother and his former wife with a discourse on the Dharma, rose from his seat and departed.
He approached his own dwelling;
having arrived, he sat down on the seat that had been prepared.
Then the monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable sir, what karma was performed by the venerable Yaśas, as a result of which, while in the midst of his harem, the perception of a cemetery arose within his own harem;
and while adorned with all ornaments, he realized arhatship in the presence of the Blessed One?
Monks, such actions were performed and accumulated by Yaśas; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a flood, and they are inevitable."
Who else shall experience the deeds accumulated by Yaśas?
Monks, deeds performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element.
Not in the fire element, nor in the wind element;
rather, actions performed ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Wholesome and unwholesome actions do not perish even in hundreds of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they indeed bear fruit for embodied beings.
The Previous Birth of Yaśas:
Monks, formerly, not far from the city of Vārāṇasī, there lived a seer who was compassionate by nature, merciful, and affectionate toward the welfare of all beings.
While he was entering for alms, he saw a dead corpse.
With a mind as if bound by the unreal, he entered for alms; having wandered for alms and returned,
he saw that corpse which had become bloated and swollen.
It burst open right before him;
by that, he conceived a sense of detachment right there,
and consequently, a sign of his realization was given here in the inner apartments.
What do you think, monks?
That seer at that time and on that occasion was none other than this Prince Yaśas.
Because he produced a state of dispassion there, he has now provided the necessary condition for [the realization of truth] while staying in the midst of his harem.
"Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black;
for those that are entirely white, the ripening is entirely white; and for those that are mixed, the ripening is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having abandoned actions that are entirely black and those that are mixed, you should apply yourselves only to actions that are entirely white."
"Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
Yaśas’s four brothers were converted and became Arhats.
In Vārāṇasī, the second son of a preeminent family, the third, the fourth, and the fifth son of a preeminent family heard [the news].
Pūrṇa, Vimala,
Gavāmpati, and Subāhu.
Having heard that Yaśas, the son of a prominent family, had shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron robes, and out of genuine faith gone forth from the home to the homeless life,
it occurred to them: "Surely,
the Buddha will not be an inferior one."
The proclamation of the Dharma is not inferior,

since now Yaśas, the son of a prominent family, while still so young and seeking such pleasures, has shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron robes, and out of perfect faith gone forth from the home to the homeless life. What if...?

"Let us too, having shaved off our hair and beards and donned saffron-colored robes, go forth from the home into the homeless state with perfect faith. Then the second son of the leading family, the third, the fourth, and the fifth son of the leading family, Pūrṇa, Vimala, [Gavāmpati, Subāhu, and Bhadrika,] likewise shaved off their hair and beards and donned saffron-colored robes. With perfect faith, they went forth from the home into the homeless state. ||| They approached the Blessed One, prostrated at his feet, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the five hundred sons of the leading families said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, we have heard that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, will before long pass into parinirvāṇa. We have also heard that the Blessed One has entrusted the entire community of monks to Mahākāśyapa. Therefore, Blessed One, if you permit us, we too would shave off our hair and beards, don saffron-colored robes, and go forth from the home into the homeless state with perfect faith. Now, who indeed might this be: a self (*ātman*), or a sentient being (*sattva*), or a living soul (*jīva*), or a creature (*jantu*), or a nourisher (*poṣa*), or a person (*pudgala*), or a human (*manuja*), or a youth (*mānava*), or an agent (*kartṛ*), or a doer (*kāraka*), or a progenitor (*janaka*), or a producer (*saṃjanaka*),
