or the experiencer— who was not a living being in the past, nor will he be one in the future;
Nor does such a thing exist even now,
who experiences here the ripening of deeds well done or ill done, whether auspicious or evil;
nor one who casts off these aggregates and links on to other aggregates.
The Discourse on the Non-existence of the Self: Then the Blessed One, having understood with his own mind the thoughts in the minds of the brahmins and householders of Magadha, addressed the monks:
"Monks, the unlearned worldling, a fool, follows after the conventional designation 'self, self,' yet herein there is neither a self nor anything belonging to a self."
Monks, this suffering arises when it arises;
this suffering ceases when it ceases;
the formative forces arise when they arise.
As they cease, they cease;
depending upon those causes and those conditions, the continuum of formations (saṃskāra-santati) of sentient beings proceeds.
Indeed, monks, having understood the reconnection of the continuum of formations, the Tathāgata designates the passing away and rebirth of sentient beings.
"Monks, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I see beings:
I see them passing away and being reborn, both beautiful and ugly."
Whether they be inferior or superior, or whether they are going to a happy rebirth, [he knows them all].
I know beings as they truly are, according to their karma, even as they go to an evil destiny:
"These worthy beings were possessed of misconduct of body, possessed of misconduct of speech and mind, and were revilers of the noble ones."

Those with wrong views, because of their undertaking of actions and dharmas based on wrong views, through that cause and that condition, after the breaking up of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, in the hells. Or again, these worthy beings, endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech and mind, not revilers of the noble ones, possessing right view, because of their undertaking of actions and dharmas based on right view...
With that as their cause and that as their condition, upon the dissolution of the body, they are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world, among the gods.
And thus, monks, I know and thus I see;
yet I do not say: "This is my self, or a sentient being, or a living soul, or a creature, or a nourisher, or a person."

Whether a human being or a man, whether an agent or an instigator, a progenitor or a producer, an arouser or an originator, a speaker or an experiencer, or one who experiences [the result], he is neither a living being, nor has he existed, nor will he exist.
Nor does such a thing exist now,
who there experiences the ripening of deeds done and not done, whether auspicious or evil;
[who] casts off these aggregates and links up with other aggregates.
It is nothing other than the conventional designation of phenomena (*dharmasaṅketa*);
therein, this is the conventional designation of phenomena: namely, "when this exists, that comes to be;
from the arising of this, that arises."
That is to say: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise;
with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises;
with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises.
With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises;
with contact as condition, feeling arises.
With feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises.
With existence as condition, birth arises;
with birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair come into being.
Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.
That is to say: when this exists, that comes to be;
from the cessation of this, that ceases.
That is to say: from the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations.
From the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness;
from the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form;
from the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases.
With the cessation of the six sense bases, there is the cessation of contact;
with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling;
with the cessation of feeling, there is the cessation of craving.
From the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging;
from the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence;
from the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth.
From the cessation of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair cease.
Thus occurs the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
For thus, monks, are conditioned phenomena suffering.
Nirvana is peace;
from the arising of causes comes the arising of suffering;
from the cessation of causes comes the cessation of suffering.
The path being severed does not proceed;
it ceases without reconnection;
this indeed is the end of suffering.
In this regard, monks, who has attained final Nirvana? None other than one for whom suffering has ceased, for whom it has been stilled.
That has become cooled;
monks, this state is peaceful, namely: the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the exhaustion of craving, dispassion, cessation, and Nirvana.
The Conversion of Bimbisāra:
Then the Blessed One addressed King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha a second time:
"What do you think, Great King, is form permanent or impermanent?"
"Venerable sir, this is impermanent.
And that which is impermanent, is it suffering or not suffering?
"Venerable sir, this is suffering."
Furthermore, that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change— would a learned noble disciple regard that as a self, thinking, "This is mine;
this I am"?
"Is this my self?
"No, venerable sir.
"Great King, are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent?"
"Venerable sir, this is impermanent.
And that which is impermanent, is it suffering or not suffering?
"Venerable sir, this is suffering."
Furthermore, that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—
would a learned noble disciple regard it as a self, thinking, "This is mine,
this I am"?
"Is this my self?
"No, venerable sir.
"Therefore, O Great King, whatever form there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior—"
Whether it be far or near, all that is not mine; this I am not.
"This is not my self"—thus should this be seen as it truly is with correct wisdom.
Therefore, O Great King, whatever feeling, perception, mental formations, or whatever consciousness there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external—
whether gross or subtle, or inferior,
whether sublime,
or whether far, or whether near.
All that is not mine, this I am not, and this is not my self; thus should this be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.
Seeing thus, O Great King, the learned noble disciple becomes weary even of form; he becomes weary of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
being weary, he becomes dispassionate.
One who is dispassionate is liberated;
for one who is liberated, there arises the very knowledge and vision of liberation:
"Birth is exhausted for me."
"The holy life has been lived;
what was to be done has been accomplished;
I know no further state of existence beyond this."
While this Dharma discourse was being spoken, the dust-free, stainless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose in King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra of Magadha,
and in eighty thousand deities,
and in many hundreds of thousands of brahmins and householders.

Then King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra of Magadha— having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, known the Dharma, and plunged deeply into the Dharma; having crossed over doubt, transcended uncertainty, being independent of others and no longer led by others, having attained confidence in the teachings of the Master regarding all phenomena—
rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"I have transcended, venerable sir; I have truly transcended!
I go for refuge to the Blessed One and to the Dharma."
And [to] the community of monks;
and consider me from this day forward as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for as long as life lasts, endowed with vitality and full of faith.
"May the Blessed One come to Rājagṛha;
I shall attend upon the Blessed One for as long as life lasts, together with the community of monks, providing robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
The Blessed One consented to King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra of Magadha by remaining silent.
Then King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha, understanding through the Blessed One’s silence that his request had been accepted,
bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from his presence.
The monks, having become doubtful, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha together with his retinue, the ripening of which resulted in their seeing the Truths in the presence of the Blessed One?"
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by King Bimbisāra himself, together with his retinue; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a flood, and they are inevitable."
King Bimbisāra, together with his retinue, performed and accumulated these karmas; who else would experience them?
Monks, karmas performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element.

Actions performed— whether wholesome or unwholesome— ripen not in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind, but rather within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases alone; for actions do not perish even after hundreds of eons.
Having obtained the necessary conditions and the right time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit.

Monks, in the past, in a former time, there appeared in the world a teacher named Aranābhi, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One. Regarding King Kṛkī: [the story follows].

Having completed all the work of a Buddha, he passed away into the realm of nirvana without remainder of substrate (nirupadhiśeṣe nirvāṇadhātau). A great multitude of people performed the funeral rites for his body and erected a great stupa on a secluded spot of ground.
At that time, a universal monarch named Kṛki, traveling through the air above with eighteen koṭis of elite troops, arrived in the vicinity of that stupa.
The deities who were devoted to the Buddha held back his wheel-treasure;
King Kṛkī reflected:
"Since this wheel-treasure has come to a halt..."
"Lest indeed there should be a depletion of my merit";
the deities informed him:
"Great King, there is no depletion of your merit."
However, in this place there is a stūpa of the Perfectly Awakened One Araṇābhi;
therefore, this precious wheel remains stationary and does not pass over it.
Then King Kṛkin, having descended with eighteen *koṭis* of the foremost of his military forces, saw that the stūpa was uncleaned.

Together with his retinue, he swept it clean and performed worship with perfumes, garlands, incense, powders, and musical instruments. Prostrating at its feet, he and his retinue made this aspiration:
"Since I have performed services for such a truly worthy recipient of offerings..."
"By this root of merit, may I become a possessor of such qualities as these;
may I please a Teacher such as this, and never displease him."

"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the universal monarch named Kṛkin together with his retinue—was he anyone else? It was this very King Bimbisāra who, at that time, on that occasion, [performed] for the Perfectly Awakened One Aranābhi..."
He performed worship at the stūpa together with his retinue;
as the ripening of that karma, he experienced divine and human pleasures of exceptional excellence for many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons.
Furthermore, because he made this aspiration, "May I become a possessor of such qualities as these," [he has attained them].
Therefore, together with his retinue, he has realized the vision of the truths in my presence;
and this was the vow he made: "May I please a Teacher such as this, and may I never displease him."
Monks, I am equal to the Arhanābhin, the Perfectly Enlightened One; I am equal in speed, equal in strength, and equal in burden.
Having attained equality and commonality,
he pleased the Teacher and did not displease him;
for thus, monks, the ripening of entirely black karmas is entirely black.
For those that are exclusively white, the result is exclusively white;
for those that are mixed, the result is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having abandoned actions that are exclusively black as well as those that are mixed, [one should cultivate those that are exclusively white].
"One should apply oneself only to actions that are entirely pure;
thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
Then the monks, having conceived doubts, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by the Venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa, such that he was converted by five hundred miracles,
while Nadīgayākāśyapa and Gayākāśyapa were converted with little difficulty?"
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, these very actions were performed and accumulated by them; having reached their full measure, as previously stated, they indeed bear fruit for embodied beings.
Thus ends the story of the three sons of a householder.

Long ago, monks, in this very Fortunate Eon, when the lifespan was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a teacher named Prayāja Kāśyapa— a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
He dwelt in dependence on the city of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana;
having performed the entirety of the Buddha’s work, he passed away into the realm of nirvana without remainder, like a fire when its fuel is exhausted;
King Kṛkin then piled a funeral pyre for him with all kinds of fragrant wood and cremated his body.
That pyre was extinguished with milk;
those bones were placed in a jar made of the four jewels, and a reliquary stūpa was erected in a secluded spot on the earth,
one yojana in height and half a yojana in width.

Now at that time, in Vārāṇasī, there was a certain householder who was wealthy, of great fortune and great enjoyment, possessing extensive and vast holdings, accumulated wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, and rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife from a family of equal status; he played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
As he was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, three sons were born to him in due course;
then that householder fell ill,
and he was attended with medicines consisting of roots, fragrances, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
And that illness did not subside;
he was overtaken by the law of time;
then his sons [dressed him] with garments of blue, yellow, red, and white.
Having decorated a palanquin and carried [the body] to the cremation ground, he was cremated;
then, having performed the consolation for their grief, they began to discuss the division of the father's property and the performance of the ancestral rites for the father;
the eldest brother said:
"Let us divide the property";
those two younger brothers did not wish for it,
but he began to insist upon it.
The two said:
"If it is so, we shall take provisions for the journey to the next world;
afterwards, we will make a division."
He asked, "What shall we do? They replied,
"We shall perform an offering to Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one."
He was difficult to convince;
he made his promise only with great difficulty.
Then, having performed an offering to Kāśyapa, the perfectly awakened one, they began to make a formal aspiration.
The two of them made this very aspiration:

"By this root of merit, may we become those who were prophesied by the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Awakened One, as the young brahmin named Uttara: 'Young man, when the lifespan of beings is one hundred years, you shall become a Tathāgata named Śākyamuni.'"
"May we go forth in the teaching of that Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and may we attain spiritual distinction.
Having heard their aspiration, the elder brother fell at their feet and began to make his own aspiration.
"I am stubborn and difficult to convince;
yet by this root of merit, may that Śākyamuni also discipline me with five hundred miracles and cause me to go forth."
"And having gone forth, may I attain distinction.
What do you think, monks? He who was that eldest brother, stubborn and difficult to inspire with faith, was none other than this Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa.
Those two younger brothers were these very Nadi-Kāśyapa and Gayā-Kāśyapa.
By the power of that former vow, Uruvilvākāśyapa was converted through five hundred miracles, whereas Nadīgayākāśyapa were converted with little difficulty.
Regarding the story of Kalandakanivāpa: when King Bimbisāra was still a prince, [he...]
At that time, there was a certain householder in Rājagṛha; he possessed a grove rich in flowers, fruits, and water, and he took great delight in it.
He was deeply attached to it;
when Bimbisāra went outside and saw that garden, he became exceedingly attached and said:
"Householder, give this park to me," he said;
but he would not grant it.
He was addressed once more with an offer of a bribe.
He said: "Prince,
I would rather abandon the country than give up the garden."
Prince Bimbisāra said:
"Householder, you must remember these words: when I become king,"
"Then I myself shall take it," he said;
"when you become king."
"Then I shall depart from Rājagṛha"; Prince Bimbisāra, having said "So be it," departed.
Subsequently, at another time, King Mahāpadma passed away.
Prince Bimbisāra was established in the kingdom, and he forcibly seized that park;
that householder fell into a state of heart-disease,
being excessively attached to that park.
He passed away and was reborn right there as a venomous serpent.
He remained constantly intent on seeking out the king's vulnerabilities.
Eventually, when the spring season had arrived and the trees were in full bloom, King Bimbisāra went out to that garden accompanied by his harem.
Having enjoyed amorous play there with the women of the inner apartments who were without men, he fell asleep;
the women, greedy for flowers and fruits, began to wander about on all sides;
one woman was stationed as the king’s guard with a sword.
By the power of the king’s merit, there were birds called Kalandakas;
they surrounded that venomous serpent and made a clamorous noise,
hearing which the woman bearing the sword deprived it of life with her blade.
Terrified, she let out a great cry;
then the king, startled, woke up and asked, "What is this?"
That woman said:

"Your Majesty, this venomous serpent set out to bite the King, but a great clamor was raised by the *kalandaka* birds, and I deprived him of his life. Upon hearing of the King's condition, the elite of the royal guards and the multitude of people residing in Rājagṛha assembled together.

That great garden, both inside and out, began to be agitated by a great clamor; the king, who was affectionate toward his subjects, [was moved], and the majority of the women of the harem stood with their eyes clouded with tears.
Then the king said:
"Sirs, what reward should be given to one who protects a consecrated Kṣatriya king with his own life?"
The body of people said,
"Half of the kingdom";
the king said:
"Sirs, my life was saved by the Kalandaka birds;
therefore, let half of the kingdom be given to them.
The ministers replied:
"Your Majesty, these birds belong to the animal realm;
what use have they for half the kingdom?
Let food be provided for them right there in the bamboo grove where they dwell."
The king said,
"Let it be done so";
that garden was surrounded by a bamboo grove.
The ministers prepared a meal for them in the vicinity of the Bamboo Grove (Veṇuvana);
thus, that Bamboo Grove became known as "Kalandakanivāpa" (the Place of the Feeding of the Squirrels).
King Bimbisāra’s maternal uncle had gone forth among the Ājīvikas.
He gave that park to him for his residence.
While the Blessed One was wandering on a tour through the Magadha country, he arrived at Rājagṛha and stayed at the foot of a certain tree.
King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha heard that the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the Magadhan districts, had arrived at Rājagṛha and was staying at the foot of a certain tree;
and having heard this, he [approached] with great royal splendor.
With great royal majesty,
he departed from Rājagṛha and approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
To King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha, who was seated to one side, the Blessed One addressed with a delightful discourse, instructing, exhorting,
and inspiring him.
He gladdens them;
having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dharma in many ways, he becomes silent.
Then King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra of Magadha—
Rising from his seat, arranging his upper robe over one shoulder, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, he said this to the Blessed One:
"May the Blessed One consent to take a meal at my home tomorrow, together with the community of monks.
The Blessed One consented to King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra of Magadha by remaining silent.
Then King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra of Magadha, understanding through his silence that the Blessed One had consented,
bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet, rose from his seat, and departed. That very night, King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra of Magadha prepared pure and excellent food, both hard and soft.
Having prepared everything, he rose early in the morning, arranged the seats, set out the water jars, and announced the time to the Blessed One by means of a messenger:
"It is time, Venerable Sir; the meal is ready; please do as you deem it the right time. Then...
In the forenoon, the Blessed One dressed,

took his bowl and robe, and, surrounded by a company of monks and preceded by the community of monks, approached the residence of Śreṇiya Bimbisāra, the King of Magadha. Having arrived, he sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.

Then King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha, perceiving that the community of monks headed by the Buddha was comfortably seated, personally served them with pure and excellent food, both hard and soft; having satisfied and served them in many ways with pure and excellent food, both hard and soft, with his own hands, he—
Knowing that the Blessed One had finished his meal, had washed his hands, and set aside his bowl, he took a golden pitcher and offered that grove to the Blessed One,
saying: "Venerable Sir, here is the Bamboo Grove,
the Kalandaka Feeding Ground."
"May the Blessed One dwell here at his pleasure";
likewise, it has been recorded by the Elders in the Sūtras:
"The Blessed One dwells at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground."
At that time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. In Rājagṛha there was a certain householder named Anāthapiṇḍada.
The Blessed One was invited to that house together with the community of monks;
at that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada arrived at Rājagṛha on some business and stayed the night in that householder’s residence.
Then that householder, having risen even during the night, addressed his household:
"Arise, noble ones! Arise, gentle sirs!
Split the firewood!"
Kindle the sacrificial fuel; cook the rice;
cook the soup.
"Prepare the snacks! Attend to the circular arena!
Then, this thought occurred to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
But what is it? Will this householder have a son-in-law arriving, or a daughter being married off,
or perhaps a royal visit?
"Either a guild,
or a corporation, or an assembly, or a king—
this Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha will have been invited by him for a meal at his home tomorrow."
Having understood this, he said this to that householder:
"Householder, will there be a wedding for you, or a marriage? Or is it the king of Magadha, Śreṇya Bimbisāra, who has invited you to his palace tomorrow?
"No, householder, there is no wedding for me."
Neither marriage, nor kingdom, nor guild;
Neither the guilds nor the assemblies,
nor even King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha, have been invited for a meal at his home tomorrow.
"However, the community of monks headed by the Buddha has been invited for a meal at home.
Upon hearing this sound—the word "Buddha"—which he had never heard before, all the hair-pores of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada bristled with joy.
With his hair standing on end, he said this to that householder:
"Householder, who is this called a Buddha?

"Householder, there is a śramaṇa Gautama, a son of the Śākyas, who from the Śākya clan shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron robes, and out of perfect faith went forth from the home to the homeless state; he has attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
He has attained perfect enlightenment;
he, O householder, is the one called the Buddha.
And who, O householder, is this one called the Saṅgha?
Householder, there are also sons of noble family from the kṣatriya caste who, having shaved off their hair and beards and donned saffron-colored robes, have gone forth out of right faith.
Having gone forth from the home to the homeless life, they followed after that very Blessed One who had himself gone forth;
noble sons— from brahmin families, from vaiśya families, and even from śūdra families— having shaved off their hair and beards and donned saffron-colored robes, [went forth] with perfect faith.
Having gone forth from the household life into homelessness, they followed after that very Blessed One who had gone forth;
this, householder, is what is called the Saṅgha.
"Tomorrow I have invited the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, to my home for a meal.
Householder, where does the Blessed One reside at present?
"Right here in Rājagṛha, in the Śītavana cemetery."
"It is possible for us, householder, to see that Blessed One; therefore, householder, wait for a moment. It is possible that you will see him tomorrow once he has arrived here."
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having fallen asleep that night with mindfulness directed toward the Buddha,
approached the Śivikā Gate at the hour of dawn, perceiving it to be day.
At that time, the Śivikā Gate remained open during the two watches of the night.
"Let there be no obstruction for the messengers coming from the east and the west, nor for those departing";
he then saw that the gate of the palanquin stood wide open.
And it was filled with light;
this thought occurred to him:
"Surely the night has turned to dawn."
For indeed, the gate of the palanquin stood open;
perceiving this, he went out from the city by that very light;
and as soon as he had gone out, that light vanished.
Darkness appeared;
he was seized by fear;
he was overcome by trembling.
A thrill of horripilation arose in him,
thinking, "May no one— whether a human, a non-human, or a rogue— cause me harm, or may I not have to pay the abundant bride-price before it has been received.
Having understood this and desiring to turn back, he circumambulated the sacrificial ground of the divine son Madhuskandha.
And he paid homage.
Then, this thought occurred to the divine son Madhuskandha:
"Today, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada must attain the vision of the Truth."

"Thinking, 'This man will this very day abandon the Buddha, the Blessed One, and pay homage to another deity,' [the god] illuminated the entire space from the gate of the palanquin to the Śītavana cemetery with a sublime radiance and said to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
'Come forward, householder!'"
Do not retreat;
for you, it is better to advance than to retreat.
For what reason?
A hundred horses, a hundred gold coins, a hundred mule-drawn chariots filled with various kinds of wealth, and a hundred mare-drawn chariots.
They do not equal even a sixteenth part of a single step forward.
Come forward, householder; do not retreat.
Advancing is better for you than retreating;
for what reason is that?
There were a hundred Himalayan elephants, adorned with gold and jewels,
possessing tusks as long as plow-poles, of massive body, and of noble breed.
They do not equal even a sixteenth part of a single step taken [toward him].
Come forward, householder; do not turn back.
It is better for you to advance; it is not better to retreat.
For what reason? Because there are a hundred maidens from Kamboja, wearing jeweled earrings,
bearing golden armlets, with gold neck-ornaments around their necks, and well-adorned.
They do not equal even a sixteenth part of a single step taken [toward him].
Come forward, householder; do not retreat.
"It is better for you to advance,
not to retreat.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada [spoke] this to that son of the gods.
He said: "Who are you, O gentle-faced one?
"Householder, I am a young brahmin named Madhuskandha, your own old friend from former times."
Thus, having developed a serene mind toward the two monks Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, I passed away and was reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings.
He is a resident right here at this very gateway of Śivikā;
therefore, I say to you:
"Go forward, householder; do not turn back."
"It is better for you to go forward, not to turn back";
then this thought occurred to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
The Buddha will not be inferior, nor will the proclamation of the Dharma be inferior,
since even the deities now exert themselves with longing to behold that Blessed One.
Having understood this, he went toward the Śītavana cemetery.
At that time, the Blessed One was walking back and forth on a walkway in the open air outside the monastery, for the most part waiting for the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada saw the Blessed One from afar.
Having seen him, he approached the Blessed One;
having approached, the householder greeted the Blessed One with words of welcome, asking:
"I hope the Blessed One has slept well?"
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"In every way, indeed, the brahmin who has attained final nirvana sleeps in peace—
he who is not defiled by sensual desires, being liberated and free from the substrate of existence."
Having cut off all attachment here and subdued the fever of the heart,
one who is tranquil sleeps happily with a mind that has attained peace.
Then the Blessed One, taking the householder Anāthapiṇḍada with him, entered the monastery and sat down on the prepared seat.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was sitting to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma.
He inspires them and gladdens them;
he delivers that Dharma discourse which is to be performed by the Blessed Buddhas at the outset [of their teaching].

Namely, a discourse on giving, a discourse on ethical discipline, and a discourse on heaven; and, in detail, the factors conducive to purification—namely, the defects, dangers, and defilements of sensual pleasures, as well as the benefits, renunciation, seclusion, and purification.
And when the Blessed One saw that his mind was joyful, pliable, glad, free from hindrances, and capable and competent to understand the exalted teaching of the Dharma, [he taught it].

Then, as the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, thoroughly proclaim in detail that preeminent teaching of the Dharma—namely, the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, while seated on that very seat, realized the Four Noble Truths:
namely, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Just as a clean cloth, free from stains and ready for dyeing, takes on the dye perfectly when placed in the dye-vat,
even so the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, while seated on that very seat, realized the four noble truths: namely, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada—having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, known the Dharma, and plunged deeply into the Dharma; having crossed beyond doubt and transcended uncertainty;

no longer dependent on others and not led by another; having attained confidence regarding the teachings in the Teacher’s instruction—rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and...

Bowing with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was, he said this to the Blessed One: "I have transcended, O Venerable One; I have truly transcended! I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks."
"Consider me a lay follower (upāsaka), from this day forward for as long as life lasts, one who has taken refuge with his very life and is full of faith.
Then the Blessed One said this to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada: "What is your name, householder?"
"Venerable sir, my name is Sudatta;
however, because I provide alms-food to those who are without protectors,
people know me as 'the householder Anāthapiṇḍada,' the householder Anāthapiṇḍada."
"Householder, from what region do you come?
"Venerable sir, there is among the eastern provinces a town of the Kosalans called Śrāvastī; there I dwell."
Anāthapiṇḍada invited the Buddha, saying: "May the Blessed One come to Śrāvastī;
I shall attend upon the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, for as long as life lasts, with robes, alms-food, and medicinal requisites for the sick."
“Are there monasteries in Śrāvastī, householder?
“No, Venerable Sir.
“Householder, wherever there are monasteries, there monks consider it proper to come, to go, and to dwell.”
"May the Blessed One come;
I shall act in such a way that there will be monasteries in Śrāvastī, so that the monks will think: 'We should come, we should go, and we should dwell here.'"
The Blessed One consented to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada by remaining silent;
the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, understanding the Blessed One’s consent through his silence, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet and departed from the Blessed One’s presence.
Then, having performed and accomplished all his business and duties in Rājagṛha, he approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable One, grant me a monk as an assistant, with whom as an assistant I may have a monastery built for the sake of the Blessed One.
The Blessed One reflected:
"Which monk is it that the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, together with his retinue, [desires]?"
The multitude of people residing in Śrāvastī was compliant;
he saw [this] regarding the monk Śāriputra.
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the venerable Śāriputra: "Recall, Śāriputra, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada together with his retinue."
"And the multitude of people residing in Śrāvastī.
The Venerable Śāriputra consented to the Blessed One by remaining silent;
then the Venerable Śāriputra, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, departed from the Blessed One's presence.
Śāriputra departs for Śrāvastī:
Then, at the end of that very night, the Venerable Śāriputra dressed in the forenoon, took his bowl and outer robe, and entered Rājagṛha for alms.
Having walked for alms in Rājagṛha and finished his meal, he returned from his alms-round after the meal, and having put away his bedding and seat exactly as he had used them, [he set out].
Having taken up his bowl and robe, he set out on a journey toward Śrāvastī.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, taking a great deal of provisions for the road, reached Śrāvastī by staying one night at each stage. As soon as he entered Śrāvastī, he went from park to park.
Wandering from garden to garden and from grove to grove, pacing back and forth and strolling about, he spoke thus:

"Which will be that spot of earth not too far from Śrāvastī and not too near, which is quiet by day with little bustle, and silent at night with little noise, and where there is little contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and creeping reptiles, so that I may have a monastery built for the sake of the Blessed One?"

The householder Anāthapiṇḍada saw Prince Jeta’s grove, not too far from Śrāvastī and not too near, which was little frequented by people during the day and free from clamor, and at night had little noise or sound, and was free from the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and crawling reptiles. Having seen it, this thought occurred to him:
"I shall have a monastery built here for the sake of the Blessed One.
As soon as he had entered his own residence, he approached Prince Jeta;
having approached him, he said this to Prince Jeta:
"Prince, grant me the grove;
I shall have a monastery built there for the sake of the Blessed One.
He replied:
"Householder, that park is not mine; rather, it is my garden.
For a second and even a third time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said this to Prince Jeta:
"O Prince, grant me the grove;
I shall have a monastery built there for the sake of the Blessed One. [The prince replied:
"It has not been relinquished."
“Householder, my park is worth ten million pieces of gold spread out.
Then again, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said this to Prince Jeta:
"You have paid the price for the grove, Prince;
accept the gold and bullion;
the grove is mine."
"Who has received the guest-offering?
"You have received it.
They fell into a dispute, saying, "I have received it," and "You have not received it."
They set out toward where the lay officials were.
In the meantime, this thought occurred to the four world-protectors:
"This householder Anāthapiṇḍada is intent on having a monastery built for the sake of the Blessed One."
"Assistance must be rendered to him.
Thereupon, having manifested themselves as judicial officers, they sat down in the court of justice.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and Prince Jeta approached the presence of the judicial officers.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika explained this matter in detail to the officials;
they said,
"Prince, you have fixed the price for the park."
"Accept this gold;
the park belongs to the householder";
he remained silent.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having brought forth abundant gold by means of carts, loads, bundles, baskets, camels, oxen, and donkeys,
began to cover the entire Jeta Grove with it;
yet it was not finished.
There remained a certain portion of ground still uncovered;
then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, reflecting on this matter, stood silent for a moment, thinking: "Which treasure-trove shall it be?"
It should be neither too little nor too much, so that this uncovered portion of ground will be covered,
yet it shall not need to be guarded again.
Prince Jeta reflected:
"Surely the householder Anāthapiṇḍada is feeling regret;
why else would he abandon such a vast heap of wealth for the sake of a grove?"
Having understood this, he said to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
"If you have regret, O householder, take back the gold;
the park belongs to me alone."
"Prince, I have no regret;
rather, it was while reflecting upon this very matter that I remained silent for a moment:
'Which of those treasures will it be?'"
Neither too little nor too much,
so that this uncovered portion of ground shall be covered,
and it will not need to be gathered up again.
Then this thought occurred to Prince Jeta:
"Surely the Buddha will not be an inferior one."
The proclamation of the Dharma is not a trivial matter,
since this householder now relinquishes such a vast mass of wealth for the sake of a grove.
Having understood this, he said to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
"Householder, give me a plot of ground that has not yet been covered;
there I shall have a gateway constructed for the sake of the Blessed One."
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada offered to Prince Jeta a portion of ground not yet covered [with grass],
whereupon Prince Jeta had a gateway constructed for the sake of the Blessed One.
[Obstruction by the Tīrthyas]

Then, as the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had begun to have a monastery built for the sake of the Blessed One, the non-Buddhist teachers— their minds agitated by intense malice— gathered together and approached the householder Anāthapiṇḍada;
having approached him, they said:
"Householder, do not build a monastery here for the sake of the ascetic Gautama.
For what reason?
We have already divided the cities among ourselves."
"The ascetic Gautama's [residence] is Rājagṛha; ours is Śrāvastī. He said:
"The cities have been divided by you, but my own property has not;
I shall cause a religious edifice to be built for whomever so desires."
They went into the presence of the king;
there too they were defeated by Anāthapiṇḍada.
The heretics, like crows with unaltered faces, said:
"Householder, we do not grant you the freedom to act as you wish;
the foremost disciple of the ascetic Gautama has arrived,
and if he defeats us in debate, then you may have the monastery built."
He said, "It is so; however, let me first look upon the noble Śāriputra.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada approached the venerable Śāriputra.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the venerable Śāriputra, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said this to the venerable Śāriputra:
"Venerable Śāriputra, the heretics say this:"
"Householder, we do not grant you the freedom to act as you wish;
the foremost disciple of the ascetic Gautama has arrived.
If he defeats us in debate,"
"Build a monastery.
"How should one proceed in this matter?
The Venerable Śāriputra reflected:
"Are there any roots of merit in these people, or are there none? He sees that there are; "To whom are they bound?
To me alone."
Again he reflects:
"Are my disciples to be converted only these many, or are there others also to be converted by means of debate? He sees that there are; he sees how long it will take for them to assemble.
"Upon the passing of seven days";
having reflected, he said:
"Householder, let it be so."
But on the seventh day, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, filled with joy and gladness, approached the place where the heretics were; having approached them, (SBV I 174)
He said this to the non-Buddhist teachers:
"Venerable Ārya Śāriputra says: 'Excellent; let it be so.'"
"But on the seventh day," they said;
they reflected,
"There must be two reasons for this."
Or perhaps he wishes to flee;
or perhaps he wishes to seek out allies;
what is the appropriate course of action here?
"We too shall seek out an ally. They began to search for an ally,
and while they were searching, they saw a wandering mendicant named Raktākṣa.
He was told by them:
"You are our fellow religious practitioner; you have been challenged by us to debate as the foremost disciple of the ascetic Gautama."
He sought an ally, saying:
"Provide us with assistance; in what length of time?"
"On the seventh day from now; that is auspicious, let it be so;
whenever your assembly takes place, you must inform me."
The Tīrthyas, their minds filled with apprehension and agitation, seek out an ally day after day and count the days. Thus do the Tīrthyas and Śāriputra contend.
On the seventh day, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had seats prepared on a wide expanse of ground,
and a lion throne was set out for the venerable Śāriputra;
meanwhile, the non-Buddhist teachers dwelling in various regions assembled there.

The multitude of people residing in Śrāvastī and many hundreds of thousands of living beings dwelling in its vicinity— some born of curiosity, and others impelled by their previous roots of merit— [assembled].
Then the Venerable Śāriputra, escorted by the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and his retinue, entered the assembly hall for debate.
Surveying those to be converted, he ascended the lion throne with a smile and with a perfectly tranquil deportment, and sat down.
The entire assembly, with attentive minds, sat watching the Venerable Śāriputra.
The Defeat of the Tīrthyas:
Then the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Tīrthyas: "Sirs, what will you do first?"
"Or will you transform it?
They replied,
"We shall do it."
"Transform yourself!
The Venerable Śāriputra reflected:
"If I were to do so..."
"Even the world together with its gods will not be able to alter it, let alone the wanderer Raktākṣa.
Having understood this, he said this to the wanderer Raktākṣa: "You do it!"
"I shall transform it";
he was skilled in the art of sorcery, and by him it was made to bloom with beautiful flowers.
A mango tree was conjured up;

the Venerable Śāriputra then unleashed a violent wind and rain, by which the tree was uprooted along with its roots and scattered here and there, becoming beyond the reach even of those who practice yoga.
Then he created a lotus pond;
the Venerable Śāriputra created a young elephant,
which trampled it on all sides.
He manifested a seven-headed nāga; the Venerable Śāriputra manifested a garuḍa by which that [nāga] was carried away;
he then manifested a vetāḍa.
The Venerable Śāriputra had pinned him down with mantras; the Vetāla, being wrongly employed, intended to kill his own master and rushed right upon him.
Then, terrified, trembling, agitated, and with his hair standing on end, he fell at the feet of the Venerable Śāriputra, saying, "Noble Śāriputra, save me! I have come to you for refuge.
Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra released the spells.
That vetāla was pacified;
the Venerable Śāriputra taught him the Dharma, and having conceived faith, he said:
"Venerable Śāriputra, may I receive the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya;
may I practice the holy life in the presence of the venerable Śāriputra.
The venerable Śāriputra then granted him the going-forth and the full ordination.
Instruction was given;
by striving, exerting himself, and making an effort, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions;
he became an arhat.

He had become one who was free from passion for the three realms, for whom a clod of earth and gold were equal, whose mind was like space or the palm of a hand, who was indifferent to the axe or sandalwood, who had split the eggshell of ignorance with knowledge,

who had attained the clear knowledges, superknowledges, and analytical insights, and who was turned away from existence, gain, and greed; he had become worthy of worship, honor, and salutation by the gods, including Indra and Upendra.
Then that assembly, their eyes wide with wonder,
became full of faith toward the Venerable Śāriputra and said:
"The noble Śāriputra has vanquished a great bull among debaters!"
Having understood this, they turned their gaze toward the face of the venerable Śāriputra.

Then, the venerable Śāriputra, having discerned the inclinations, latent tendencies, elements, and natures of that assembly, delivered a Dharma teaching conducive to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.
Upon hearing it, many thousands of beings attained great spiritual distinction.
Some generated the aspiration for the enlightenment of a śrāvaka;
some for the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; and some for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Some took up the training precepts for going for refuge;
some realized the fruit of stream-entry; and some realized the fruit of once-returning.
Some attained the fruit of non-returning;
some, having gone forth, realized arhatship through the complete abandonment of all afflictions;
for the most part, that assembly was inclined toward the Buddha.
Inclined toward the Dharma,
leaning toward the Saṅgha,
she was established [in that state].
The non-Buddhist teachers reflected:
"It is not possible for us to defeat him in debate; we must devise a stratagem."
"Let us work here for wages; then, having found an opportunity, we shall have him killed by a hired assassin.
Having all come together, they went into the presence of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and said:
"Householder, you have cut off all our means of livelihood;
therefore, have mercy on us.
Let us perform work for wages in your monastery."
"We have resided here for a long time;
let us not abandon this country," Anāthapiṇḍada said.
First, I shall look for the noble Śāriputra;
he approached the venerable Śāriputra, and having approached, he said this to the venerable Śāriputra: "Noble one," [he said].
The non-Buddhist ascetics said,
"All our means of livelihood have been cut off by you;
therefore, please show us compassion."
"We perform work for hire in your monastery;
we have resided here for a long time,
so let us not be forced to abandon our country."
The Venerable Śāriputra began to reflect:
"Do they possess any roots of merit, or do they not? He saw that they did possess them; he then considered with whom those roots were connected.
Thinking, "It shall be mine alone," he reflected and said: "Householder, let it be so."
"What contradiction is there in this? they thought, and they began to perform work for wages in that monastery;
then the Venerable Śāriputra manifested a fierce man as a supervisor of the ropes.
He began to have that work performed;
the Venerable Śāriputra, knowing it was the time for their conversion, stood walking back and forth near them at the foot of a tree.
He was seen by them, and they reflected:
"This is the time to kill him; he is staying in a secluded place.
They approached him and stood surrounding him.
The Venerable Śāriputra reflected:
"With what kind of mind have these approached me? he thought;
as soon as he saw that it was with a murderous mind, he released that created being who was the cane-guardian.
Therefore, they were pursued by him with the command, "Go! Perform your work!
They said, "Noble Śāriputra, protect us!"
He said: "Venerable one, go;
let them rest for now."
They reflected:
"Such is this Great Being;
yet we harbor murderous intent toward him."
Knowing, "This one has a mind of loving-kindness toward us," they became full of faith.
Then, the Venerable Śāriputra, having understood their intentions, latent tendencies, elements, and dispositions, delivered a Dharma teaching conducive to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.

Having heard which, they shattered with the vajra of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity that rose up with its twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry. Those who had seen the truth said:
"May we, Śāriputra, obtain the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of monks within this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya;
may we, Venerable Śāriputra, practice the holy life in your presence.
They were then granted the going-forth and the full ordination by the Venerable Śāriputra.
Instruction was given; by them, as they were applying themselves and striving, [it was attained].

Exerting themselves, they understood this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra to be moving and unstable; having struck down all conditioned states by means of their nature of decay, fall, scattering, and destruction, and through the abandonment of all defilements, they realized arhatship and thus became arhats.

They became free from passion for the three realms; regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal; possessing minds as even as space or the palm of a hand; being like an axe and sandalwood (indifferent to harm or honor); having split the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge;

having attained the superknowledges, the higher faculties, and the analytical insights; turning their backs on existence, gain, greed, and honor; and becoming worthy of worship, veneration, and salutation by the gods, including Indra and Upendra.
Regarding the construction of the monasteries there, the venerable Śāriputra took up the monastery-measuring cord at one end, and the householder Anāthapiṇḍada likewise took it up at the other end.
The Venerable Śāriputra began to manifest a smile; the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said:
"Noble Śāriputra, Tathāgatas or the disciples of a Tathāgata do not manifest a smile without cause or condition."
"What, noble Śāriputra, is the cause? What is the condition for manifesting this smile?
"It is so, householder."
It is so; neither Tathāgatas nor the disciples of the Tathāgata manifest a smile without cause or condition.
You have taken up this sūtra here, and in the Tuṣita realm of the gods, a golden palace has been manifested.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, his eyes wide with wonder, said: "Noble Śāriputra, if that is so,
then please spread out the cloth once more, to an even greater extent."
"I shall clarify my mind";
the Venerable Śāriputra took up that discourse;
and the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, with an even greater degree of intense and fervent faith, clarified his mind.
Immediately upon that arising of faith, that golden mansion became composed of the four jewels;
and this was reported to him by the Venerable Śāriputra.
Thereupon, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada’s stream of merit increased further and further.
Sixteen large monasteries were constructed,
as well as sixty small dwellings.
Having had the sixteen large monasteries and the sixty small dwellings built, and having filled them with all necessary requisites, he approached the Venerable Śāriputra.
Having approached, he said this to the venerable Śāriputra:
"Venerable Śāriputra, by how many stages of travel does the Blessed One proceed on the road?
It is, for example, like that of a universal monarch, householder."
"By what measure does a wheel-turning monarch travel?
Householder, a wheel-turning monarch travels a distance of ten *krośas* per stage of his journey.
Then, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having calculated the number of halting places along the route between Śrāvastī and Rājagṛha, had rest-houses constructed.
A hall for giving was constructed; a man was appointed as the announcer of the time;
and archways were erected, adorned with parasols, banners, and flags, sprinkled with sandalwood water, and hung with censers of fragrant incense.

The blind regain their sight; the deaf their hearing;
and the mute become capable of speech.
Those with impaired sense faculties regain their senses;

"Whichever messenger I send, he goes forth into homelessness right there, because the Dharma and Vinaya are so well-proclaimed. Udāyin saw him and asked,

The tree of the Victor has been planted by one scorched by the fire of the afflictions.

By whom you were nurtured like a young tree when you had only sprouts for wings, thinking, "This child is my offspring," now that you have reached the enjoyment of the fruits of your domain as a son.

"When you were first born, this was promised by you:

"Make your mind inclined toward coming;

Having taken the letter, Udāyin arrived at Śrāvastī on the seventh day; having dispelled the fatigue of the journey, he approached the presence of the Blessed One,

By what path will you lead that Buddha, whose range is infinite and who is trackless— He for whom there exists nowhere any guiding craving, with its web and its attachments?
By what path will you lead that Buddha, whose range is infinite and who is trackless— one for whom there is no guiding leader of craving, nor any web-like attachment clinging anywhere?
How will you lead by means of any path that Buddha, whose conquest never increases, whose victory is never followed by anything whatsoever, and who has an infinite range and is trackless?
How will you lead by means of any path that Buddha, whose victory never increases and whose victory is never followed by anything whatsoever, who has an infinite range and is trackless?
Failing to find a reply, he said:

He then explained to him in detail the rules of proper conduct, saying, "This is what you must do."
"From this day forward, Udāyin, you must not lie down in a single room together with a woman.

Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he said this to the Blessed One:

The Blessed One said: "Udāyin, go;

Standing at the gate, one should say,
"A Śākya bhikṣu has arrived"; if they say, "Enter," [then enter].
One should enter;
once having entered, if they ask, "Are there other Śākya bhikṣus as well? [one should answer accordingly].
It should be said, "They exist.
If they say, "The prince Sarvārthasiddha also has such a dress," one should say, "He indeed has such a dress."
And you must not reside in the royal palace; if they ask why Prince Sarvārthasiddha does not take up residence in the royal palace, you should say, "He does not."
If they ask where he dwells, it should be said: "In the forest or in a monastery.
If they ask what kind of monastery this is, [it should be described].
It should be depicted and shown in the form of the Jeta Grove;
and if they ask, "Will Prince Sarvārthasiddha come? [one should say he will].
It should be said:
"He will come; after how long?"
Udāyin replied: "After the passing of seven days."
"Lord, I am going.
The Blessed One said, "Go. By his word, the kings' prosperity was fulfilled.
"By the mind of the gods, and by the mere arising of a thought, everything is thus accomplished for those who meditate.

Like the sun and a firefly,

And at the site of Kuṭikāvastu,

"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied to the Blessed One, and having done so, he announced to the monks:

"Whoever among you is able to behold the reunion of father and son, let him take up his robes.
Then the Blessed One—tamed, with a tamed retinue; calm, with a calm retinue; liberated, with a liberated retinue—[proceeded].

Like the moon surrounded by a host of stars,
like the sun surrounded by a thousand rays,
like Dhṛtarāṣṭra surrounded by a host of gandharvas.
Like Virūḍhaka surrounded by a host of kumbhāṇḍas, like Virūpākṣa surrounded by a host of nāgas,
and like Dhanada surrounded by a host of yakṣas.
Like Vemacitrī surrounded by a host of asuras, like Śakra surrounded by a host of the thirty-three gods, like Brahmā surrounded by the Brahmakāyika gods.
Like the ocean when it is still,
