like a lordly elephant whose rut has subsided.
With his sense faculties well-tamed, his conduct and deportment were undisturbed;
he was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
and his body shone with the eighty secondary characteristics.
His body was adorned with a fathom-wide radiance;
possessing a brilliance exceeding that of a thousand suns,
he was like a moving mountain of jewels.
The Samantatabhadra, endowed with the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses.
Endowed with the three unique applications of mindfulness and great compassion,
he arrived at Rohaka together with a great community of monks.
King Śuddhodana heard that Prince Sarvārthasiddha had reached the Rohakā River.
Upon hearing this, King Śuddhodana had the city of Kapilavastu cleared of stones, pebbles, and gravel;
it was sprinkled with sandalwood water and adorned with various censers of fragrant incense.
Garlands and bundles of silk ribbons were hung [along the way], and between the Rohaka River and the Nyagrodha Grove, a great adornment of the road was prepared;
on a wide expanse of ground, a variegated arrangement of seats was made.
There, at the Rohaka River, some monks were washing their hands;
some were discarding tooth-sticks;
and some were bathing.
The Śākyas of Kapilavastu heard that Prince Sarvārthasiddha had arrived;
having heard this, they all went out to the Nyagrodha Grove.

Some were urged on by their previous roots of merit, while others were filled with curiosity, wondering: "Will the father pay homage at the feet of his son, or will the son pay homage at the feet of his father?"
Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One:
"If I enter Kapilavastu on foot, the proud Śākyans will express their lack of faith, saying: 'The Prince Sarvārthasiddha went to the forest of asceticism and obtained nothing.'"

For he who was indeed followed by many hundreds of thousands of deities as he departed through the upper air, and having practiced hundreds of thousands of difficult austerities for so long a time and attained the deathless (*amṛta*), has now entered on foot— such is his magical power.

Then the Blessed One entered such a state of meditative concentration that, with his mind thus composed, he rose up into the air above in the eastern direction and performed the four modes of conduct: namely, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.
He sits down,
he prepares his bed,
and he also enters the fire-element concentration.
From the body of the Blessed One, the Buddha, who had entered the fire-element concentration, various rays of light issued forth—
blue and yellow.
Red,
white, and madder-colored.
They are the color of crystal;
he displays even twin miracles;
his lower body blazes with fire.
From the upper part of his body, cool streams of water flow forth;
the upper part of his body blazes with fire;
from the lower part of his body, cool streams of water flow forth.
Just as in the eastern direction, so too in the southern, western,

and northern directions— having thus displayed the fourfold miraculous power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) in the four directions— he withdrew those miraculous performances and stood at a height of only seven palm trees.
At a height of seven palm trees, O monks, was the Blessed One; at six palm trees, the monks.
In five [cases] the Blessed One [is the authority],
and also in five [cases] the monks;
in four [cases] the Blessed One.
Furthermore, monks, [the Saṃgha] consists of four; the Blessed One [is the fifth]; furthermore, monks, [the Saṃgha] consists of three; the Blessed One [is the fourth].
The Blessed One [stood] at a distance of two [tālas] from the two; the monks [stood] at a distance of two [tālas] from the Blessed One; the Blessed One [stood] at the height of a palm tree.
O monks,
when [the Buddha] stood at the height of a palm tree, the Blessed One was seven men's height,
and the monks were seven men's height.
The Blessed One [is proficient] in six [factors],
the monks in six;
the Blessed One [is proficient] in five.
In five matters, monks, the Blessed One [is the authority]; in four matters, monks, the monks [are the authority].
In three cases, the Blessed One [is the authority];
in three cases, the monks [are the authority]; in two cases, the Blessed One [is the authority].
"O monks, there are two [cases];
[in the case] exceeding a man's height, [the Blessed One said],
'In the case exceeding a man's height.'"
The monks,
having seen such a miracle on earth by King Śuddhodana and [his] attainment of monkhood, were overcome with confusion;
they did not know which of the two was the Blessed One.
Then he addressed the venerable Udāyin:
"Udāyin, there are many here who have gone forth, clothed in saffron robes; which one is the prince?"
The Venerable Udāyin, pointing out the Blessed One, said:
"This is that Blessed One, the ender of existence, the Lord of the mind, the Guide;
he is the destroyer of the afflictions, the sun that reveals the true meaning of reality."
O King, this son of yours, the Lord of Dharma, shines forth today—pure, having attained his heart's desire, possessing the ten powers, and having reached the further shore in all things. Behold him!
Then King Śuddhodana, bowing his body toward the Tathāgata, paid homage at his feet and spoke this verse:
"O you of vast wisdom, this is the third [time] for you."
I pay homage at the feet of the All-Seeing One;
when he was being born, the earth trembled,
yet the shadow of the Jambu tree did not leave his body.
Then the Śākyas and Śākyāyanīs, seeing King Śuddhodana prostrate at the feet of the Blessed One, expressed their displeasure, saying:
"How is it that a father now performs a salutation at the feet of his son?
King Śuddhodana, addressing the Śākyas and Śākyāyanīs, spoke thus:
"O venerable ones, it was not only now that I prostrated at the feet of Prince Sarvārthasiddha;
rather, when Prince Sarvārthasiddha was born, there occurred a great earthquake and this entire world was suffused with a sublime radiance—

even those intermediate spaces between worlds, which are blind, shrouded in darkness, and enveloped in thick gloom, where even these two, the sun and the moon, despite being so powerful and majestic, do not experience their own light."
At that time, they too were suffused with a sublime radiance;

and those beings who had been reborn there, by means of that light, saw one another and recognized each other, saying, "Other beings, sirs, have also been reborn here; other beings, sirs, have also been reborn here."

Even then, I performed the prostration at the feet of the Blessed One, the Bodhisattva; and also when the prince Sarvārthasiddha, while traveling among my fields of labor, sat in the shade of a rose-apple tree and,

secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, entered upon the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion.
Having attained and dwelling in the first dhyāna, which resembles the untainted state,
the shadows of the other trees slant toward the east (or incline toward the east).
At Prācīnaprāgbhāra,
the shade of the Jambu tree did not leave the body of the Bodhisattva;
even then, my mind being captivated by that marvelous and wonderful phenomenon, I again bowed my head at the feet of the Blessed One.
Now for the third time I bow at the feet of the Blessed One, since I speak thus: "O you of vast intelligence, O you with all-seeing eyes, this is the third time I pay homage to your feet."
"As he was being born, the earth trembled,
yet the shadow of the Jambu tree did not leave his body.

Then the Blessed One, having withdrawn those miraculous manifestations, entered among the assembly of many hundreds of thousands and sat down upon the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.

Then King Śuddhodana, his heart choked with tears and his eyes clouded with weeping, questioned the Blessed One with verses and song: "Having dwelt in magnificent palaces within your father’s house..."
How do you dwell alone in forests filled with danger?
The Blessed One said:
"O lord of men, I dwell in the ten noble abodes where sages reside,
liberated from the bonds of the household."
The king said:
"Having previously slept upon comfortable couches with legs of ivory and gold, spread with fine coverings, how is it that you now sleep upon a mere mat?"
The Blessed One said:
"O King, I sleep without attachment and free from all feverish distress upon the delightful bed of liberation, strewn with the flowers of the factors of enlightenment."
The king said:
"O hero, having gone to your own home by means of elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles."
How is it that you tread with your feet upon this earth filled with thorns?
The Blessed One said:
"Mounted upon the chariot of the bases of psychic power, which provides right effort,
I traverse the entire earth unharmed by the thorns of the afflictions."
King Śuddhodana said:
"O Hero, formerly you shone resplendent, clothed in garments of Kāśī silk;
how does your body now endure this coarse saffron robe?"
The Blessed One said:
"O King, the garment of modesty is my outer robe; my upper cloak is the covering [of shame].
Clad in these, the sages shine in peace within the forest."
King Śuddhodana said: "In former times, you indeed ate śāli rice of manifold flavors served in golden vessels."
O Lord, having eaten alms-food, how is it that today you eat such coarse food, and how does it even reach your throat?
The Blessed One said:
"Indeed, for one who is devoted to renunciation and established in meditative concentration, my food of the essence of the Dharma is supreme."
Having indeed abandoned all craving for food, I wander for the sake of compassion toward the world.
The king said:
"Having drunk the juice of grapes and sugar, which is so pleasant for the throat,
why do you drink waters that are hot and turbid?"
The Blessed One said:
"O lord of men, I drink the blissful flavor of the Dharma;
having drunk it, all other drinks appear to me like poison."
King Śuddhodana said:
"Formerly, you indeed dwelt in palatial mansions and on the rooftops of the palace, according to the seasons."
O Subuddhi, as you dwell alone in the forest today, why does fear not enter you?
The Blessed One said:
"Gautamas, those roots of all fear which were my impurities along with their latent tendencies have been abandoned."
Thus, free from sorrow, I dwell in fearlessness;
not even the slightest bit of fear exists for me here.
King Śuddhodana said:
"In the past, indeed, you always bathed in a most beautiful bathing chamber with the finest and most excellent perfumed waters."
O Lord of Sages, who here today shall bathe you, now that you are alone and engaged in dwelling in the forest?
The Blessed One said:
"O Gautama, the Dharma is a lake with morality as its bathing ford;
it is indeed untroubled and praised even by the virtuous."
Having bathed in which, men cross to the further shore by means of the qualities of the Vedas, their limbs remaining dry.
King Śuddhodana said:
"O Hero, having bathed in your own home with jars of gold and silver..."
How can you bathe in waters that are both hot and turbid?
The Blessed One said: "O Gautama, the river Śuddhā has holy bathing places; it is indeed untroubled and praised even by the virtuous."
Having bathed in which, men cross to the further shore with their limbs remaining dry, by means of the qualities of the Vedas.
King Śuddhodana said:
"O Hero, you shone in the past with your limbs anointed with yellow sandalwood and draped in the finest garments of Kāśī; now, deprived of those, you do not shine."
The Blessed One said:
"Virtue is indeed the foremost ornament; virtue is like an unguent.
What use have I for earrings of gold and jewels that produce madness?"
King Śuddhodana said:
"From where has this sense of inferiority arisen, and from where this fear of existence? Or from what has this world-weariness been born? Being questioned, tell me that."
The Blessed One said: "Listen, I shall tell you that from which my contempt arose, from which my fear of existence arose, or from which my world-weariness was born."
If these three— old age, disease, and death— did not exist,
even for me there would be delight in the most charming sense objects.
King Śuddhodana said:
"Excellent, O hero! You are well-born, the delight of the Śākya clan, since you are thus unstained by the eight worldly concerns."
Then, filled with joy and with a blossoming serenity, he circumambulated the Saṅgha and the Ṛṣi,
and bowed his head at the feet of the Lord of Munis.
Standing there, he gazed all around at the Sugata.
Then this thought occurred to King Śuddhodana: "It is a great gain for me, a well-attained fortune, that my son has realized such a multitude of virtues."
Then the Blessed One, having understood the inclinations, latent tendencies, dispositions, and natures of that assembly in the Nyagrodha Grove,
gave such a Dharma teaching that, upon hearing it, seventy-seven thousand Śākyas headed by King Śuddhodana realized the fruit of stream-entry, with the exception of King Śuddhodana himself.
Devadatta was evil-intentioned and conceited;
therefore, he did not realize the vision of truth.
Overcome by anger, he said:
"What if I were to learn such an art of subjugation by which I might win over the entire world?
Thus he was addressed by the Śākyas, who had shown him affection and goodwill.
"Enough, Devadatta; do not speak thus:
'The Blessed One is of great supernatural power and great majesty'";
he remained silent.
In the Brahmāvarta garden, such a Dharma was taught that, upon hearing it, seventy-six thousand Śākyas headed by Droṇodana realized the fruit of stream-entry,
with the exception of King Śuddhodana;
Devadatta, however, continued to revile him in the same manner.
In the Rohītaka grove, such a Dharma was taught that, upon hearing it, seventy-five thousand Śākyas headed by Amṛtodana realized the fruit of stream-entry,
with the exception of King Śuddhodana;
Devadatta, however, continued to revile him in the same manner.

Among the remaining assembly, some generated the aspiration for the enlightenment of a śrāvaka; some for the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; and some for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Some realized the fruit of stream-entry; some the fruit of once-returning;
and some the fruit of non-returning.
Some, having gone forth, realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.
Some went for refuge to the Buddha; some to the Dharma;
and some to the Saṅgha.
For the most part, that assembly was established as being inclined toward the Buddha, leaning toward the Dharma, and directed toward the Saṅgha. Then,
this thought occurred to King Śuddhodana:
"Previously, the Blessed One was worthy of worship, honor, and salutation by the world including the gods and asuras; now he is honored by humans but no longer honored by the gods.
Then, a certain Śākya youth spoke this verse:
O Great Sage, best among speakers, this multitude has been satisfied by you with the rain of the True Dharma,
having been lifted up from the path of terrible ruin.
"For this world is indeed established upon the path to liberation.
King Śuddhodana, however, out of excessive joy, did not perceive the truths, thinking: "My son alone possesses such great supernatural power and such great majesty."
The Blessed One reflected:
"For what reason does King Śuddhodana not perceive the truths?
Then this thought occurred to him:
"Because of excessive joy, thinking, 'My son alone possesses such great supernatural power and such great majesty,' one must by all means effect the removal of his pride.
Truths are not perceived for two reasons: through excessive dejection and through over-excitement."
His mind was sluggish and he was elated;
"What if I were to remove his sluggish continuity and his elation?
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Pay attention, Maudgalyāyana, to King Śuddhodana.
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied to the Blessed One, and having done so, he approached King Śuddhodana.
King Śuddhodana saw the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana from afar.
And having seen the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, he spoke this to him: "Come, venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana;
welcome to you, venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana."
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, please sit on this very seat that has been prepared.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana sat down on the prepared seat;

then, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana entered such a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that, with his mind thus composed, he vanished from his own seat and rose up into the air in the eastern direction.
He adopts the four modes of conduct; namely, he walks and stands.
He sits down,
prepares his bed,
and even enters the fire-element concentration.
As the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had entered the fire-element concentration, various rays of light issued forth from his body—
namely, blue, yellow, red, white, madder-colored, and crystal-colored—
and he even displayed the twin miracles.
The lower part of his body blazes forth;
from the upper part of his body, cool streams of water flow;
the upper part of his body blazes forth.
Cool streams of water flowed from his lower body;

just as in the eastern direction, so too in the southern, western, and northern directions— having thus displayed the fourfold miraculous power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) in the four directions, he withdrew those miraculous performances and sat down upon the very seat that had been prepared.
Then King Śuddhodana said this to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana, are there other disciples of the Blessed One who possess such great supernormal power and such great majesty?
"There are, Great King."
And he spoke this verse:
"The disciples of the Sage are many— of great majesty, possessing the three knowledges, skilled in discerning the minds of others, having exhausted their outflows, and being Arhats."
Then this thought occurred to King Śuddhodana:
"It is not only for me alone that my son possesses such great supernatural power and such great majesty; rather, there are other renunciants as well who possess such great supernatural power."
"Thus great is his power";
the elation he had felt vanished.
At that moment, the Blessed One generated a worldly thought:
"Oh, if only Śakra, Brahmā, and the other gods would come!
I would teach the Dharma in the pure assembly of gods.

Now, it is the very nature of things that whenever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, give rise to a worldly thought, at that time even such creatures as ants and termites perceive the mind of the Blessed One with their own minds.
How much less so the gods such as Śakra and Brahmā!
At the very moment when they give rise to a supramundane mind, even the great śrāvakas do not know the Blessed One’s mind with their own minds;
what need then to mention the gods such as Śakra and Brahmā?
How much less so for living beings such as ants and termites?
Then, this thought occurred to Śakra, the lord of the gods, as he was teaching the devas:
"What was the purpose for which the Blessed One produced a mundane thought?
It occurred to him:
"He wishes to teach the Dharma to the pure assembly of gods."
He gave an order to the divine son Viśvakarman:
"Viśvakarman, construct in the Nyagrodha Grove a gabled chamber made of the four jewels, and arrange a variegated seating."
"The Blessed One desires to teach the Dharma in the assembly of the Śuddhāvāsa gods. "Excellent indeed, Kauśika!
Having thus responded to Śakra, Lord of the Devas, the divine son Viśvakarman manifested a gabled hall made of the four precious gems in the Nyagrodha Grove.
And there was a variegated arrangement of seats;
there, the four great kings were stationed at the four gates, [namely] Dhṛtarāṣṭra, ...
Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa,
and Kubera; and Dhṛtarāṣṭra at the eastern gate.
Adorned with armlets, earrings, and various garlands and ornaments;
on the right, Virūḍhaka, adorned with divine ornaments;
and on the west, Virūpākṣa, adorned with various jewels.
To the north was Kubera, adorned with all ornaments;
then Śakra, the lord of the gods, having caused a great display of splendor to be made in the Nyagrodha Grove, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, surrounded by Śakra and many hundreds of thousands of deities, entered the gabled pavilion and sat upon a lion throne adorned with various jewels before a great assembly of gods.
Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, taking King Śuddhodana with him, approached the place where the Blessed One was;
having approached, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana entered.
King Śuddhodana was restrained by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the king of the gods:
"Wait, O Great King! Do not enter!"
What is the reason?
The Blessed One is teaching the Dharma in an assembly of pure gods;
there is no entry here for one who is merely human.
Then King Śuddhodana went to the southern gate;
having seen him, Virūḍhaka, the king of the gods, addressed him:
"Stop, stop, Great King! Do not enter!"
King Śuddhodana said:
"Who are you, gentle-faced one?
"I am Virūḍhaka, Great King."
The Blessed One was teaching the Dharma in the assembly of the Śuddhāvāsa gods;
"No human being may enter here.
Then King Śuddhodana went to the western gate.
Having seen him, Virūpākṣa, the king of the gods, said:
"Stop, stop, O Great King! Do not enter!"
King Śuddhodana said,
"Who are you, gentle-faced one?
Virūpākṣa replied.
"I am Virūpākṣa, O Great King;
the Blessed One is teaching the Dharma in the assembly of the Śuddhāvāsa gods,
where entry is not obtained by one who has become a human."
Then King Śuddhodana went to the northern gate;
having seen him, the Great King Vaiśravaṇa addressed him, saying, "Stop, stop, Great King! Do not enter!"
King Śuddhodana said,
"Who are you, noble sir?
Vaiśravaṇa replied:
"I am Vaiśravaṇa, O Great King;
the Blessed One is teaching the Dharma in the assembly of the Śuddhāvāsa gods;
no entry is possible here for one who has become a human being."
Then a longing arose in King Śuddhodana:
"Oh, would that I might see the Blessed One teaching the Dharma in a pure assembly of gods!
Thereupon, that sluggish disposition of King Śuddhodana's mind vanished.
The Blessed One reflected:
"If King Śuddhodana does not see me, it is possible that he will vomit hot blood and pass away. Then... (SBV I 198)
"A strategic arrangement must be made," [he thought].
Thereupon, the Blessed One transformed that gabled chamber composed of the four jewels into one made of crystal,
so that King Śuddhodana could see the Buddha’s body unobstructed.
Having seen him, he was filled with joy and gladness; having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Then, knowing the disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature of King Śuddhodana, the Buddha delivered a discourse on the Dharma such that it led to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.
Upon hearing it, King Śuddhodana shattered with the thunderbolt of wisdom the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up with its twenty peaks, and he realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the truth, he uttered this inspired exclamation three times:
"Venerable Sir, this was not done for us by our mother, nor by our father."
Neither by the king, nor by the deities,
nor by the ancestors.
Neither by ascetics nor by brahmins, nor by any other circle of kinsmen and relatives, has that which has been done for us by the Blessed One been done.
The oceans of blood and tears have been dried up;
the mountains of bones have been crossed;
the gates to the lower realms have been closed.
The gates to heaven and liberation have been opened wide; he has established [the Dharma] among gods and humans. And it is said:
"That which ought to be done by a good son who seeks to repay his father..."
By that act of yours, our minds have been directed toward liberation.
Having rescued us from the miserable realms, we have been established in heaven and liberation through your great effort; well done, you have performed a difficult task.
O Lord, like merchants driven by greed, we— who were longing for the enjoyments of worldly existence— have been brought [to this state] by Your affection through the desire for heaven.

Then King Śuddhodana, rising from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, accept my invitation for a meal at my home tomorrow."
The Blessed One consented to King Śuddhodana by remaining silent.
Then, King Śuddhodana, understanding the Blessed One’s consent through his silence, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet and departed from the Blessed One’s presence.
He approached Śuklodana and said this to him:
"Prince, the consecration for the kingdom has come upon you;
accept the kingdom. For whose sake?
Because the truths have been seen in the presence of the Blessed One."
"On which day? "On this very day;
on the same day that the Dharma was taught by the Blessed One in the Nyagrodha Grove, seventy-seven thousand Śākyas together with me perceived the Truths.
Having been told thus, Droṇodana was addressed: "Accept the kingdom."
He said: "When the Dharma was taught by the Blessed One in the Brahmāvarta garden, seventy-six thousand Śākyas together with him perceived the Truths.
Having been told thus, "Amṛtodana, please accept the kingdom," he replied:
"When the Blessed One was teaching the Dharma in the Rohītaka grove, I, together with seventy-five thousand Śākyas, perceived the truths.
If this is so, whom shall we now establish in the kingdom?
They said:
"Bhadrika, the Śākya king!
Thus, acting together, they consecrated Bhadrika, the Śākya king, in the sovereignty and lordship of the kingdom.
The Dedication of the Nyagrodhārāma.
Then King Śuddhodana, having prepared pure and exquisite hard and soft foods during that very night, rose early at dawn, arranged the seats, set out water-jars,
and announced the time to the Blessed One by messenger: "It is time, Venerable Sir."
"The meal is ready;
may the Blessed One now do as he deems timely.

Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, surrounded by a company of monks and preceded by the community of monks, approached the place where King Śuddhodana’s meal was being served.
Having approached, he sat down on the seat prepared right in front of the community of monks;
then King Śuddhodana, seeing that the community of monks headed by the Buddha was comfortably seated, personally satisfied and served them with pure and excellent food, both hard and soft.

In many ways, having personally satisfied and served the Blessed One with pure and exquisite foods both hard and soft, and knowing that the Blessed One had finished eating, had washed his hands, and had set aside his bowl, he took a golden pitcher and offered the Nyagrodha Grove to the Blessed One.
And with a voice endowed with the five qualities, the Blessed One bestowed a blessing:
"Whatever merit arises from this gift, may it go to the Śākyas;
may they attain the eternal state or their desired wishes. Thus he spoke.
There, the Blessed One was dwelling in Kapilavastu at the Nyagrodha Monastery; likewise, it is recorded in the sūtras by the Elders that the Blessed One was in Kapilavastu at the Nyagrodha Monastery.
The Blessed One, residing in Kapilavastu, ate at the royal palace one day and in the inner apartments another day;
thus the Śākyas followed the Buddha.
King Śuddhodana saw the matted-hair ascetics who had gone forth as monks;

because of their peaceful deportment, they were pleasing to the mind, yet not pleasing to the body, for their bodies were emaciated by the hardships of various specific ascetic vows. Having seen them, this thought occurred to him:
"Or rather, these matted-hair ascetics, because of their peaceful deportment, are pleasing to the mind but not pleasing to the body;
with what kind of retinue would the Blessed One be beautiful?
Thus he reflected.
"By the retinue of the Śākyas";
then, having assembled all the Śākyas, he said: "Sirs, had the prince Sarvārthasiddha not gone forth into the religious life,"
Who would have become [the king]?
A universal monarch (cakravartin);
and who would you all have become?
"Followers! Now Prince Sarvārthasiddha is the unsurpassed King of Dharma;
why do you not become his followers?"
"Your Majesty, shall we go forth into homelessness? "Go forth. "Shall we all do so?"
"By a single family;
let us do so.
King Śuddhodana then had a proclamation made by the ringing of bells throughout the city of Kapilavastu.
"The King issues this command: 'The Śākyas residing within my realm must renounce the world one family at a time.
Now, Aniruddha and Mahānāman were the two sons of Droṇodana—Aniruddha and Mahānāman."
Of those two, Mahānāman was exceedingly devoted to the performance of agricultural labors,
whereas Aniruddha, having gone to the upper terrace of the palace, sported, enjoyed himself, and amused himself with instrumental music performed by women alone.
Mahānāman was addressed by his mother:
"My son, the king has caused a proclamation by bell to be made that the Śākyas must renounce the world one family at a time; therefore, you should renounce the world.
He replied:
"I am not going forth; rather,
let him who is your beloved son, who remains sitting at ease, go forth— O son, you who possess great merit and majesty."
"He is a being; do not compete with him.
Mother, you have placed your faith in him, which is why he is one of great power through merit.
Mother, today do not send him anything at all."
"I shall find out whether or not I am one of great merit and power.
"Son, let it be so; I shall make it manifest."
Having filled a basket with those empty jars, covered it with a white cloth, and marked it with a seal, she sent it in the hand of a maidservant; she was instructed:
"If he should ask, 'What is here? [you must answer thus]."
"It is nothing that needs to be said";
taking him with her, she set out.
Śakra, the lord of the gods, exercises his vision of knowledge from below.
He reflected:
"Since Upāriṣṭa the Pratyekabuddha was indeed provided with almsfood by him, how could there be a lack of food for him today?"
"The preparation of food for him must be made";
thus, he filled that basket with food consisting of various soups, sauces, and side dishes.
Then, the girl took it and went into the presence of Aniruddha.
Then he said to the girl,
"What is here? She replied,
"Prince, there is nothing."
Aniruddha reflected:
"I am dear to my mother;
why would she send me empty-handed?"
"Surely no food at all has been placed here; let me see," he said, and opened it;
he found that the entire garden was filled with various implements and fragrant scents.
Having smelled it, Aniruddha was filled with supreme wonder;
being devoted to his mother,
he sent her the finest alms-food.
And she sent word: "Mother, you ought to send such food as this every day, nothing less.
Upon seeing it, she was filled with great wonder, and she showed it to Mahānāman.
"Son, did you see it?
"Mother, I saw it.
"Therefore, I told you before: that being is called 'of great merit' and is fortunate among men."
"Do not engage in rivalry with him.
He replied,
"Mother, let him be one of great power through merit or not."
"I am not going forth";
and because Mahānāma did not consent to the going forth under any circumstances,
Aniruddha was then addressed by her:
"My son, the king has caused a proclamation by bell to be made:
'The Śākyas must renounce the world one family at a time.
Why then do you renounce the world?"
"Or do you remain at home?
He replied,
"Mother, what is the benefit in the life of renunciation?"
What is the disadvantage?
What is the benefit in living as a householder? What is the disadvantage?

My son, when the life of renunciation is successfully accomplished, it leads to nirvana; when it fails, it leads to rebirth among gods and humans. Likewise, the household life, when properly maintained, leads to rebirth among gods and humans.
If not properly maintained, it leads to rebirth in the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts;
Mother, that which is a disadvantage in the life of renunciation is an advantage in the household life.
"Therefore, enough with living at home; give me your permission; I shall go forth."
She said:
"Son, excellent; do so. Bhadrika, the Śākya king, is a friend of Aniruddha."
He went into his presence;
at that time, Bhadrika, the Śākya king, was playing the lute, and as he was playing it, a string broke.
One tone passed into another;
Aniruddha was skilled on the lute,
and by him the sign was grasped according to the sound.
Standing at the gate, he addressed the doorkeeper:
"Go, my good man,
inform King Bhadrika that Aniruddha is standing at the gate, desiring to see the king."
The doorkeeper went and informed Bhadrika, the Śākya king:
"Your Majesty, Aniruddha is standing at the gate."
"I wish to see the deity.
He replied,
"May you, Aniruddha, enter."
"Who prevents you, venerable Aniruddha?
He entered;
the king embraced him and had him sit down.
And it was asked, "How long has it been since you arrived?
He replied,
"When the string of your lute snapped as you were tuning it."
"The tone has moved to another tone";
he was struck with great wonder and said,
"You are highly skilled on the lute."
Bhadrika, the Śākya king, said:
"Prince, what is the purpose of your coming?
Aniruddha replied:
"Your Majesty, King Śuddhodana has caused a proclamation by bell to be made:
'The Śākyas must renounce the world one family at a time.
Therefore, please look upon this."
"I shall go forth";
the king said,
"If that is so, I too shall go forth."
"Let us deliberate together;
you should take up residence right here today."
He arrived right here at his lodging;
the attendant in charge of the bedchamber had spread cloths with the scent of fever over the bed and scattered flowers about it.
Aniruddha was seated on his bed;
a stalk of jasmine was placed beneath him,
and he experienced its touch.
He said: "What is this stone figure standing here below?
They began to investigate;
[they found] a stalk of a *mallikā* flower.
Having seen this, they were struck with great wonder;
Aniruddha had slept uncomfortably during the night.
When the night had turned to dawn, the king asked:
"Has Aniruddha slept happily? He replied:
"Your Majesty, it is not a pleasant sleep," he said.
The king asked, "For what reason? Aniruddha replied:
"Your Majesty, garments fragrant with fever have been spread out; flowers have been scattered about;
and the body is being scratched by the flower-stalks."
The king summoned the bed-maker and said, "For what purpose have you prepared these garments that smell of fever? The bed-maker replied:
They were supplied by my treasurer;
the king summoned the treasurer and said:
"For what reason have you supplied garments that smell of fever?"
He said,
"Your Majesty, they were given to me by a weaver.
The king summoned the weaver and spoke to him.
"For what purpose were these garments smelling of fever given by you?
The weaver replied,
"Your Majesty, while the garments were being woven, a small portion remained unfinished."
When I was feverish, I spoke [of it], and the king said:
"Prince, how did you come to know this?"
He replied: "Because of the experience of a hot touch,
and because of the smell of fever."
The king was struck with great wonder and said, "Sirs, Aniruddha is truly a fortunate Śākya.
Thereupon, Bhadrika, the Śākya king, addressed him:
If I go forth into homelessness,
Devadatta will become the king of the Śākyas;
he will bring harm to the Śākyas.
"What if we all join together and incite Devadatta?
Thus, Devadatta was summoned by Bhadrika, the Śākya king, having been ensnared.

Devadatta reflected:

therefore, by means of a stratagem, I shall deceive them."
Indeed, on the very day the Blessed One displayed the miracle of supernatural power in the Nyagrodha Grove, this thought arose in me:
"Just as he has won over the great multitude of people by means of this converting illusion, so too must I win them over."
Having understood this, he said:
"Your Majesty, you are going forth into the religious life; for what purpose should I remain?"
Bhadrika, the Śākya king, reflected:
"This man is a liar;
having made him stand by his promise, I must inform the great multitude."
Then the king, having had those words committed to writing on a leaf, caused a proclamation by bell to be made in the city of Kapilavastu:
"Listen, O citizens residing in Kapilavastu!
Five hundred Śākyas, headed by Bhadrika, Revata, Aniruddha, and Devadatta, are about to go forth into the religious life."
"Upon hearing this, you should give rise to joy";
however, upon hearing it, Devadatta experienced great pain and mental distress,
thinking, "If I had known for certain that Bhadrika, the Śākya king, would definitely go forth into homelessness..."
"I would not have made this vow;
if I do not go forth now, I shall not obtain even the kingdom, for I will be considered a liar."
"In every respect, what is the appropriate course here?
I shall go forth into the religious life; once I have gone forth, I will rule the kingdom."

Then this thought occurred to King Śuddhodana:

He had that city cleared of stones, pebbles, and gravel;

it was sprinkled with sandalwood water, with banners and flags raised, draped with bundles of silk ribbons and garlands, hung with incense burners of fragrant smoke, and strewn with various flowers so that it was delightful.

The Śākya women and Śākya maidens, filled with curiosity, stood at the windows, air-holes, and balconies,
desiring to behold the splendor of the Śākyas; and the multitude of people arrived from various regions gathered in the streets, lanes, squares, and crossroads.
The Brahmins who were interpreters of omens and experts in analysis had been summoned for the examination of the Śākyas, to determine who among them was worthy and who was not.
Then the Śākyas, having taken leave of their parents and adorned themselves with necklaces, bracelets, armlets, and other ornaments, each mounted his own chariot and began to depart.
Previously, Bhadrika, the Śākya king, went out; he was seen by the fortune-tellers, who said:

thus Revata, Aniruddha, and the others departed,
and they too were prophesied by the soothsayers.
Then Devadatta went out;
as he was departing, his crest-jewel was snatched away by a hawk;
this was observed by the fortune-tellers.

as Kokālika, Khaṇḍadravya, Kaṭamorakatiṣya, and Samudradatta were departing, a donkey brayed.
They too had been prophesied by the fortune-tellers:
"These, having committed verbal misconduct against the great śrāvakas, will be destined for hell.

he too was prophesied:
"Because of extreme greed, he is destined to be reborn in the hells."
Then five hundred Śākyas, headed by Bhadrika, Aniruddha, and Devadatta, approached the Blessed One with great splendor, vying with one another to go on a pleasure-trip to the park.
The Blessed One reflected:
"If I were to ordain these Śākyas by the 'Come, monk' formula, some might become successful [in their practice]."
Some are non-attainers;
for those who are non-attainers, there will be a change [in their state].
And every monk here is in his final existence.
"What if I were to ordain and confer full admission upon all the monks by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations?
Having thought this, he addressed the monks:
"Monks, let the Śākyas of Kapilavastu go forth;
let them receive full ordination through a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations.
"So be it, Venerable Sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One.
Upāli, King Śuddhodana sent the barber named Upāli, a Śākya shaver, to shave the hair of those who were going forth;
while shaving the hair of Bhadrika, the Śākya king, his face was clouded with tears and his heart was choked with sobs as he wept again and again.
Absorbed in deep sighs, he let his hair fall;
Bhadrika, the Śākya king, said:
"Upāli, why do you weep?"
With words faltering, piteous, and drawn out by compassion, he said: "Your Majesty, having performed service for the foremost men of Jambudvīpa, I shall now have to perform service for common men."
"Let there be separation from life as you wish, but not the life of one abandoned by you";
thus spoke Bhadrika, the Śākya king.
Enough, Upāli! You have demonstrated your devotion and affection for your master;
restrain your grief.
I shall act in such a way that you will no longer perform attendance upon ordinary men.
Having understood this, he spread out a cloth in one place and addressed the Śākya youths: "Listen, young men! This Upāli, our barber, has performed his service for us."
"Therefore, place these ornaments, intended for his livelihood, upon the cloth;
we shall not dwell in the house again.
They then made a great heap on the cloth of various kinds of ornaments—necklaces, half-necklaces, bracelets, armlets, and earrings—all inlaid with diverse gems.
Upāli shaved their hair in due order;
they went to bathe,
and he reflected:
"These princes, endowed with noble lineage, wealth, and youth, have gone forth into homelessness, casting aside their vast harems and their abundant treasuries and granaries;
yet I am attached to this mere ornamentation and shall fall into ruin through such a lack of wisdom."
If I were not born into a low family,
I too would strive and exert myself toward going forth in the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya.
I would strive for the crossing over of the floods and for the transcending of the yokes.
For this is the nature of things: just as the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, survey the world with their Buddha-eye three times during the night and three times during the day,
so too do the great śrāvakas.
The venerable Śāriputra saw Upālī the barber, who was extremely distressed;
having seen him, he approached where Upālī the barber was, and having approached, he said this to Upālī the barber:

"Upāli, why are you so deeply distressed, sitting with your cheek resting on your hand, lost in thought? He replied, "How could I not be lost in thought, venerable Śāriputra, when now these young men— endowed with noble lineage, wealth, and youth— possess flourishing harems and flourishing treasuries and granaries?"
Having cast it aside, they went forth into homelessness.
Am I, being attached to this mere ornament, to fall into calamity through such misconduct?
If I were not born of a low family, I too, having gone forth into the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, would exert myself and strive.
"I shall strive for the crossing over of the floods and for the transcendence of the yokes. The Venerable Śāriputra said:
"O gentle-faced one, this teaching of the Lord of Sages does not have birth as its essence, nor lineage as its essence, nor learning as its essence."
Moreover, this teaching of the Lord of Sages has practice as its essence;
the Tathāgatas do not examine birth, family, or lineage,
but they do examine actions, even those performed long ago.
"If you desire the going forth, the full ordination, and the state of a monk within this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya,
come, let us go into the presence of the Blessed One;
the Blessed One will grant you the going forth."
He consented.
Then, Upāli was ordained.
Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra took the barber Upāli with him and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he said this to the Blessed One:

"Venerable Sir, this Upāli desires the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya; may the Blessed One therefore grant him the going forth."
"May he grant me full ordination out of compassion.
He was addressed by the Blessed One: "Come, monk; lead the holy life."
Immediately upon the conclusion of the Blessed One’s speech, he became shaven-headed,
clad in the outer robe (saṅghāṭī),
with his hands occupied by a bowl and a water-pot.

With his hair and beard shorn seven days ago, he stood with the deportment of a monk who had been ordained for a hundred years. And regarding this, it is said: "And having been addressed by the Tathāgata, 'Come!'"
With his head shaven and his body wrapped in the saṃghāṭī robe,
he stood there with his senses immediately calmed,
adorned by the very desire for Buddhahood.
The Śākyas who had gone forth performed the formal salutation according to seniority;
while Bhadrika, the Śākya king, was performing the salutation, he recognized the feet of Upāli,
whereupon he looked up at his face.
He said: "Lord, this is Upāli;
should I also prostrate at his feet?"
The Blessed One said:
"Child, renunciation is for the sake of abandoning conceit; this elder of yours has already destroyed intoxication and pride."
He prostrated himself;
he fell at his feet,
and the earth shook in six ways.
This great earth shakes, trembles,
and quakes violently; it is agitated.
It trembles, it trembles violently;
the eastern direction rises up,
while the western direction sinks down.
The west rises;
the east sinks; the south rises.
The north sinks down;
the north rises up; the south sinks down.
The middle rises up and the ends sink down; the ends rise up and the middle sinks down.
The middle one bowed down; thus they fell down one after another in succession;
Devadatta did not fall.
The Blessed One said: "Child, one goes forth into homelessness for the sake of abandoning conceit; therefore, humble yourself. He replied:
"What do you have [to offer]?
"I will not prostrate at his feet.
Because he did not prostrate, Devadatta was the first there to reject the Blessed One’s command.
The monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, behold! When Bhadrika, the Śākya king, performed his salutation to Upāli, an earthquake occurred in six ways.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now; this was the natural law even in the past: that he who fell at his feet [was saved]."
And an earthquake occurred with sixfold quaking;
listen to that, O student Sundara.
And Bhadrā, the courtesan.
Formerly, monks, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king named Brahmadatta reigned; his kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people and inhabitants.
At that time, there lived in the city of Vārāṇasī a courtesan named Bhadrā; and there was a young brahmin named Sundara who approached her and said:
"Come, my lady, let us enjoy ourselves.
She replied,
"Do you have those five hundred kārṣāpaṇas?"
He said,
"There are none; go, take five hundred kārṣāpaṇas and return."
He had no wealth;
he was excessively attached to that [tree],
and from time to time [he gathered] various and wonderful flowers.
She also presented fruits to her;
she conceived an affection for her.
Then, at another time, a festival occurred in Vārāṇasī.
All the women, adorned with garments, garlands, and ornaments, remained in their respective places, full of play, delight, and joy;
seeing them, the young man Sundara became agitated.
Bhadrā, the courtesan, reflected:
"Today the people of Vārāṇasī, adorned with garments and ornaments, will enjoy themselves together with their respective wives;
the young man Sundara will enjoy himself with me.
And she thought thus:
And the young brahmin Sundara arrived at that place;
seeing him, she, her mind filled with joy born from his previous kindness, said:
"Young brahmin, go!"
"Come, taking fragrant flowers;
you shall enjoy yourself with me.
Like one who has regained his life after it was lost, his heart overcome with wonder, he departed.
Imagining her beauty, youth, and cleverness, he remained awake the entire night, overcome by passion;
when the night had turned to dawn, his eyes were so excessively agitated by sleep that he slept until sunrise;
and he only woke up when all the flowers had been gathered by people for every kind of use.
He wandered here and there for the sake of flowers,
but he did not find them.
Having taken śirīṣa flowers, he approached her;
she spoke this verse:
"The lazy one who wears a deerskin is devoid of industriousness."
This young man Sundaraka, who possesses not even a single worthless masha,
now gives a shirisha flower at this time when the trees are in full bloom.
Having understood this, he said:
"Go, and return having taken other flowers.

For indeed, as one indulges in sensual pleasures, the fetters increase. Thus, with his passion for sensual desires intensified, during the last month of summer, on a cloudless day when the clouds had vanished—
When it was the time of midday,
he was gathering flowers while singing *vaktra* and *aparavaktra* verses in forests located at a great distance from the city;
and King Brahmadatta had gone out for the purpose of hunting deer.
Scorched by the heat of the sharp rays of the sun, he reached a cool spot in the shade;
hearing the sound of singing, he spoke this verse:
"The sun burns from above, and the sand burns from below."
"Why do you sing? The sun's heat does not burn your limbs? Thus addressed, Sundaraka spoke this verse:
"The sun does not torment me; it is my own volitions that torment me."
"In this world, it is actions done and left undone that cause suffering, not the heat of the sun";
the king reflected:
"Surely this young man is skilled in accounts of coolness, since he gathers flowers while it is midday."
He was addressed by him:
"Young man, tell a cool story first; I shall listen."
He reflected:
"Surely this king is burning with grief for his body, which is why he speaks thus."
He gave him a wonderful discourse on coolness,
hearing which the king’s bodily burning subsided;
the king was filled with faith.
He asks his ministers:
"Sirs, what is the recompense for one who grants life to an anointed Kṣatriya king?"
"Your Majesty, half the kingdom.
Then he was addressed by the king:
"Young man, take up residence in the royal palace this very day."
"I shall grant you half of the kingdom.
An elegant bed and seat were provided for him in the royal palace;
while lying upon it, he fell asleep and, recollecting Bhadrā, began to reflect.
"I shall take that half-kingdom where Bhadrā, the courtesan, resides.
He further reflected:
"What kind of king is he, under whom she enjoys half the kingdom?"
"What if I were to deprive him of life? he thought;
then he reflected again:
"Enough with this kingdom, which involves the slaughter of a king!"
And he says:
"Thirst for objects does not cease even when an object is attained; rather, there is distress regarding what has not yet been attained.
Therefore, the mind set upon objects leads to misfortune. (SBV I 209)
When the night had turned to dawn, he became filled with remorse; rising from his bed, he spread out a black antelope skin and lay down upon the ground.
When the night had brightened, the king said:
"Gentlemen, summon that young brahmin;
we shall bestow half the kingdom upon him.
The royal messengers went and saw him.
Having descended from his great couch, he lay upon the ground;
and seeing this, they reported it with displeasure and went into the presence of the king, saying:
"Your Majesty, he does not deserve the kingdom."
The king asked, "For what reason?

They replied, "Your Majesty, how can one who has abandoned an exquisite bed and seat to lie upon the bare ground on a black antelope skin— who is thus of inferior inclinations— possibly desire sovereignty?"
The king said: "Sirs, he is wise;
there must be a reason for this."
"Call him," they were told; he was summoned by them and questioned by the king.
"O young brahmin, for what reason have you lain down upon a black antelope skin instead of a great bed?
He related to the king exactly what had occurred, and then the king said:
"Your Majesty, please grant me permission; I wish to go forth. The king said, "I grant you permission on one condition."
"If you, having gone forth, should attain any collection of virtues, you must inform me"; he promised, "So be it.
Then, having gone to a secluded place, he attained the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha without a teacher and without a preceptor.

"I made a promise to that king;
I shall go and fulfill that former promise."
Having gone into the presence of the king, he rose high into the air and began to perform the miraculous feats of blazing, heating, raining, and flashing lightning;
the king fell at his feet and spoke this verse:
"Behold the ripening of even a small deed performed in a former age!"
Indeed, a great distinction has been attained by Upaga!
Truly well-obtained are the gains by this young man,
who has gone forth as a seeker of what is wholesome.
Gaṅgāpāla, the barber: King Brahmadatta had a barber named Gaṅgāpāla;
by him, that Sundaraprokta was made to learn a verse, and he was told:
"Gangapala, you shall remind me of this verse again and again.

whenever he performed the shaving of King Brahmadatta, the king would fall into a state of drowsiness.

and having been awakened,
he invited Gaṅgāpāla to choose a boon.
"Tell me, what boon shall I grant you?
He replied,
"Your Majesty, I shall inform you."
When Gaṅgāpāla reminded the king of the verse, the king’s mind did not incline even toward talk of sensual pleasures, much less toward the actual practice of them;
he then looked about his inner apartments.
The women of the inner apartments, overcome by the intoxication of their afflictions, said to Gaṅgāpāla:
"Uncle, when the King offers you a choice of boons, then you should say this:"

"If the King is well-disposed toward me, then may he explain the meaning of this verse in detail. The King then analyzed the meaning of that verse for him in detail. Deeply moved, he prostrated at his feet and said:
"Your Majesty, I have been attended upon; I shall go forth from the home to the homeless state.
The king said:

he replied, "Your Majesty, let it be so; I shall inform you."
Having gone there, he went forth among the ṛṣis;
by him the five super-knowledges were realized;
this thought occurred to him:
"I made a promise to King Brahmadatta: 'I am going; I shall fulfill that former promise.
He then approached where King Brahmadatta was."
Having approached and ascended high into the air, he began to perform miracles of blazing, heating, raining, and flashing lightning;
for the supernatural power of an ordinary person can be captivating.
He prostrated at his feet and said:
"Noble one, have you attained such a multitude of virtues? "I have. King Brahmadatta prostrated at the feet of the seer Gaṅgāpāla.
An earthquake occurred with sixfold manifestations,
and his mother spoke this verse:
"This is the Devāmravana grove belonging to the wise Brahmadatta."
"For having distributed [his wealth], he went forth as a renunciant with a razor-case.
King Brahmadatta, consoling his mother, spoke this verse:
"Do not speak thus of Aṅgapāla."
Training in some of the stages of silence,
he is indeed the performer of that which is difficult to do,
by accomplishing which those of broad intelligence become so.
For by austerity one overcomes all evil,
and by austerity one also overcomes the entire world;
indeed, by austerity one overcomes the vessel of karma.

"He shines by means of asceticism; he is not to be spoken to about anything. (SBV I 211) "What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the king named Brahmadatta, was none other than this Bhadrika, the Śākya king.
He who was the seer named Gaṅgapāla was none other than this Upāli."
Even then, when Bhadrika the Śākya king, having become Brahmadatta, performed a prostration before Upāli who had become the seer Gaṅgapāla, an earthquake of sixfold movement occurred;

a) The Buddha Subdues a Nāga (CPS 24a.1): Then, having departed from the village of Senāyanī, this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "Is there here in the Magadha country some ascetic or brahmin of good conduct who is highly esteemed, whom I might convert; and upon his conversion, a great multitude of people would [be converted] with little difficulty?"
At that time, the matted-hair ascetic Uruvilvākāśyapa was aged, decrepit, and advanced in years;
he was two hundred years old by birth. Among the people of Magadha, he was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped as one recognized as an Arhat.
With a retinue of five hundred followers, he was practicing austerities at a hermitage on the bank of the river Nairañjanā.
Then this occurred to the Blessed One:
“This matted-hair ascetic Urubilvākāśyapa is old and aged, as previously described, up until ‘he is at peace.
Suppose I were to convert the matted-hair ascetic Urubilvākāśyapa; when he has been converted, a great multitude of people will be converted with little difficulty.”
Then the Blessed One went to the hermitage of the matted-hair ascetic Uruvilvākāśyapa.
The matted-hair ascetic Uruvilvākāśyapa saw the Blessed One from afar;
having seen him, he prepared a seat for the Blessed One and said this to the Blessed One:
"Come, Great Śramaṇa! Welcome, Great Śramaṇa!
It has been a very long time since the Great Śramaṇa last made an occasion to come here. Let the Great Śramaṇa sit upon the seat that has been prepared."
The Blessed One sat down on the very seat that had been prepared.
Then Urubilvākāśyapa, having exchanged various greetings and pleasantries with the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
As he was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to the matted-hair ascetic Urubilvākāśyapa:
"If it does not trouble you, Kāśyapa, I would stay one night in your fire-hut.
"It does not trouble me, Great Śramaṇa; however, a venomous serpent-nāga dwells there."
"He will not harm you;
come now, Kāśyapa, give your permission, for he will not harm me.
If, Great Śramaṇa, he does not harm you, then stay there, Great Śramaṇa, exactly as you please."
Then the Blessed One, having washed his feet outside the fire-hall, entered the fire-hall and sat down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
The serpent Āśīviṣa saw the Blessed One from afar;
having seen him, he emitted smoke through the power of his wrath.
The Blessed One also caused smoke to issue forth through the power of his supernatural might;

(CPS 26.1) The Sermon at Gayāśīrṣa:

Then the Blessed One, having caused that thousand of matted-hair ascetics to go forth and having given them full ordination, dwelt in Uruvilvā as long as he pleased and then set out on a journey toward Gayā.
Traveling by stages, he arrived at Gayā;
he stayed at the Gayāśīrṣa shrine together with a thousand monks, all of whom were formerly matted-hair ascetics.
There, the Blessed One instructed those thousand monks through the three miraculous displays.
By the miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*), the miracle of mind-reading (*ādeśanāprātihārya*), and the miracle of instruction (*anuśāsanīprātihārya*).
In this regard, this was the Blessed One’s miracle of supernatural power:
then the Blessed One entered such a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that, with his mind thus composed, he vanished from his own seat.
Having ascended into the sky above in the eastern direction, he assumes the four modes of conduct: he walks, stands, sits, and lies down;
he also enters the fire-element meditative attainment.
From the body of the Buddha, the Blessed One, who has entered the fire-element concentration, various rays of light issue forth— blue, yellow, red, white, madder-colored, and crystal-colored—
and he displays twin miracles:
his lower body blazes with fire.
From the upper part of his body, cool streams of water flow forth;
the upper part of his body blazes with fire;
from the lower part of his body, cool streams of water flow forth.
In the same way, he did so in the southern, western,

and northern directions; then, having displayed these four kinds of various miracles of supernatural power in the four directions, he withdrew those supernormal feats and sat down on the seat prepared in front of the community of monks.
This is the Blessed One’s miracle of supernatural power there;
this is the Blessed One’s miracle of mind-reading there: "O monks, such is your thought."
"This is the mind; this is consciousness;
one should apply discursive thought to this; one should not apply discursive thought to that."
Attend to this;
do not attend to that;
abandon this.
"Do not abandon this;
having realized it with your own bodies and attained it, abide in it.
This was the miracle of mind-reading performed by the Blessed One there.
In this regard, this is the miracle of the Blessed One’s instruction:
"Monks, everything is ablaze. And what is everything that is ablaze?"
The eye is ablaze, as are forms, eye-consciousness, and eye-contact;
whatever internal feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by eye-contact, that too is ablaze.
Likewise, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are ablaze.

The mental consciousness is ablaze, as is the contact of the mind; and whatever feeling— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— arises internally conditioned by that mental contact, that too is ablaze.
By what is it set ablaze?
By the fire of passion, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion;
it is set ablaze by birth, aging, sickness, death, lamentation, suffering, mental distress, and despair.
"It is ablaze with suffering"—
this was the miracle of instruction performed by the Blessed One on that occasion.
While this Dharma discourse was being spoken, the minds of those one thousand monks were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging.

Thus shall be the seventh [dream];
and he shall have a full thousand sons— heroes, warriors, handsome in form, crushers of enemy armies— who,

"If he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on saffron robes, and goes forth from the home to the homeless life with perfect faith, he will become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, whose fame will resound throughout the world.
